Man United transfer news: Red Devils 'set sights' on Brentford defender for Mauricio Pochettino signing

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 15 Nov 2026 14:13.
  • Manchester United are allegedly considering whether to make an approach for Brentford defender Nathan Collins during the winter transfer window.
  • With Mauricio Pochettino having been confirmed as the successor to Michael Carrick, the Red Devils hierarchy can start to work with the Argentine regarding new additions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 15 Nov 2026 14:13.

Manchester United are allegedly considering whether to make an approach for Brentford defender Nathan Collins during the winter transfer window.

With Mauricio Pochettino having been confirmed as the successor to Michael Carrick, the Red Devils hierarchy can start to work with the Argentine regarding new additions.

Reports have suggested that a upcoming forward could be a priority for Pochettino, a consequence of Benjamin Sesko expected to be sidelined for a number of months.

However, the majority of United's supporters will argue that defenders should be the focus in the next market.

According to Football Insider, Collins could be the subject of interest from United in January.

The report suggests that the Republic of Ireland international would be a target for club chiefs, rather than Pochettino.

Nevertheless, it is plausible that Pochettino could give the green light to a move for the 25-year-old.

While Collins has missed a significant period of 2026-27 through injury, he is fit again after a six-week absence.

Collins is in his fourth campaign at the Gtech Community Stadium, contributing eight goals from 124 appearances.

United are said to value Collins's leadership skills and presence in Keith Andrews's defence.

Despite the perception that Collins may be keen on a move to Old Trafford, Brentford are highly unlikely to consider any offers during the winter transfer window.

Not only does Collins have a contract until 2029, Brentford are attempting to qualify for Europe.

Brentford's transfer business is meticulously planned, and their strategy will not involve cashing in on a key player at the midway point of the campaign.

Breaking: Rangers star saved by Man Utd man as team secure quarter-final place with stunning comeback

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Despite starting Belgium’s 2-1 win away over Turkiye on Thursday night, the Rangers star had to be content with a place on the bench against Italy as Mark van Bommel’s side looked to seal a place in the quarter-finals of the Nations League at the Stade Roi Baudouin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin breathed a sigh of relief after seeing the penalty he conceded just minutes after his introduction to the pitch saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens during Belgium’s thumping 4-1 win over Italy in the Nations League on Sunday night.

Despite starting Belgium’s 2-1 win away over Turkiye on Thursday night, the Rangers star had to be content with a place on the bench against Italy as Mark van Bommel’s side looked to seal a place in the quarter-finals of the Nations League at the Stade Roi Baudouin.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Two points ahead of their visitors ahead of the Group A1 clash on nine points, the game got off to a disastrous start for the hosts when Italy went into an 11th-minute lead when Brentford defender Michael Kayode's cross to Pio Esposito to score 10th international goal in 15 appearances.

However, the lead was short-lived, and Belgium found themselves back on level terms just four minutes later when Brighton wing-back Maxim de Cuyper slammed home to restore parity in Brussels, before centre-back Nathan Ngoy rifled home from close range after a scramble in the box on 22 minutes.

It has been revealed that jeremy Doku then completed the turnaround when he added a third for Belgium just four minutes later, dancing through the Italian defence with stunning footwork before firing a low drive beyond his Manchester City teammate Gianluigi Donnarumma in the visitor’s goal. The strike put his side temporarily top of Group A1, with Turkiye holding France to a 0-0 draw at half-time.

It has been revealed that with 10 minutes to spare, Diego Moreira made sure of the win when he neatly placed home his side’s fourth of the game after being teed up by Kevin De Bruyne. However, it was not enough to seal top spot in the group, with Belgium forced to be content with qualification to the Nations League quarter-finals via second place as France ran out 2-1 winners in Paris.

Despite the Group standings being all but confirmed, the action did not cease, with Italy awarded a last-minute penalty after VAR ruled that Raskin had handled Alphadjo Cisse’s shot in the area. The Rangers man had replaced Romeo Lavia just over 10 minutes earlier, but needn’t have worried, as goalkeeper Lammens pulled off an excellent save to deny Esposito a brace.

Sources indicate that “If Donnarumma had not been in goal, then we would've scored six,” noted new Belgium head coach van Bommel. “I'll be honest, I didn't expect this when we started two months ago, but even before that first match with Italy, I could tell this was a really intelligent group of players. That makes it a pleasure for a coach to work with them.

“These players can anticipate an opponent, are flexible, and can adapt to different situations. Today you saw that reflected. Not only was the idea right, individually many players stepped up too. And ultimately we managed to dominate an opponent like Italy for long periods. That is the most notable thing to me.".

Belgium will discover their Nations League quarter-final opponents on Friday, November 20, 2026, with the draw set to take place at 11am UK time in Nyon, Switzerland.

Napoli 3-3 AC Milan Women: Lead lost twice as Rossonere claim just one point

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (408 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sempremilan

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AC Milan Women were held to a 3-3 draw in their away game against Napoli on Saturday afternoon, despite having the lead twice.
  • Recent findings suggest that it has been a rough start to the season for Suzanne Bakker and her side, clinching a mere seven points in the first seven games.
  • In the derby against Inter last week, the Rossonere only had themselves to blame for the 0-3 defeat after missing several good chances, while conceding two penalties and getting a red card.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AC Milan Women were held to a 3-3 draw in their away game against Napoli on Saturday afternoon, despite having the lead twice.

Recent findings suggest that it has been a rough start to the season for Suzanne Bakker and her side, clinching a mere seven points in the first seven games. Even worse, the form seems to be declining as with today’s game included, they haven’t won in the last three games (1D, 2L).

In the derby against Inter last week, the Rossonere only had themselves to blame for the 0-3 defeat after missing several good chances, while conceding two penalties and getting a red card. They didn’t exactly make things better today either.

After just five minutes of play, the former Milan player Chante Dompig opened the scoring for the hosts. In fairness to the Rossonere, it was a cracking finish from outside the box to stun Sally Rainey in goal, so not much could be done.

Industry observers note that milan responded in the best way possible as Sara Kanutte Fornes pounced on a huge mistake by the Napoli defence, tapping in the equaliser after 16 minutes of play. Just ten minutes later, Abi Brighton found the striker on a corner, heading it home nicely for an early brace.

In a recent development, the Rossonere played well after that and headed into the break with a 2-1 lead. It wasn’t a poor start to the second half, but in the 58th minute, a really poor offside trap (of sorts) meant Napoli only had to play one pass to play Kinga Kozak through, and she made no mistakes.

Sources indicate that sloppy defending that Milan thought they had cancelled out in the 78th minute after a lovely move. Thea Kyvåg found Christy Grimshaw in the box with a great cross and the veteran headed it to Emma Koivisto, who in turn headed it into the back of the net.

The lead only lasted about six minutes, though, as Napoli suddenly had loads of space on the right flank and played a smart low cross into the box. Considering the lack of coverage on the flank, the Milan players at least should have kept tabs on things in the box, but they didn’t.

In a recent development, and so, Michela Giordano made it 3-3 and that was also the final result in the end. Two points dropped for Milan against another struggling side.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester United made enquiries to secure Hurzeler as they sought a replacement for the sacked Michael Carrick.
  • Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brighton rebuffed "high-level' contact from Manchester United for their head coach Fabian Hurzeler.

Manchester United made enquiries to secure Hurzeler as they sought a replacement for the sacked Michael Carrick.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The Red Devils also considered Aston Villa manager Unai Emery before settling on Argentine boss Mauricio Pochettino, who last week joined Manchester United on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Hurzeler, 33, has impressed at Brighton since arriving from German club St Pauli in 2024. He has led the Seagulls to two eighth place finishes and qualification to this year’s Uefa Conference League.

Brighton have also had a fine to start to this campaign and are currently second in the Premier League, five points adrift of leaders Arsenal.

Hurzeler is contracted to the south coast club until June 2029 and is believed to have a release clause of between £15m to £20m.

The Athletic reported that there was “high-level contact” from Manchester United to Brighton and to asked about the possibility of taking the Albion boss.

Brighton chairman owner Tony Bloom reportedly told the Red Devils that the price of prising their impressive boss away was around “£15million ($20m).”.

The Athletic added that Hurzeler “wants to complete this season with Brighton” and that Emery and Cesc Fabregas were also on the radar.

Brighton have the potential to achieve something special this season and it’s little wonder Hurzeler wants to see the season out.

Recent findings suggest that “I am really focused on my job here,” Hurzeler mentioned last month. “I have no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days.

“Beside that, I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick, for what he has done with Manchester United at the end of last season.

“He is a great human being, he is a great personality.

“Every time we meet each other, we have a really good relationship, so therefore I really respect him and there is nothing more to say about that.”.

Brighton resume action after the international break on November 22 at Hull City and then turn attention to the Conference League as they welcome Romanian outfit Craiova.

“I am really privileged to be in this situation here, and I always mention that I am part of a journey,” he stated.

“I always emphasise as well that I still have this feeling when I go to bed that we are not finished with our journey, and I am not 100 per cent satisfied and happy with where we are.

“There is still improvements we can do, still a lot of potential to get out of the players, and therefore I really want to work on that together with my players, together with my staff.

“I have great experts around me. I have a great group of players who support me, who give everything for this club and we built this over the last years.

“We had tough periods, we have good periods, but I think to build these kind of relationships, you need time, you need connections and you don’t take these things for granted.”.

Already relegated to League B before the game, the visitors entered the clash without a win in eight, and had lost all five of their Nations League games, conceding 12 goals and scoring just twice.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Naderi, who opted to represent Czechia last month despite also being eligible to represent Germany and Bulgaria, made his international debut as a second-half substitute in a 3-1 defeat to world champions Spain in October before making his full debut against England at Wembley a few days later.

In a recent development, he had to be content with a place on the bench, though, as Czechia went in search of their first Nations League points against Croatia on Sunday. However, they started the game in the worst possible fashion, with veteran winger Ivan Perisic putting the home side ahead after just 87 seconds via a clinical left-footed strike from the edge of the penalty area.

Industry observers note that searching for a quickfire second, Croatia piled on the pressure following their early opener, but Czechia stood firm until half-time. Looking to restore parity, Czechia began to get back into the game after the restart, with Antonin Kinsky, Idris Hopi and Adam Hlozek all attempting to get past Barcelona stopper Dominik Livakovic in the home side’s net. With the game entering the final stages, Rangers forward Naderi was introduced in the 74th minute as a substitute for Christophe Kabongo, and he helped Czechia level the score shortly afterwards.

Industry observers note that scoring nine goals and assisting five more for Rangers this season, he was on the field just 10 minutes before he found strike partner Adam Hlozek in a dangerous scoring position. His initial effort was blocked, but Hlozek reacted quickest to rifle home a left-footed finish to level the level. However, just as it appeared that Naderi’s had helped his side steal a late point, Croatia restored their lead three minutes later through substitute Lovro Majer.

Taking a pass from Brighton centre-back Luka Vuskovic in the away side’s area, he drilled a low drive into the net to condemn Czechia to a seventh consecutive defeat and the worst losing streak in their history.

Beginning in the group stages of this summer’s World Cup in North America, Czechia’s slide began with a 3-0 defeat to Mexico and has carried straight through into a brutal Nations League campaign against Spain, England, and Croatia.

Recent findings suggest that won by Portugal last year, they claimed a second title with a penalty shootout win over Spain after playing out a thrilling 2-2 draw with Spain in Munich, Germany. Winners of the inaugural tournament in 2019, they are now the most successful team in Nations League history, ahead of Spain and France, who have one win each.

Sources indicate that want to know when the draw for the Nations League quarter-final takes place, who has qualified and when the games will take place? Here’s everything you need to know:.

Get our daily football newsletter by clicking here.

It has been revealed that the draw for the Nations League quarter-finals will take place on Friday, 20 November. The draw begins at 11am UK time and will take place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

As of November 15, the following teams have confirmed a place in the Nations League quarter-finals: France, Belgium, England, Portugal and Spain.

Recent findings suggest that in total, eight teams qualify for the quarter-finals via League A. The four League A group winners are seeded and placed in Pot 1 of the draw, with the four League A group runners-up are placed in Pot 2 and unseeded. Each group winner is drawn against a runner-up from a different group. Teams from the same group cannot play each other in the quarter-finals.

Teams placed in Leagues B, C and D all compete for promotion and relegation, and are unable to qualify for the knockout stage of the competition.

It has been revealed that the upcoming quarter-final ties will be played over two legs during the March 2027 international break. The seeded group winners will play the first leg away from home, with the second leg on home soil. First legs are scheduled to take place from 25–27 March 2027, and second legs follow from 28–30 March 2027.

Sources indicate that the draw will not be broadcast in the UK and Ireland. However, they are several options to stream the draw live, which are detailed below.

If you want to stream the draw via your smart TV, laptop, tablet or mobile phone, the entire ceremony will be streamed for free via UEFA.tv and via the official UEFA YouTube channel.

Hamilton Academical 1 Ross County 2.

The depth of the descent of Hamilton Accies and Ross County would make it understandable if tickets for a fixture between the two carried warning about the bends when leaving New Douglas Park.

Industry observers note that the decompression sickness caused by emerging from a League One fixture for two sides who should be much higher must be severe. There may, however, be a positive prognosis.

Accies, despite their defeat, are whispering about stability, even though ‘legacy debt’ has to be faced, perhaps contested.

Sources indicate that county, meanwhile, will not say it even in a whisper but Saturday’s victory takes them eight points clear at the top and heavily fancied for the title. The Staggies have one set of hooves in the Championship.

Sources indicate that scottish football, of course, does not restrict itself to the cliched fare of top of the table clashes so New Douglas Park hosted a striker who is 39 later this month, a winger who was once a Scottish international, and a gentleman in the stands who once played against George Best. And a Ross County fan who regularly travels up from North Wales.

These exotic avenues demand to be explored but perennial questions about the financial health of the Accies had to be asked, too, after reports this week stating that hospitality packages at the club were being suspended.

An Accies fan feels the pain of defeat during Saturday's home loss to Ross County.

Allan Currie, chairman, answered them over a half-time pie.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We have come on in leaps and bounds but every week seems to throw up different challenges,’ he mentioned. ‘We have a level of debt that we have inherited and we are working with the creditors to try to navigate our way through that.’.

Matters on the field are positive, despite Saturday’s defeat.

‘The guys on the pitch, manager, and his staff have been unbelievable. Surviving in this league last season was phenomenal given what they were going through but it couldn’t be better now,’ he said. ‘Off the pitch, we are fighting with the different challenges we have. We are in a much better place even if we are not out the woods yet.’.

Asked what the level of pressure on him, he mentioned: ‘I am the guy on the ground but Rob Edwards is carrying out negotiations.’.

Edwards, through his Morley Group, took over the club earlier this year but has been sideswiped by a number of claims for payment. However, Currie has faith in the owner.

Sources indicate that ‘Without him, the club would not survive. Rob should take all the credit,’ he said.

Asked what the short-term aims for the club were, Currie replied with a smile: ‘A goal in the second half would be good.’ A goal was scored but not for the Accies.

But the club remain in second place and the play-offs seem a more than reasonable prospect.

Ross County goalscorer Kieran Phillips battles with Hamilton's Kai Smutek.

Recent findings suggest that with 10 minutes to go, Hamilton brought on their latest signing. Barrie McKay, who has played for Scotland and scored for Rangers in a Scottish Cup semi-final against Celtic. His considerable achievements, though, paled in comparison to the subject of a casual conversation in the bar before the match.

‘I played against George Best,’ said Alan McDougall, with an air so off-hand one could have believed he was merely ordering another pint.

‘Yes, I played 200 games for the Accies. Davie McParland brought me here as a 21-year-old and I played for about six years. I went to Stranraer for a year and then went down south. I played against Best with the Accies.’.

Sources indicate that the Northern Irish genius played for Hibernian in 1979-80. ‘He was well past his best and that was sad,’ said McDougall. Best’s addiction to alcohol had taken a severe toll.

‘I came back to watch games five or six years ago,’ said McDougall. ‘When the club went to Clyde, it destroyed me. What is fantastic is that the people that are now in control seem to be turning it around.’.

Sources indicate that there was a mood of cautious optimism from other fans. ‘I have been a fan since forever, well the 1980s at least,’ noted Gavin Fullarton. ‘I have seen this team in every division. I have seen them in the downs and downs. But I think we are going in the right direction. So far.’.

According to recent reports, he added: ‘The upcoming guys seem to know what they are doing. They are communicative.’.

There were 1,216 fans in the ground on Saturday with 300 stalwarts travelling down from the north. Colin Richardson, an Accies supporter, was asked why so many had stuck by the club.

Sources indicate that ‘It’s about loyalty,’ he noted. ‘You can’t pick and choose when you support your team. At the moment it is all about small steps. It has to be about stability.’.

A Ross County fan had travelled up from North Wales. The journey to Scotland is a familiar one for Ian Ellson. ‘I have been all over Scotland to watch Ross County,’ he said. ‘Twenty years ago I visited Ross County and I was spoiled rotten. I decided to follow them.’.

A social worker, he averages one visit a month. ‘I live and breathe Ross County,’ he said. ‘This season we are going up.’.

Welsh Staggies fan Ian Elson and Englishman Ray Griffiths travelled far for Saturday's game.

In a recent development, brian Graham would not be so bullish. He is 39 this month and has learned enough about football to know that predictions are made only to make the speaker seem foolish down the line.

Industry observers note that he was, though, expansive about what is happening at County. He joined the club for the second time in the summer after Stuart Kettlewell, the manager, convinced him of the ambitions in Dingwall.

It has been revealed that ‘This is a club where I have had success before so I know how good a club it can be,’ he stated. ‘It’s not been great for a couple of seasons but in the summer the manager set out his stall very early. It was about leaving egos at the door, building a togetherness and having a change of culture at the club. I think you are seeing that now.’.

The early signs were good for the striker who dropped down from Falkirk in the Premiership to play in Dingwall.

‘We had good pre-season performances against Aberdeen and Dundee and that was a solid building block,’ he said.

Brian Graham celebrates after scoring his 21st goal of the season for County.

Graham converted a first-half penalty to reach a tally of 21 goals this season and the Christmas trees are not up yet. ‘I get a lot of plaudits for scoring goals but others in the team are scoring a lot too,’ he mentioned. ‘We are scoring team goals.’.

Has he set a target for the season? ‘When I came back I knew I had to score 13 to reach 50 goals for the club in two spells,’ he noted. ‘I always set down targets in a wee black book but now I might need to readjust that.’.

It was a night of adjustment for Darian MacKinnon. He had set a victory target but was condemned to accept defeat. He would not concede the league race was over. ‘We have to play them twice,’ he said.

In a recent development, he added ‘We are going in the right direction. The owners have put money in and they have backed us.’.

Asked to pinpoint a factor that has contributed to the team sitting second, he mentioned: ‘The most positive thing for me this season is that this is now a good place to come into your work after the last three or four seasons. We are all actually enjoying coming to our work.’.

According to recent reports, there is work to be done on and off the pitch but the Accies are surviving. And that is the biggest result.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scotland end their Nations League campaign with a clash against Switzerland on Monday, with their slim hopes of qualifying for the promotion playoffs still intact.

Placed in Group B1 alongside Slovenia, North Macedonia and the aforementioned Switzerland, fresh head coach Sebastien Pocognoli kept alive Scotland’s chances of claiming second spot in the group with a narrow 2-1 home win over North Macedonia on Friday, thanks to two goals from John McGinn.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Here’s what Scotland needs to happen to nab a promotion/relegation playoff spot, how to watch the draw and what a third-placed finish would mean for Pocognoli’s men.

First and foremost, Scotland MUST beat Switzerland to stand any chance of finishing in second place in the group. Should they achieve that, they will also have to hope Slovenia fail to beat North Macedonia. If Slovenia beat North Macedonia this evening, it is impossible for Scotland to finish in second place regardless of their result against Switzerland.

Sources indicate that in the scenario that Scotland draw with Switzerland, and Slovenia lose to North Macedonia, both sides would be level on eight points. However, Slovenia would take second place following their 2-1 win at Hampden Park last month, with UEFA prioritizing head-to-head results between tied teams rather than overall goal difference. Currently in third place on seven points, they trail Slovenia in second place on eight points.

Recent findings suggest that the draw for the Nations League playoffs will take place on Friday, 20 November. The draw begins at 11am UK time and will take place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland.

You can stream the draw live via your smart TV, laptop, tablet or mobile phone, the entire ceremony will be streamed for free via UEFA.tv and the official UEFA YouTube channel.

If Scotland fail to beat Switzerland in their final Group B1 game, they will be guaranteed to finish in the third place and will remain in League B for the next edition of the tournament. North Macedonia are already guaranteed to finish fourth place will face a promotion/relegation playoff game with a second-placed League C team to remain in League B. Scotland are safe from relegation to League B.

Meanwhile, Switzerland have already won the group and have been promoted to League A. As detailed above, the second place team [currently Slovenia] will face a playoff against a third placed League A side.

Sources indicate that A third placed finish will have a direct effect on Scotland’s Euro 2028 qualifying campaign, which begins in March 2027. The tournament, which takes place across the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland, will require all four co-hosts - England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland - to compete in the standard qualifying campaign. They are not given a bye.

Where teams finish in their Nations League groups will directly decide how they are seeded for Euro 2028 qualifying, with each nation seeded based on their final group position. If Scotland finish in third, then Pocognoli’s side would drop into pot three for the draw, which could result in them facing high-ranking opponents from Pot 1 and Pot 2.

Sources indicate that the Euro 2028 qualifying draw sees teams separated into 12 groups of either four or five teams. Those who win their groups groups qualify automatically for the finals, alongside the eight highest ranked second place finishers. The four lowest ranked second place finishers enter the play-offs. Team who finish third or lower will not qualify.

In a recent development, the one caveat is that the host nations have two spots in the finals reserved if they fail to qualify. If more than two host teams do not qualify via the usual route, these two places will be allocated to the hosts placed highest in the European Qualifiers overall rankings. If only one or neither of the spots be used, the remaining places will be reallocated via the play-offs.

AC Milan devise £53m Endrick transfer plan with Real Madrid buy-back clause

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 14:51.
  • AC Milan are reportedly preparing a fresh approach to sign Real Madrid forward Endrick in January, with a proposed buy-back arrangement designed to convince the Spanish giants to sanction his departure.
  • The Italian club have previously explored a loan move for the 20-year-old Brazilian, who has struggled for regular playing time under Jose Mourinho despite showing considerable promise during his spell at Lyon last season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 15 Nov 2026 14:51.

AC Milan are reportedly preparing a fresh approach to sign Real Madrid forward Endrick in January, with a proposed buy-back arrangement designed to convince the Spanish giants to sanction his departure.

The Italian club have previously explored a loan move for the 20-year-old Brazilian, who has struggled for regular playing time under Jose Mourinho despite showing considerable promise during his spell at Lyon last season.

However, Milan are now considering a more ambitious proposal that could see Endrick eventually join them on a permanent basis while allowing Madrid to retain control over his long-term future.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the Rossoneri are weighing up an initial loan with an option or obligation to buy for approximately €60m (£53m), plus bonuses.

Crucially, the agreement would also include a buy-back clause worth around €80m (£70m), giving Real Madrid the opportunity to bring Endrick back to the Santiago Bernabeu if he develops into the player they believe he can become.

The proposed structure resembles Madrid's arrangement with Como for Nico Paz and could provide a potential solution to the disagreements that have previously prevented Endrick from leaving.

Milan's interest in Endrick is not new, but their latest reported strategy represents a change from the short-term loan previously considered.

Rather than simply borrowing the striker for six months, the Serie A club would be prepared to make a substantial financial commitment while offering Madrid assurances over the player's future.

An eventual €60m purchase would represent a major investment for Milan, who are expected to have around €70m available for the January transfer window.

The proposed €80m buy-back clause would give Madrid the possibility of reversing a permanent departure, although there is right now no indication that the Spanish club have accepted the arrangement.

There is also uncertainty over whether Milan would seek an obligation to buy or merely an option, with Italian reports discussing both possibilities.

Either structure would require an agreement over the conditions attached to the purchase and Madrid's subsequent right to re-sign the player.

Real have so far been reluctant to sanction Endrick's exit despite his limited opportunities.

Mourinho has publicly expressed his desire to retain the Brazilian, acknowledging that he has found it difficult to provide him with the playing time his development requires.

Endrick has made only limited appearances this season, contributing one goal and one assist in 141 minutes of football.

His situation follows a productive loan spell at Lyon during the 2025-26 campaign, when he registered eight goals and seven assists in 21 appearances.

Those performances demonstrated his ability to make an impact with regular minutes, strengthening interest from clubs seeking attacking reinforcements.

Real Madrid's previous reluctance to approve a permanent move for Endrick has complicated Milan's efforts, but the inclusion of a buy-back clause could offer a different basis for negotiations.

Milan may also have an advantage through their connections with Endrick's representatives.

Club owner Gerry Cardinale reportedly maintains a positive relationship with Roc Nation, the agency responsible for the Brazilian's career.

Cardinale had already expressed an interest in bringing Endrick to San Siro during the summer and is said to have requested updates whenever Madrid make a definitive decision about the youngster's future.

Former Milan and Real Madrid midfielder Kaka could also become involved in attempts to persuade Endrick to consider the move.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the Brazilian legend is viewed as a potentially influential figure because of his connections with both clubs and his standing in Brazilian football.

There is no confirmation that Kaka has formally entered negotiations or spoken directly to Endrick about joining Milan.

Nevertheless, his possible involvement adds another dimension to the club's pursuit.

Another former Milan favourite, Ronaldinho, has also offered an encouraging assessment of Endrick's ability to succeed in Italian football.

Speaking in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport, the 2005 Ballon d'Or winner insisted that his compatriot possesses the qualities required to adapt to Serie A.

"He is a player who can play anywhere in the world," Ronaldinho said.

"He has played in different leagues and done well, in France, Brazil and Spain. He is very young and can play well, yes.".

Ronaldinho's comments were an assessment of Endrick's qualities rather than an indication that he is involved in Milan's transfer prepares.

The Rossoneri face competition from Roma, where Gian Piero Gasperini is also interested in strengthening his attacking options.

The capital club have been linked with a January loan, while interest from England and France has also been reported.

However, a recent report from Corriere dello Sport suggested that Endrick was not particularly enthusiastic about moving to Milan, potentially presenting another obstacle even if the clubs can agree financial terms.

Milan are therefore maintaining alternative options, with Club Brugge striker Nicolo Tresoldi also under consideration.

The 22-year-old has scored 14 goals in 17 appearances this season and is reportedly valued at approximately €60m (£53m).

Brugge would prefer to retain Tresoldi until the summer, meaning Milan could explore signing one of their attacking targets in January before returning for the other at the end of the campaign.

For Endrick, the decisive factor remains Real Madrid's willingness to reconsider their position. Milan's proposed buy-back arrangement may offer a compromise, but no formal agreement has been reached and Mourinho has not changed his publicly stated desire to keep the striker.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Sporting director Graeme Jones has pinpointed European football and a latest playing style among the key reasons for Hearts' "unprecedented" injury situation.

The Tynecastle side were missing 11 first-team players for most recent match - a 5-2 home defeat by Falkirk before the international break - and then lost another when Malachi Fagan-Walcott limped off.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The absences have coincided with a run of just one win in eight matches across all competitions, leaving Wouter Vrancken's side fourth in the Scottish Premiership and 32nd in the Uefa Conference League.

"I need to look beyond the bad luck theory and dig into possible circumstances or reasons as to why we find ourselves where we are," Jones noted in a club interview. "We've got a latest head coach that's brought in an intended new front foot style philosophy of how we play. We have new players who are adapting to a more competitive league than what they've been used to previously.

"We have European football which is becoming the standard we want every season but the demands that Thursday-Sunday brings on the team. And then there's also the part of the bad luck which is we've suffered a huge amount of contact injuries so far this season, more in this short period than the whole of last season.

It has been revealed that "So, unfortunate as it is, it's a convergence of all these factors. But I also think it's notable to realise that there is light at the end of the tunnel. We have players returning for the game coming up on Saturday [away to Dundee].

According to recent reports, "We're hoping to have up to six, maybe even seven players possibly back into contention for first team training. Whether they're included in the squad, it just might be too soon, but we'll manage that accordingly. I can be confident that things are going to improve in the second half of the season, I've got no doubts on that.".

Jones reassured fans that Hearts are "not sitting on our hands" with regards to addressing their injury challenges.

He added: "We conducted an external review of our performance area at the turn of this year. We utilised one of the top performance practitioners in the the UK and he conducted an in-depth review that came with a numerous recommendations of things that we needed to improve. We've implemented all of these things.

"We have invested heavily in our medical department and even though it might not feel like it from the outside looking in, we're in a much better place to deal with this unprecedented level of injuries than we would have been a year ago.".

Hearts came into the campaign looking to build on last season's runners-up finish in the Scottish Premiership after narrowly missing out on a first title in 66 years to Celtic on the final day. However, after 12 matches, they have collected 10 points less than they had at the same stage last season with 12 more goals conceded. They also lost their 18-month unbeaten home record against Falkirk and were beaten by rivals Hibs at Hampden for the first time in the semi-finals of the Premier Sports Cup.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not been good enough," Jones admitted. "I know that, Wouter knows that, the players know that and we're doing everything during this international week to recalibrate and rest and put things right as best we can.

Recent findings suggest that "It's crucial to have the substantial picture in mind when you're in my role and looking towards the future. But I totally understand the short-term results have a massive effect on the general harmony across the board, particularly with our fans.

"I would never sit here and tell fans to be patient and calm during these periods. I am a fan, I've sat in the stand during some of the worst times throughout the club's history so I do understand. But we as a club and me as the sporting director have to remain focused on the objectives and the long-term future of the club and the success of the club that we are striving for.".

Addressing Hearts' plans for the January transfer window, Jones, who was appointed sporting director two years ago, stated the focus would be on balancing the squad.

"We've got a very large squad with double figures number of players that are unavailable recently so as they return back we will naturally have to look at creating balance within the squad," he said. "So we will look to decrease the size of the squad but also only add with quality. So it will be an active window like all transfer windows are but as we all know January is notoriously difficult.

Industry observers note that "We've got plenty of evidence in the last two years that the players that sign in January don't always come in and hit the ground running. So we have to focus our attentions on the quality that can make a difference but we will be very much looking to create a bit of balance within the squad. Once all our players come back are fit and available and then looking to add quality and also help people move on that aren't getting the opportunities.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mario Gila has explained how he managed to get through a difficult time at the start of his Italy adventure, eventually performing at such a high level that AC Milan decided to sign him.

Recent findings suggest that gila left Real Madrid and Spain in the summer of 2022, when he was just 21 years old, as Lazio secured his services. In his first season, however, he only got 765 minutes on the pitch and didn’t play a single game in the second half of the campaign.

The following season, it was as if things had changed completely, as the centre-back started performing really well and was rewarded with a lot of playing time. The growth only continued from there, resulting in Milan paying good money for him in the summer.

In a recent development, in his long interview with AC Milan for the interview series The Chamber, Gila discussed his initial struggles in Italy, hitting ‘rock bottom’ in his first season with Lazio. A psychologist and a changed mindset helped him get through it all.

When you make a mistake, are you very demanding and hard on yourself? I mean, how do you treat yourself when something doesn’t go the way you wanted?

It has been revealed that “In the past, for example… I’ve changed a great deal. I went through a really difficult time early in my career here in Italy and hit rock bottom, but with outside help, psychological support, I got through it.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s why I keep saying ‘before’. Back then, I was very hard on myself. I didn’t allow myself to fail. If I did, I was extremely negative towards myself, I couldn’t accept that I might fail or make mistakes.

Sources indicate that “Now I handle it much better. Now I feel that making mistakes is part of the job, it’s something that helps you improve, something that helps you grow. So I deal with it much more calmly, I process it much better internally.

“I think you still need to hold yourself to high standards and you also need to know how to find a solution to that mistake, whether in your career or in your personal life, but with much more calm and more kindness towards myself.”.

Regarding that difficult period you went through, which helped you grow and taught you so many things, you mentioned therapy. Could you tell me, not so much what happened, but what your experience with therapy was like? I mean, what did it give you at first?

It has been revealed that “I sought help from a psychologist because I was going through a very difficult time and couldn’t find a way to move forward. We’re expected to deal with situations… that I find mentally overwhelming, at just 21 years old, when you have no professional experience, because in the end, everything comes at you so fast.

“So I went to a psychologist, and completely changed my perspective. I mean, I started seeing everything negative that happened to me as a step forward, thinking: this is something that will help you improve, something you needed to go through.

Industry observers note that “Everything changed when I changed my perspective. I used to be very hard on myself, very hard, I demanded so much of myself. Now I’m someone who feels much more at ease.

“We can all fail, make mistakes, go through difficult situations, So the way I treat myself, the way I respond to myself, the way I talk to myself, I think it plays a crucial role in maintaining a consistently positive mindset.”.

By Matthew Cooper | 15 Nov 2026 14:52.

Denmark will be looking to secure their place in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League when they welcome Norway to Parken Stadium on Tuesday.

The hosts currently sit second in their League A group, just three points above the visitors in third.

Denmark head into Tuesday's match knowing that they will reach the quarter-finals if they can simply avoid defeat.

However, Brian Riemer's side will be looking to pick up another victory, having comprehensively beaten Portugal 4-1 away from home on Saturday.

Rasmus Hojlund bagged a brace for Denmark, while Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg and Joachim Andersen also found the back of the net.

The Danes will be keen to build on that performance, which Riemer described as "perfect", and gain revenge for the 3-2 defeat they suffered to Norway back in September.

It is also worth noting that was their first defeat to Norway since 1998, with Denmark going unbeaten in six games across all competitions before September's loss.

Norway, meanwhile, need to win by a three-goal margin if they are to reach the quarter-finals and they head into the game off the back of a massive win over Wales.

Stale Solbakken's side beat Wales 3-1 at home on Saturday, with Antonio Nusa, Andreas Schjelderup and Erling Haaland on target.

It was an important victory for Norway, who were bottom of the group heading into the match after suffering three consecutive Nations League defeats to Portugal, Wales and Portugal again.

Solbakken will be hoping his side can carry the momentum of Saturday's victory into Tuesday's clash with Denmark and they will draw confidence from the fact they beat the Danes back in September.

Hojlund is expected to continue up front for Denmark, having bagged a brace against Portugal, with support out wide from Gustav Isaksen and Andreas Skov Olsen.

Morten Hjulmand and Hojbjerg are likely to continue their partnership in midfield.

Norway could reward Schjelderup with a start after he came off the bench to score against Wales, while Haaland is expected to lead the line once again.

Martin Odegaard was able to start against Wales despite struggling with illness the night before and Norway will be hoping the Arsenal star is back to his best on Tuesday.

Denmark possible starting lineup:.

Hermansen; Kristensen, Andersen, Nelsson, Maehle; Hojbjerg, Hjulmand; Isaksen, Damsgaard, Skov Olsen; Hojlund.

Norway possible starting lineup:.

Selvik; Ryerson, Ajer, Heggem, Wolfe; Berg, Berge; Bobb, Odegaard, Nusa; Haaland.

Both sides will be full of confidence after impressive performances at the weekend and we are expecing a tough, hard-fought contest on Tuesday.

#2022. UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 101m • 📚 Deep Dive (20168 w)

UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 101 min read (20168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~101 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8.
  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative condition.
  • Sources indicate that genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have shown that single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within and proximal to a cryptic exon in UNC13A increase the risk of developing ALS and accelerate disease progression14,15,16.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressive and fatal neurodegenerative condition. Recently, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting SOD1 and FUS have shown early promise in clinical trials9,10, but these approaches only benefit patients with SOD1 and FUS mutations—less than 3% of patients with ALS—leaving an urgent need for therapies for the remaining roughly 97% of patients with ALS. A common feature of all non-FUS and non-SOD1 ALS is the aggregation of TAR DNA binding protein-43 (TDP-43) in neurons1,2, a finding also observed in roughly 50% of both frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer’s disease2,11. However, no therapies that directly target TDP-43 are available, leaving the underlying nuclear loss of function (LoF) unaddressed. TDP-43 is an RNA-binding protein that is normally located in the nucleus and has crucial roles in the regulation of RNA splicing12,13. Cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43 induces a nuclear LoF resulting in cryptic exon inclusion, cryptic alternative polyadenylation and/or exon skipping in some mature messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts3. These events occur in hundreds of transcripts, including genes with crucial neuronal functions, such as STMN2, UNC13A and KCNQ2 (refs. 4,5,6,7,8). Whereas the impact of STMN2 mis-splicing on axonal regeneration and KCNQ2 exon skipping on intrinsic excitability has been studied, the direct impact of TDP-43 LoF on synaptic function has not been addressed.

Sources indicate that genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have shown that single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) located within and proximal to a cryptic exon in UNC13A increase the risk of developing ALS and accelerate disease progression14,15,16. Under normal physiological conditions, these risk SNPs do not induce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, but after TDP-43 LoF, risk SNPs exacerbate cryptic exon inclusion leading to increased loss of functional RNA transcripts and protein6,7. UNC13A is a presynaptic protein that is required at the active zone to properly dock and prime synaptic vesicles for fusion with the plasma membrane17. Genetic deletion of Unc13a in mice leads to a roughly 90% reduction in spontaneous and evoked glutamatergic excitatory synaptic transmission18,19,20. Although the UNC13A genetic association strongly implicates this event in ALS pathogenesis, the contribution of TDP-43 LoF to synaptic dysfunction and the role of UNC13A cryptic splicing—particularly in the context of many mis-splicing events in other synaptic transcripts—is unaddressed. Resolving these outstanding questions is crucial for establishing whether correcting UNC13A splicing represents a viable therapeutic approach for restoring normal neuronal function.

Industry observers note that here we report that TDP-43 loss in mature human induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell-derived neurons induces loss of presynaptic UNC13A and a notable reduction in AMPA (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole propionic acid) receptor-mediated synaptic transmission, leading to a loss of coordinated network activity. Despite the widespread roles of TDP-43 in RNA regulation, isolated genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon rescues these deficits, demonstrating that this single event is a key driver of synapse dysfunction in ALS. To this end, we developed splice-switching ASOs that can rescue UNC13A mRNA splicing, UNC13A protein levels and UNC13A presynaptic localization, and restore both spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ASO treatment rescues UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion in a humanized mouse model that recreates this human-specific mis-splicing event. Thus, ASOs targeting the UNC13A cryptic exon represent an innovative therapeutic strategy for treating ALS and FTD, and their use for treating sporadic ALS is supported by genetic evidence.

TDP-43 plays vital roles in development and therefore, to avoid interfering with neuronal maturation by depleting TDP-43 from the iPS cell stage, we used CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to generate a cell line in which both endogenous copies of TDP-43 harbour a HaloTag to allow for proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC)-mediated21 knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a–d). TDP-43 is degraded by HaloPROTAC in a dose-dependent manner and in a process blocked by proteasome inhibition or the NEDD8 E1 inhibitor (Extended Data Fig. 1e–g). HaloTag-TDP-43 iPS cells were differentiated into mature excitatory cortical-like neurons (HaloTDP iNeurons) that expressed the layer V excitatory cortical marker CTIP2 and lacked expression of the inhibitory marker NKX2.1 or the neuronal progenitor marker PAX6 (Extended Data Fig. 1h). TDP-43 was also found to be correctly localized to the nucleus (Fig. 1b). Tagging of TDP-43 can alter its function and, whereas the HaloTag partially affected TDP-43 function (Extended Data Fig. 1i), UNC13A cryptic splicing and mRNA downregulation were robustly detected only on HaloPROTAC knockdown of TDP-43 (Fig. 1c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2a), similar to CRISPR interference (CRISPRi)-mediated knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Loss of UNC13A mRNA led to a time-dependent decrease in UNC13A protein whereby less than 5% of protein remained after 10 days of HaloPROTAC treatment (Fig. 1e,f). Immunofluorescence staining revealed a loss of synaptic UNC13A staining at synapsin-positive puncta (Fig. 1g,h). HaloPROTAC-mediated knockdown of TDP-43 in mature neurons did not lead to alterations in the RNA levels of N-methyl-d-aspartate and AMPA receptor subunits as assessed by reverse transcription–quantitative PCR (RT–qPCR) (Extended Data Fig. 2g).

Recent findings suggest that previous investigations of the physiological functions of UNC13A have been mainly conducted using primary rodent neurons with limited studies in human neurons18,19,20,22. We therefore sought to assess the impact of UNC13A loss in human iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Whole-cell patch clamp recordings indicated that depletion of UNC13A through CRISPRi impaired synaptic transmission, as evidenced by a reduction in the frequency of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) (Fig. 1i), consistent with a presynaptic deficit and in line with previously published work19,20. HaloPROTAC-mediated TDP-43 depletion also reduced mEPSC frequency (Fig. 1j), mirroring the presynaptic deficit observed on UNC13A loss. Treatment with 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) blocked mEPSCs, confirming that synaptic events were mediated primarily by means of fast AMPA receptor-mediated glutamatergic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3a). Whereas UNC13A depletion had no effect on mEPSC amplitude, consistent with a purely presynaptic deficit (Extended Data Fig. 3b), TDP-43 depletion led to a modest reduction in amplitude (Extended Data Fig. 3c), suggesting extra postsynaptic deficits independent of UNC13A depletion. Passive membrane properties remained comparable between control and UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e).

Industry observers note that to investigate the effect of UNC13A and TDP-43 loss on network activity, we carried out multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings. We found that either UNC13A or TDP-43 depletion induced a disordered and asynchronous pattern of network activity, measured by a reduction in the normalized electrode cross-correlations (Fig. 1k–m). This result indicates that UNC13A–TDP-43 depleted neurons fail to support network-level activity. The number of active electrodes remained consistent (Extended Data Fig. 3g) and phase-contrast images showed comparable cell coverage between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 3h), ruling out complications with electrode coverage as a confounding factor. CNQX treatment of control neurons confirmed network synchrony was highly dependent on fast AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic transmission (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Whereas extra MEA metrics were also affected by both TDP-43 and UNC13A loss, the network synchrony deficit was the largest and most consistently observed change (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Thus, we show that TDP-43 depletion substantially impairs fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission and synchronized network activity in human neurons, mirroring a comparable loss of synaptic function and network activity induced by direct UNC13A loss.

It has been revealed that knockdown of TDP-43 leads to cryptic exon inclusion within UNC13A intron 20 along with an independent downstream intron retention event at intron 31 and other lower-frequency splicing abnormalities throughout the UNC13A mRNA transcript6,7. To determine the degree to which protein loss is dependent on the UNC13A intron 20 cryptic exon, we performed CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing to remove the cryptic exon from the genome of SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Using two single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) we made a homozygous deletion of 233 nucleotides (nt) that contain both splice acceptors and the common donor splice site of the cryptic exon. In wild-type (WT) cells containing the full UNC13A gene there was robust induction of UNC13A mis-splicing after TDP-43 depletion as assessed by reverse transcription–PCR (RT–PCR) (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d), whereas in cells with genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon, no cryptic splicing was detected (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Cryptic exon deletion rescued correctly spliced levels of UNC13A mRNA, as determined by RT–qPCR, and led to roughly 75% rescue of UNC13A protein following TDP-43 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 4e–g). We subsequently deleted the UNC13A cryptic exon in iPS cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a–e) and detected a similar rescue in UNC13A RNA and protein following CRISPRi-mediated knockdown of TDP-43, confirming the relevance of this event in iPS cell-derived neurons (Extended Data Fig. 5f–k). In the UNC13A cryptic exon deletion cell line, we performed further CRISPR–Cas12 gene editing to add a HaloTag in the TARDBP gene to efficiently induce TDP-43 loss after differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 6). Similar to results in SH-SY5Y cells, genomic deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in HaloTDP iNeurons rescued UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction and restored mRNA and presynaptic protein levels (Fig. 2a–h), demonstrating this splicing event is the main driver of TDP-43-dependent UNC13A loss.

It has been revealed that TDP-43 knockdown yields synaptic transmission defects similar to those induced by direct depletion of UNC13A. However, TDP-43 has hundreds of validated RNA targets, regulating splicing, stability and transport of transcripts involved in virtually every aspect of neuronal function. Therefore, the reduction in synaptic transmission could reflect a multi-gene insult affecting pathways including synaptic vesicle trafficking, Ca2+ signalling and active zone organization. To determine the extent to which UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion contributes to impaired synaptic function following loss of TDP-43, we performed whole-cell patch clamping experiments in WT and cryptic exon deletion lines. Rescue of this single cryptic exon largely restored synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion with an 80% recovery in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 2i,j). mEPSC amplitude was still marginally (roughly 10%) reduced, supporting the conclusion that UNC13A cryptic exon deletion rescues specifically presynaptic function (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Passive membrane properties were similar between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7b). As mEPSC frequency is influenced by synapse number, we measured excitatory synapse density along the dendrites of iNeurons. We found that TDP-43-knockdown neurons had fewer synapses than controls, a feature that persisted even when the UNC13A cryptic exon was deleted (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d), suggesting a strong recovery in synapse function in the remaining synapses.

According to recent reports, despite the small reduction in synapse number, MEA recordings demonstrated that deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in TDP-43-depleted neurons restored synchronous network activity, indicating effective neurotransmitter release and propagation of signalling across the network (Fig. 2k,l and Extended Data Fig. 7e). This represented the most robustly rescued MEA metric (Extended Data Fig. 7f). Taken together, these findings show that correction of a single cryptic exon splicing event (intron 20 UNC13A cryptic exon) is sufficient to restore synaptic transmission and rescue the asynchronous patterns of network activity caused by TDP-43 loss. Active electrodes and cell coverage were comparable across conditions (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Likewise, analysis of neuronal survival confirmed that network-level changes were not attributable to changes in viability due to TDP-43 loss (Extended Data Fig. 7h) demonstrating that TDP-43 driven UNC13A loss drives a functional synaptic deficit in otherwise structurally intact, viable neurons.

Recent findings suggest that the rescue of UNC13A levels and restoration of synaptic signalling conferred by deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon in the context of TDP-43 knockdown highlights the therapeutic potential of targeting this event in patients. We therefore sought to identify ASOs that can induce splice switching similar to those successful in targeting splicing events in SMN2 and STMN2 (refs. 23,24). We first designed locked nucleic acid-modified ASOs that targeted regions covering the cryptic exon acceptor and donor splice sites (Extended Data Fig. 8a). We screened the ASOs by transfection in SK-N-BE(2) cells and assessed their ability to restore UNC13A splicing at the exon 20–21 junction by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 8b) and found that 21-nt ASOs targeting the donor splice site could restore UNC13A splicing. We confirmed splicing rescue and ability to restore UNC13A RNA and UNC13A protein levels in SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 8c–g). To improve therapeutic tolerance, we adapted the best performing ASOs to have full 2′-O-methoxyethyl (MOE) ribose-modified bases and tested their ability to rescue UNC13A splicing and restore protein levels in HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3a–c and Extended Data Fig. 8h). We found these could restore splicing to more than 90% and protein levels to 30–50% of normal levels. Treatment with the M21-4 MOE ASO led to increased presynaptic UNC13A protein expression at synapsin-positive puncta following TDP-43 depletion compared with treatment with the control scrambled ASO (Fig. 3d). To identify ASOs that could increase protein rescue above 50% of normal levels, we carried out a secondary screen by performing an ASO walk along the cryptic donor site with 18-nt MOE-based ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 9a). We evaluated the ability of the 18-nt ASOs to rescue splicing in SH-SY5Y cells by RT–PCR (Extended Data Fig. 9b) and confirmed that the best performing 18-nt ASOs could rescue correct UNC13A mRNA splicing to more than 90%, and protein to more than 50% in SH-SY5Y cells and HaloTDP iNeurons (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 9c–h). In addition, we performed amplicon sequencing, which confirmed the ability of ASOs to rescue both reference and risk alleles in our HaloTDP iNeurons (Extended Data Fig. 9i).

To validate the efficacy of UNC13A ASOs to rescue cryptic splicing in an in vivo model, we generated humanized UNC13A (hUNC13A) reporter mice, in which mouse intron 20 was replaced with human UNC13A intron 20 containing the cryptic exon. TDP-43 knockdown was performed by tail vein injection of an adeno-associated virus encoding a synthetic microRNA targeting the mouse Tardbp gene (Fig. 3g). On the same day, intracerebroventricular injections were performed in hUNC13A reporter mice with the M21-4 MOE ASO or artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Three weeks post-injection, spinal cords were dissected from the mice. RT–PCR analysis from spinal cord tissue following knockdown of TDP-43 demonstrated no cryptic exon inclusion in WT mice and robust cryptic exon inclusion in hUNC13A reporter mice, which was partially rescued by administration of UNC13A splice-correcting ASO (Fig. 3h–k). Overall, these results show that ASOs can reduce inclusion of the UNC13A cryptic exon on TDP-43 knockdown both in vitro and in vivo, and can rescue UNC13A protein expression to above 50% in cultured neurons.

Unc13a heterozygous knockout mice and individuals with heterozygous LoF UNC13A mutations are viable and do not present with abnormal neurophysiology18,25. Recovery of UNC13A expression to WT levels after TDP-43 LoF is probably not required to restore synapse function, in agreement with previous work in primary mouse cultures that highlighted that clear deficits in synapse function are only observed when expression of Unc13a falls below 30% of normal physiological levels20,25. Indeed, treatment with M18-17 ASO, which rescues UNC13A levels to more than 50% of control, was able to rescue synaptic transmission as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4a). We then tested our M21-4 ASO, which rescues UNC13A protein levels to roughly 30% of normal levels. Despite the lower level of protein rescue, treatment with M21-4 ASO also rescued synaptic transmission following TDP-43 depletion as measured by an increase in mEPSC frequency (Fig. 4b). mEPSC amplitude and passive membrane properties were unaffected by treatment with ASOs (Extended Data Fig. 10a–d), suggesting that ASO treatment specifically rescues presynaptic deficits caused by the cryptic exon in UNC13A.
