Whereas mEPSC recordings allowed us to detect deficits in spontaneous vesicle release, we also sought to determine whether TDP-43 depletion affected evoked synaptic transmission, the physiological mode that drives circuit function, and whether UNC13A ASOs could be beneficial. We conducted whole-cell voltage clamp recordings to examine evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (eEPSCs) in autaptic micro-island cultures in which single neurons are grown on astrocytes and form synaptic connections onto themselves26,27. We performed experiments in two different ALS-affected neuronal subtypes: cortical-like excitatory iNeurons expressing the layer V marker CTIP2 and human iPS cell-derived spinal motor neurons expressing Islet-1 and the marker VAChT, performed in two laboratories with different methods for TDP-43 depletion (days in vitro (DIV) 14 PROTAC or DIV45 gapmer ASO knockdown). In both neuronal subtypes, TDP-43 depletion caused a substantial reduction in eEPSC amplitude, which was partially rescued by UNC13A splice-correcting ASOs (Fig. 4c,d and Extended Data Fig. 10e,f). Furthermore, the spontaneous vesicle release phenotype (decrease in mEPSC frequency) and ASO-mediated rescue were also confirmed in the separate spinal motor neuron model (Extended Data Fig. 10g–k). The amplitude of eEPSCs depends on several factors, including presynaptic probability of neurotransmitter release, postsynaptic strength (quantal amplitude) and synapse density. Our previous observations have already described UNC13A-independent decreases in both postsynaptic strength (Extended Data Fig. 7a) and synapse density (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). Therefore, we decided to directly measure evoked presynaptic release probability at the level of single synapses in conventional iNeuron cultures (not autaptic), using live imaging of a genetically encoded reporter of glutamate release, iGluSNFR3 (ref. 28). TDP-43 depletion led to both a reduction in the number of active synapses as well as a reduction in the release probability of those synapses (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 11a). UNC13A splice-correcting ASOs did not rescue the number of active synapses (Extended Data Fig. 11a), consistent with the morphological analysis showing UNC13A splice correction also failed to rescue synapse density along dendrites following TDP-43 loss (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d and Extended Data Fig. 11b). However, UNC13A splice correction was associated with improved release probability at the remaining synapses, although this effect narrowly missed statistical significance (P = 0.052) (Fig. 4e).

According to recent reports, next, we tested the effectiveness of UNC13A splice-switching ASOs in rescuing network synchrony in neurons in which we induced TDP-43 depletion at DIV14. MEA recordings showed a small but statistically significant rescue in network synchrony following treatment with M18-17 ASO compared with a scrambled control (Fig. 4f,g and Extended Data Fig. 11c). To better mimic the disease, in which TDP-43 loss occurs in adult neurons, we induced TDP-43 depletion at DIV33, when neurons have already developed mature network activity (Extended Data Fig. 11d,e). As with earlier knockdowns, synchrony was the metric most affected by TDP-43 depletion (Extended Data Fig. 11f). In this case, ASO rescue experiments showed a greater recovery of network synchrony (Fig. 4f,g and Extended Data Fig. 11g). Across all MEA metrics, network synchrony showed the most consistent and pronounced rescue (Extended Data Fig. 11h).

Together, these data demonstrate that therapeutic targeting of the UNC13A cryptic exon using an antisense oligonucleotide can rescue synaptic function: from neurotransmitter release at individual synapses through to emergent network-level function.

Sources indicate that in this study, we show that TDP-43 LoF leads to a drastic loss of spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission, leading to a disordered and asynchronous pattern of network activity in human neurons. Of the many hundreds of widespread cryptic mis-splicing events driven by TDP-43 LoF, we demonstrate that a single cryptic exon in the disease progression modifier gene UNC13A is a main driver of this synaptic breakdown. By designing splice-correcting ASOs targeting the UNC13A cryptic exon, we demonstrate how synaptic function can be restored, supporting UNC13A splice correction as a genetically anchored therapeutic strategy amenable to most patients with ALS and patients with FTD with TDP-43 pathology.

It has been revealed that out of the numerous cryptic splicing events induced by loss of nuclear TDP-43 that affect proteins that are predicted to affect neuronal health and function3,4,5,6,7,8,29, the cryptic exon in intron 20 of the UNC13A gene has attracted considerable interest. Risk SNPs accounting for the second strongest ALS and frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 aggregation GWAS signal are located within this intron and enhance cryptic splicing, exacerbating transcript and protein loss6,7,14,15,16,30,31,32. Among patients with ALS, homozygous carriers of UNC13A risk SNPs (rs12608932 and rs12973192) show a 5–12-month reduction in median survival15,16,33,34,35,36. Therefore, genetic data strongly support targeting this event to modify disease progression.

According to recent reports, the functional implications of UNC13A cryptic splicing in ALS and/or FTD remain unknown. UNC13A protein is crucial for synaptic vesicle priming; Unc13a-null mice die at birth from respiratory failure, and primary cortical cultures from these mice develop normally but have substantially reduced excitatory synaptic transmission18,19,20. Although ALS-linked mutations in TDP-43 have been shown to cause excitability and synaptic deficits in human neurons37,38,39, these studies did not establish a mechanistic role for cryptic exon inclusion or altered UNC13A protein levels. Therefore, we sought to determine whether direct depletion of TDP-43, modelling TDP-43 LoF in patients with sporadic ALS and associated alterations in RNA splicing also drive impaired synaptic function. Here we demonstrate TDP-43 depletion in iPS cell-derived neurons drives a reduction in both spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, leading to a failure of network-level signal propagation and asynchronous network activity. These results mirror the LoF we observed following direct UNC13A knockdown, as well as the synaptic defects described in previously published reports of Unc13a depletion in primary rodent neurons18,19,20.

TDP-43 LoF causes widespread mis-splicing in hundreds of transcripts, many of which are involved in synaptic transmission. Therefore, to specifically assess the contribution of the UNC13A cryptic exon to the decreased synaptic activity observed in TDP-43 depleted neurons, we selectively deleted the UNC13A intron 20 cryptic exon in human neurons. We found that rescuing this single mis-splicing event could restore spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release in two independent models (cortical-like iNeurons and spinal motor neurons), and re-establish network synchrony, demonstrating that loss of UNC13A protein is a main driver of synaptic breakdown caused by TDP-43 LoF. Other synaptic genes are also likely to contribute to the broader range of observed phenotypes. For example, we observed changes in mEPSC amplitude on TDP-43 loss in iNeurons that are not recapitulated by direct UNC13A loss, nor rescued by deletion of the UNC13A cryptic exon. Similarly, we observed a reduction in synapse density following TDP-43 knockdown that does not appear to be driven by altered UNC13A protein levels. Further studies, focusing on mis-spliced transcripts whose products either localize to the postsynapse or are involved in synapse turnover40, will explain the functional mechanisms underpinning these changes. Despite this strong deficit in synapse density that is independent of UNC13A, we found that rescuing UNC13A led to a robust recovery in both spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission as measured across two independent model systems and cell types relevant to ALS and/or FTD (cortical-like iNeurons and spinal motor neurons). Live imaging of individual synapses revealed that, although the number of active synapses was not restored, there was a trend towards higher release probability of these remaining synapses after splice correction, highlighting the importance of vesicle release kinetics at individual synapses in contributing to emergent network-level function.

Data assessing UNC13A protein levels in patient neurons are not available, but transcriptomic data on fluorescence-activated nuclei-sorted postmortem cortex from patients with ALS and/or FTD with TDP-43 pathology show that the UNC13A cryptic exon can be included in more than 90% of UNC13A transcripts within the cell population lacking nuclear TDP-43, which is thus predicted to greatly inhibit production of functional UNC13A protein6,41. These findings support the validity of using iPS cell-derived neuronal models in which TDP-43 loss induces a near-total loss of UNC13A, although models that recapitulate both nuclear loss and cytoplasmic aggregation will be beneficial in future work. Previous electrophysiology studies have demonstrated that the level or activity of UNC13A needs to be reduced below roughly 30% before strong synaptic deficits appear20,25. This agrees with studies using Unc13a-heterozygous mice, which demonstrated no defects in synaptic activity. Our results show that restoring roughly 30% or more of UNC13A protein levels can rescue synaptic transmission. Altogether, this suggests that splice-switching therapeutic rescue of UNC13A to more than 30% in patients with ALS could be beneficial for the recovery of synaptic function.

Although loss of UNC13A effectively leads to synaptic silencing, transcranial magnetic stimulation studies have detected cortical hyperexcitability at an early stage in patients with ALS that worsens with disease progression42 and is associated with poorer survival outcomes43. Although other factors, such as KCNQ2 mis-splicing, may contribute to this hyperexcitability, it is possible that UNC13A loss also plays a role in this. Rare patients with inherited biallelic UNC13A mutations can present with seizures at a young age25,44,45, and one individual with a biallelic truncating mutation in UNC13A developed myasthenia and had cortical hyperexcitability on electroencephalography analysis44. Cortical hyperexcitability has also been shown in individuals with variants in other presynaptic proteins that reduce synaptic vesicle release through LoF or dominant-negative mechanisms, such as STX1B (syntaxin-1B)46, STXBP1 (Munc18-1)47 and SNAP25B (ref. 48). The impaired excitatory synaptic output driven by UNC13A mis-splicing could drive hyperexcitability through more complex circuit alterations, such as the reduction in microcircuit feedforward inhibition and an overall skew of the excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio49. Our experimental system consisted exclusively of excitatory neurons, in which impaired synaptic transmission manifested as a loss of network synchrony, rather than hyperactivity. Future studies should incorporate inhibitory interneurons to more precisely assess how TDP-43 loss and UNC13A dysfunction affect network dynamics. The humanized mouse model described here could provide a valuable platform for assessing network changes in an in vivo setting.

Our experiments were carried out in populations of neurons that had a homogeneous loss of TDP-43 and in which its presynaptic and postsynaptic effects are inevitably compounded. As such, our experimental setup represents a more extreme condition than the mosaic pattern of TDP-43 loss seen in patients with ALS, in which affected neurons can still project onto unaffected neurons. It is conceivable that UNC13A-mediated presynaptic release rescue could be sufficient to restore normal synaptic signalling in connections in which the postsynaptic neuron remains unaffected, and future studies in more complex models will help resolve how circuits are affected by mosaic UNC13A mis-splicing.

The cellular events that lead to TDP-43 aggregation in ALS are unknown and it is therefore challenging to correct this directly, but aggregation is associated with a loss of TDP-43 nuclear function that produces numerous cryptic splicing events, which may represent more tractable therapeutic targets than targeting mislocalization directly. Splice-modifying ASOs have been successfully developed to treat spinal muscular atrophy by correcting SMN2 splicing23,50. This same strategy can be used to correct cryptic splicing in ALS and has the advantage of being able to restore physiological transcript levels, without the risk of overexpression. Yet there is still a need to identify splicing events that have the strongest impact on neuronal function and hold the most promise of improving disease symptoms. Our findings, along with results from GWAS suggesting that modulation of UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion affects disease progression15, strongly support UNC13A as a key candidate for splice-modifying therapy development in ALS. TDP-43 LoF drives sufficient UNC13A reduction to impair synaptic transmission and network synchrony.

According to recent reports, we show prevention of UNC13A mis-splicing by means of CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing or application of ASOs can rescue UNC13A protein expression and restore defects at many layers of complexity: from single-synapse release probability to spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission and emergent network synchrony. This points to a stage of TDP-43-linked neurodegeneration in which neurons lose the ability to contribute to meaningful synaptic communication before overt neuronal death. This functional death provides a unique therapeutic opportunity: a pool of structurally intact neurons unable to contribute to normal network function that are recoverable through splice-correcting ASOs targeting a single TDP-43 dependent cryptic exon in UNC13A. Notably, therapies targeting UNC13A splicing would be amenable to most patients with ALS and/or FTD and TDP-43 pathology that is supported by clear genetic evidence and a clearly defined molecular and functional mechanism.

SH-SY5Y cells (American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)) and SK-N-BE(2) (ATCC) with stable doxycycline-inducible short-hairpin RNA (shRNA) to TARDBP were described in ref. 6 and were maintained in DMEM–F12 with GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and split with TrypLE Express (Thermo Fisher Scientific) when 80% confluent. The WTC11 iPS cell line derived from a healthy human participant (GM25256) with stable integration of doxycycline-inducible expression of NGN2 at the AAVS1 locus and stable integration of dCas9-BFP-KRAB at the CLYBL locus was a gift from M. Ward51. This iPS cell line is heterozygous for UNC13A risk SNPs (rs12608932 and rs12973192). Cells were maintained in E8 Flex Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in Geltrex-coated (Thermo Fisher Scientific) plates and passaged with Versene solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) or Accutase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) when 80% confluent. All cell lines were authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling and were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination, with negative results throughout. For induction of iPS cells to iNeurons, iPS cells were passaged with Accutase (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and plated into Geltrex-coated plates with induction media: DMEM–F12 with GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1× N2-Max Supplement (R&D Systems), 1× non-essential amino acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 2 μg ml−1 doxycycline hyclate (Sigma-Aldrich), 2 μM XAV939 (Cayman Chemical), 10 μM SB431542 (Cayman Chemical) and 100 nM LDN-193189 (Cayman Chemical)52,53. Medium was changed daily for 3 days. On the third day, cells were replated to poly-l-ornithine-coated (10 μg ml−1; Sigma-Aldrich) plates for RNA and protein experiments or on 50 μg ml−1 poly-d-lysine (PDL) (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 10 μg ml−1 laminin-coated (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) 18-mm coverslips (Deckglaser) with primary rat astrocytes for electrophysiology, live imaging and immunofluorescence experiments. Differentiated neurons were maintained in neuronal medium (synaptic medium) with extra supplements: BrainPhys (StemCell Technologies), with 1× N2-Max Supplement (R&D Systems), 1× N21-Max Supplement (R&D Systems), 10 ng ml−1 NT3 (StemCell Technologies), 20 ng ml−1 glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (Peprotech), 2.5% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1× Non-Essential Amino Acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 0.2 mg ml−1 cAMP (Sigma-Aldrich), 1× GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 200 nM ascorbic acid (Sigma-Aldrich)54. This medium was used for all experiments, with the exception of MEA recordings that were carried out without FBS. Half-medium changes were performed twice per week for all cultures, or after recording on MEA cultures.

Recent findings suggest that for rat astrocyte preparation, primary cortices were dissected from E18 Wistar rat embryos (Charles River Laboratories) and treated with 0.5 mg ml−1 trypsin (Worthington) for 15 min at 37 °C. Cortices were washed with Hanks’ balanced saline solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and triturated with fire-polished glass Pasteur pipettes of decreasing diameter in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) + 10% FBS (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were collected by centrifugation at 900 r.p.m. for 10 min, resuspended and passed through a 70-µm cell strainer. Roughly 15–18 million cells were plated in a T-75 flask and cultured in DMEM + 10%FBS + 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After 2 days a complete medium change was conducted to remove antibiotics and medium was replaced every 3 days thereafter. Once reaching confluence, the cultures were enriched for astrocytes by shaking at 180 r.p.m. on an orbital shaker for 30 min, after which the medium was removed. Fresh medium was added and shaking increased to 240 rpm for 6 h, after which the medium was replaced. These steps remove microglia and oligodendrocyte precursor cells. Astrocyte-enriched cultures were passaged using 0.25% trypsin–EDTA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and cultured in fresh T-75 flasks for 12–14 days, with a medium change every 2–3 days, until confluent. Astrocytes were then passaged and either stored in liquid nitrogen or plated on 50 μg ml−1 PDL (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 10 μg ml−1 laminin-coated (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) 18 mm coverslips (Deckglaser) for culturing with iNeurons.

Recent findings suggest that the GM25256 human iPS cell line, which is heterozygous for UNC13A risk SNPs (rs12608932 and rs12973192) (Coriell Institute for Medical Research) was maintained in mTeSR1 stem cell culture media on Matrigel-coated plates (StemCell Technologies, 85850; Corning, 354277). Human iPS cells were fed daily and split every 4–5 days. Differentiation of iPS cells into motor neurons (iMNs) was carried out using three-dimensional developmental pathways for 14 days (refs. 7,55). On day 14, neuronal spheroids were dissociated, counted and frozen using 70% KnockOut Serum Replacement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10828010), 20% 1 M Trehalose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 182550250) and 10% DMSO (Sigma-Aldrich, D2650). Neurons were thawed, and plated on PDL–laminin-coated coverslips or directly on PDL-coated coverslips on which mouse astrocytes were plated25, and maintained in a medium containing Neurobasal medium (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 12348017) supplemented with 1× N-2 supplement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 17502001), 1× B-27 supplement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, A1486701), 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15140-122), 20 µM l-ascorbic acid (Sigma-Aldrich, A4403-100MG), 1% KnockOut Serum Replacement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 10828010), 5 µM ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (StemCell Technologies, 72304), 10 ng ml−1 GDNF (R&D Systems, 212-GD-050), 10 ng ml−1 CNTF (R&D Systems, 257-NT-050) and 20 ng ml−1 BDNF (R&D Systems, 11166-BD-050) for the first 2 days. After 2 days, half of the medium was exchanged with neuron maintenance medium without the ROCK inhibitor and supplemented with 5 µM DAPT (Sigma-Aldrich, D5942) and 10 ng ml−1 BDNF. Five days later, iMNs were fed with neuron maintenance medium without ROCK inhibitor and DAPT. iMNs were supplemented with fresh medium every 7 days.

In a recent development, spinal iMNs release the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, but do not express postsynaptic nicotinic receptors. As such, iMN cultures express synaptic markers, but the cells are not synaptically connected. To record synaptic transmission properties in these neurons, we expressed the vesicular glutamate transporter (VGlut1) tagged by green fluorescent protein (GFP) in iMNs 1 week before electrophysiological recordings, on the basis of previous observations that its expression can confer the release of glutamate in inhibitory neurons56. Complementary DNA (cDNA) encoding rat VGlut1 tagged with enhanced GFP (EGFP) at the carboxy terminus was used to prepare lentiviral particles (Viral Core Facility of the Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin). The FUGW vector57, in which the ubiquitin promoter was exchanged with the human synapsin 1 promoter, was used according to a previously published57, modified protocol58, using helper plasmids59 (Addgene, 8454 and 8455).

Sense and antisense bridging oligonucleotides 5′-AAAGTCCAGATTCAGGG TCACCTCCTCTGGGAAGCCCACC TTGGCCTCCBGGATGGATAGATGGATGAGTTGGTGGGTAGATTCGTGGCTAGATGGATGA-3′ and 5′-TCATCCATCTAGCCACGAATCTACCCACCAACTCATCCATCTATCCATCDTGGAGGCCAAGGTGGGCTTCCCAGAGGAGGTGACCCTGAATCTGGACTTT-3′, which include degenerate base B (C, G or T) and D (A, G or T) were designed as homology-directed repair templates. Locked nucleic acid-modified ASOs were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies. The 21-nt MOE-modified UNC13A splice-correcting ASOs or TDP-43 gapmer ASOs were purchased from Dharmacon, Wuxi or Biospring, and a gift from Trace Neuroscience. A panel of 18-nt MOE-modified ASOs was designed to tile across the region of interest before being subjected to further selection on the basis of potential sequence-driven off-target effects and secondary structure. The resulting panel of 24 ASOs was generated by solid-phase synthesis using MerMade12 automated synthesizer using prepacked controlled pore glass columns (1-µmol scale, 1,000 Å). Phosphoramidites (TheraPure by Thermo Fisher Scientific) were prepared at 0.08 M using acetonitrile. Cleavage and deprotection of oligonucleotides were performed using concentrated ammonia for 6 h at 55 °C. After deprotection, samples were dried and resuspended in water. Purification of the oligonucleotides was performed by reversed-phase high-performance liquid chromatography using 0.1 M triethylammonium acetate pH 7 and acetonitrile in an XBridge BEH C18 Prep column (Waters). Oligonucleotides were desalted using ethanol precipitation and quantification performed measuring the absorbance at 260 nm and the corresponding molecular extinction coefficient for each ASO. Quality control of the synthesized oligonucleotides was performed by liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry. ASO sequences are in Supplementary Table 2.

SH-SY5Y cells with stable integration of a shRNA cassette for TARDBP were treated with 25 ng ml−1 doxycycline (Sigma-Aldrich) for 5 days and then transfected while replating into 12-well plates using Lipofectamine RNAiMax (6 μl per well, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ASOs at 50 nM final concentration. Following transfection, doxycycline concentration was increased to 1 μg ml−1 and cells were collected 5 days after transfection. To test 18-nt MOE-based ASOs, shTARDBP SH-SY5Y cells were treated with 25 ng ml−1 doxycycline for 5 days, then 100 ng ml−1 doxycycline for 24 h, plated into 96-well plates and transfected using Lipofectamine RNAiMax (0.72 μl per well) and ASOs at 10 nM or 50 nM final concentration. Cells were collected 48 h after transfection.

Following transfection doxycycline concentration was increased to 1 μg ml−1 and cells were collected 3 days after transfection.

On day 45 after neuronal plating, TRTDP43 ((moeA)*(moeA)*(moeG)*(moeG)*(moe5C)*(dT)*(dT)*(d5C)*(dA)*(dT)*(dA)*(dT)*(dT)*(dG)*(dT)*(moeA)*(moe5C)*(moeT)*(moeT)*(moeT); where moe denotes MOE base, d denotes DNA base, 5C denotes 5-methylcytosine) (2–4 μM)) was added to the culture wells to knock down TDP-43. Sources indicate that RNA was extracted from SH-SY5Y cells, SK-N-BE(2) cells and iNeurons with a RNeasy kit (Qiagen) using the manufacturer’s protocol including homogenization of samples with QIAshredder spin columns (Qiagen). Industry observers note that RNA extraction and cDNA synthesis were performed as in RT–qPCR methods. The UNC13A cryptic exon was amplified with a forward primer in exon 19 5′-CAGACGATCATTGAGGTGCG-3′ and reverse primer in exon 22 5′-ATACTTGGAGGAGAGGCAGG-3′ using Q5 Hot Start High Fidelity 2× Master Mix (New England Biolabs). PCR products were resolved on a TapeStation 4200 (Agilent) and bands were quantified with TapeStation Systems Software v.3.2 (Agilent). For the primary screen of ASOs in SK-N-BE(2) cells, PCR products were analysed with a QIAxcel capillary electrophoresis machine (Qiagen). Raw data were exported and analysed with the QIAxcelR package (v.0.1) (https://github.com/Delayed-Gitification/QIAxcelR).

According to recent reports, genomic DNA from SH-SY5Y cells and iPS cells were extracted with the Monarch Genomic DNA Purification Kit (New England Biolabs). PCR was performed with Q5 Hot Start High Fidelity 2× Master Mix (New England Biolabs) and purified with Monarch PCR cleanup kit (New England Biolabs). Purified amplicons were sequenced using the Premium PCR long-read sequencing service (Plasmidsaurus). Raw FASTQ reads were mapped to UNC13A and TARDBP genes using Minimap2 (ref. 62) with the -x splice flag enabled (v.2.26-r1175) and converted to BAM files with SAMtools63 (v.1.21). Results were visualized with the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) browser64. For quantification of UNC13A allele-specific rescue, RT–PCR was performed as described above and amplicons were sequenced by Plasmidsaurus. Raw FASTQ reads were mapped to UNC13A using Minimap2, converted to BAM files with SAMtools and SNPs were quantified with custom Python scripts.

Genomic DNA was extracted from iPS cells using the Monarch Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Fresh England Biolabs). Low-pass whole-genome sequencing (roughly 10× mean coverage) was performed by Azenta Life Sciences. Adapter trimming and quality control of FASTQ files were carried out with fastp65 (v.0.23.4). Reads were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38 (GCA_000001405.15) using bwa-mem2 (ref. 66) (v.2.2.1), and the resulting alignments were converted to sorted BAM format with SAMtools (v.1.21). Copy-number variant analysis was performed with CNVkit67 (v.0.9.12) using the batch command with the whole-genome sequencing pipeline (--method wgs). Sequencing-accessible regions were defined by masking gaps and repeat tracks from the UCSC genome browser (--access access-hg38.bed). Bins of 20-kilobase average size were used (--target-avg-size 20,000), GC bias and low-coverage bins were corrected (--drop-low-coverage), gene annotations were added from refFlat.txt (--annotate) and a flat male reference was constructed (--male-reference --normal --output-reference WTC11-WT_flat.cnn). Segmented copy number profiles were generated with the default circular binary segmentation algorithm.

Cells were collected with RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with cOmplete mini protease inhibitors (Sigma-Aldrich) and protein concentration was quantified using the Pierce bicinchoninic acid (BCA) Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Protein lysates were resolved on 4–12% precast Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher Scientific) or poured 7% Bis-Tris gels and transferred to 0.2-μm polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (Merck Millipore). Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in tris-buffered saline with Tween (TBST) and then probed overnight with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 6) in 5% non-fat milk in TBST at 4 °C. Blots were washed 3 times with TBST and subsequently probed with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h (Goat anti-Mouse HRP Bio-Rad 1706516; 1:10,000 or Goat anti-Rabbit HRP Bio-Rad 1706515; 1:10,000) and developed with Chemiluminescent substrate (Merck Millipore, WBKLS0500) on a ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad). Band intensity was measured with Fiji (ImageJ)69 (NIH version 2.0.0-rc-69). Band intensities were normalized to loading control (Tubulin) within each lane. Normalized values were log10-transformed before analysis. The effect of treatment was assessed by repeated-measures one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), with biological replicate (blot) as the matching factor and the Geisser–Greenhouse correction applied (sphericity not assumed), followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test for all pairwise comparisons between groups.

Industry observers note that motor neurons were lysed in RIPA buffer (25 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% (w/v) SDOC, 1% IGEPAL (NP-40), 0.1% (w/v) SDS) with 0.1% of each protease inhibitor (aprotinin, leupeptin, phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride), sonicated and centrifuged in a tabletop centrifuge at 4 °C for 45 min at 15,000 r.p.m. Supernatants were transferred into a fresh tube, and protein concentration was determined using Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225). Samples were diluted in Laemmli buffer (3% (w/v) SDS, 41.6 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 10% (v/v) glycerol, 0.06% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 0.77%, (w/v) dithiothreitol in double-distilled H2O (ddH2O)) and incubated for 10 min at 95 °C. Then 10 µg of the lysed samples was loaded onto a commercial 4–12% Bis-Tris gels (NuPAGE 4–12% Bis-Tris Gel (1.0 mm × 10 wells), Invitrogen, NP0321BOX) and separated in cold MOPS buffer (20 mM MOPS free acid, 5 mM sodium acetate, 1 mM Na2EDTA) at a constant voltage of 120 V. Transfer of the proteins was conducted in transfer buffer (192 mM glycine, 25 mM Tris, 10% methanol) on a nitrocellulose membrane for 14 h at 65 mA. Membranes were then stained for total protein as a loading control with Pierce Reversible Protein Stain Kit for Nitrocellulose Membranes (according to the manufacturer’s manual; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 24580). The membranes were blocked with 5% milk in TBST buffer (10 mM Tris/HCl, 100 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween 20, pH 7.5) for 1 h at room temperature. After this step, the membranes were cut and incubated with primary antibodies: rabbit anti-Munc13-1 (Synaptic Systems, 126 103, 1:250), rabbit-TDP-43 (Proteintech, 10782-2-AP, 1:1,000), mouse anti-Vinculin (Sigma-Aldrich, V9131-100UL 1:1,000) and rabbit anti-Stathmin-2 (Bio-Techne, NBP1-49461, 1:1,000). The corresponding secondary antibodies used were: anti-mouse HRP (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 115-035-146, 1:3,000) and anti-rabbit HRP (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111-035-144, 1:3,000). The chemiluminescence signal was detected with Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 32106) on an ECL ChemoStar imager (Intas). Protein signals were analysed in Fiji (ImageJ). Protein levels were first normalized to the total protein staining in the corresponding lane, and then to the control condition. Finally, statistical analysis was conducted in GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software) using one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons. Error bars represent mean ± s.e.m.

Industry observers note that maestro 96-well cytoview MEA plates (Axion Biosystems M768-tMEA-96B) were drop-wise coated in 0.05 mg ml−1 PDL (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific, A38904-01) at room temperature for 2 h, washed 3× in 50 μl of ddH2O and left to dry overnight. Wells were then drop-wise coated with 10 μg ml−1 laminin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1–2 h at 37 °C. 50,000 neurons and 12,500 primary rat astrocytes were drop-wise plated in synaptic media (described above) containing ROCK inhibitor (Y-27632; Tocris, 1254) at 1 μM. Cells were left to attach for 1.5 h before media containing CultureOne Supplement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added for 3 days. Half-medium changes (without ROCK inhibitor or CultureOne) were thereafter performed every 2–3 days and HaloPROTAC-E 30–300 nM was added to cultures with each media change starting on DIV14 for early TDP-43 KD and at DIV33 for late TDP-43 KD. ASO treatment was performed every 2 weeks starting at DIV14, at a final concentration of 0.5 μM. MEA plates were recorded from every 2–3 days on the Maestro Pro (Axion Biosystems). Plates were left inside the Maestro Pro for 15 min preceding each recording to allow for acclimatization and recordings occurred immediately after and continued for 15 min. Data were processed using the Neural Metric Tool (Axion Biosystems). Active electrode criteria were set to five spikes per min. Single electrode burst parameters used an inter-spike interval threshold, consisting of a minimum of five spikes and a maximum inter-spike interval of 100 ms. Network bursts used envelope analysis, with a threshold factor of 1.25, minimum inter-burst interval of 100 ms, 35% minimum electrode and a burst exclusion of 75%. All synchrony metrics were measured with a synchrony window of 20 ms. Wells with fewer than three active electrodes were excluded from the analysis. For visualization of combined replicate time-course traces, data were normalized to the maximum mean of each control condition. All quantification was done using raw data and all log2[fold changes] shown were derived from raw data. Statistical analysis was performed on area under the curve values of each individual experiment. This was done for time-course data between day 28 and the last day of neuronal survival for early TDP-43 KD and UNC13A KD, between day 37 and the last day of survival for late TDP-43 KD phenotype recordings and between day 43 and last day of neuronal survival for late TDP-43 KD with ASO rescue experiments. The last day of neuronal survival was defined as the last day that every replicate plate had a viable set of recordings, regardless of whether individual plates lasted longer.

In a recent development, for whole-cell patch clamp recordings, 500,000 neurons were plated onto 18 mm no. 1 coverslips (Deckglaser) coated with 50 μg ml−1 PDL (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and mouse 10 μg ml−1 laminin (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Primary rat astrocytes were plated 1 week before and treated with CultureOne Supplement (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) 2 days before. mEPSCs were recorded at 4-weeks maturation on rat astrocytes, in extracellular solution containing: 136 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 1.3 mM MgCl2, 2 mM CaCl2, 10 mM glucose, pH 7.3, 300 mOsm l−1, supplemented with 1 μM tetrodotoxin (Tocris) and 10 μM gabazine (Tocris). Patching pipettes were filled with caesium methanosulfate-based internal solution: 135 mM CsMeSO3, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM Na2-phosphocreatine, 5 mM glutathione, 4 mM MgCl2, 4 mM Na2ATP, 0.4 mM NaGTP supplemented with 5 μM QX-314 (Tocris). Pipettes were pulled from borosilicate glass (outer diameter 1.5 mm, inner diameter 0.86 mm, Sutter Instruments) to a resistance of between 3 MΩ and 5 MΩ. Whole-cell patch clamp recordings were then made, without whole-cell compensation applied, for 5 min at the soma. Cells were held at −70 mV using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices) and the data were acquired using a Digidata 1440A digitizer (Molecular Devices). All recordings were carried out on a heated stage set to 37 °C. Data were acquired with Clampex software (Molecular Devices) and Axon Multiclamp Commander Software (Molecular Devices), data were sampled at a rate of 20 kHz and filtered at 10 kHz. mEPSCs were analysed in a fully automated manner using Clampfit v.10.7 software (Molecular Devices). Passive membrane properties were measured by applying a subthreshold voltage step and analysed using custom MATLAB scripts. Series resistance (Rs) was calculated as proportional to the current response amplitude, membrane capacitance (Cm) was estimated from the transient time constant by fitting the current transients to exponential functions and membrane resistance (Rm) was estimated from the steady-state response following the current transients. Passive membrane properties and series resistance were measured at the beginning and at the end of all recordings to ensure proper access (Rs < 30 MΩ) had been maintained.

It has been revealed that autaptic micro-islands were prepared according to a previously published protocol27. Briefly, 18 mm No.1 coverslips (Deckglaser) were etched in 1 M HCl for 2 h, neutralized in 1 M NaOH for 1 h then washed 3× in ddH2O, 1× in 70% ethanol and then stored in 100% ethanol. Coverslips were then briefly coated for 30 s with heated (55 °C) 0.0015% agarose type II-A and left to dry overnight. Microdots were then applied using a solution of 0.16 mg ml−1 PDL (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1.16 mg ml−1 rat tail collagen (BD Biosciences) and 5.6 mM acetic acid using a custom rubber stamp with a dot diameter of 250 μm (gift from M. Verhage). Around 10,000 primary rat astrocytes were plated in DMEM–F12 (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) with 10% ES-FBS (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1 week before plating 2,000 NGN2 forward-programmed iNeurons. Cultures were then matured in synaptic media (above) for 10 weeks before electrophysiology recordings, with HaloPROTAC and ASO treatments started at 2 weeks post-plating. Recordings were carried out in extracellular solution containing: 136 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 1.3 mM MgCl2, 2 mM CaCl2, 10 mM glucose, pH 7.3 (300 mOsm l−1) and intracellular solution containing 125 mM KMeSO4, 5 mM MgCl2, 10 mM EGTA, 10 mM HEPES, 0.5 mM NaGTP and 5 mM Na2ATP, pH 7.4 (290 mOsm l−1). Cells were recorded in voltage clamp and given an 80-mV stimulus for 1 ms and a paired-pulse interval of 100 ms. Passive membrane properties were measured before and after recordings to ensure proper access (Rs < 30 MΩ) had been maintained.

WT astrocyte micro-island cultures were prepared according to a published protocol70. Roughly 7 days after astrocyte preparation, 10,000 iMNs per well were plated to obtain a low-density culture. Cultures were kept at 37 °C and 5% CO2 until recordings were made at DIV60–70. Whole-cell voltage-clamp data were acquired using a HEKA EPC10 USB amplifier and the PATCHMASTER software (HEKA Elektronik, Harvard Bioscience). All recordings were performed using a standard external solution containing 140 mM NaCl, 2.4 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM glucose, 2 mM CaCl2 and 2 mM MgCl2 (320 mOsm l−1). The standard internal solution contained 136 mM KCl, 17.8 mM HEPES, 1 mM EGTA, 4.6 mM MgCl2, 4 mM NaATP, 0.3 mM Na2GTP, 15 mM creatine phosphate and 5 U ml−1 creatine phosphokinase (315–320 mOsm l−1), pH 7.4. eEPSCs were evoked by depolarizing the cell from −70 mV to 0 mV for a 1-ms duration. Basal eEPSCs were recorded at a frequency of 0.1 Hz and mEPSCs were recorded for 50 s. mEPSC traces were filtered at 1 kHz, and miniature events were identified using a sliding template function in Igor Pro (5–200 pA; rise time, 0.15–1.5 ms; half-width, 0.5–5 ms). Analyses were performed using custom-made Igor Pro macros (WaveMetrics). Data were obtained from three cultures. Recordings were made at room temperature (roughly 22 °C).

In a recent development, for live imaging, iNeurons were transfected with pAAV.CAG.iGluSnFR3.v857.PDGFR, a gift from K. Podgorski28 (Addgene plasmid no. 178333). Transfections were conducted after 3 weeks maturation on rat astrocytes using Lipofectamine LTX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Imaging was conducted when neurons reached 5–6 weeks’ maturation in extracellular solution containing: 136 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 1.3 mM MgCl2, 2 mM CaCl2, 10 mM glucose, pH 7.3, (290 mOsm l−1), supplemented with 10 μM NBQX, 25 μM AP-V and 10 μM gabazine (Tocris) to prevent recurrent activity. Neurons were transferred to a field stimulation chamber with parallel platinum electrodes (RC-49FS, Harvard Bioscience) and imaged on an inverted Olympus IX71 microscope equipped with a ×60/1.42 numerical aperture oil objective. Images were acquired with an ORCA-Flash4.0 V2 C11440-22CU scientific CMOS camera (Hamamatsu Photonics) cooled to roughly −20 °C with an Exos2 water cooling system (Koolance) and controlled using HCImageLive Software (Hamamatsu Photonics). The excitation light source was a 470 nm LED (CoolLED) set at 70% power, filtered with an excitation–emission filter set optimized for EGFP (49002 ET-EGFP, Chroma). Full frame images were acquired with 4 × 4 binning (pixel size 433 nm), frame bundling at 4 images and 10 ms exposure to achieve a frame rate of 100 Hz. Stimulation was delivered by an SD9 stimulator (Grass Technologies) using a pulse of 80 V for 1 ms to elicit a single action potential per pulse and consisted of 15 action potentials at 1 Hz in 3 separate images, which were combined during analysis. The triggering of LEDs, camera acquisition and stimulation were controlled externally through Clampex software (pCLAMP10, Molecular Devices) and a Master-8 programmable stimulator (A.M.P.I). The investigator was blinded to the treatment condition for iGluSNFR3 imaging.

iGluSNFR3 images were analysed using a custom-built MATLAB pipeline (https://github.com/f-hamidlab/iGluSNFR3/tree/publication_branch). Dendrites of iNeurons were first traced manually using the NeuronJ plugin71 for Fiji (ImageJ), converted to binary images and dilated twice. Binary masks were used to segment the region to be analysed using pixel-based analysis in the iGluSNFR3 pipeline. The gradient of the rising slope in the raw data trace was determined for each pixel and pixels with low signal-to-noise were removed. A sliding window was used to determine the baseline fluorescence (F0) for each pixel, pixels with high baseline drift were removed and ΔF/F0 was calculated. iGluSNFR3 events were detected using thresholds of three times the standard deviation of the baseline for both rising slope and peak ΔF/F0. Pixels with no events were removed resulting in punctate structures along the segmented dendrite that represented putative synapses. Pixels were then clustered into individual synaptic regions of interest (ROIs) both spatially (less than 5 pixels apart) and temporally (event peaks within 2 frames) and the number of evoked events per synapse was calculated by detecting peaks in the ΔF/F0 trace within a 150-ms time window after stimulation that were greater than 2.5 times the standard deviation of the baseline. Locations of synaptic ROIs were compared across the 3 images, and those within 5 pixels were considered to represent the same synapse. The overall release probability per synapse was calculated as the number of detected events divided by the number of stimulation trials (45).

Sources indicate that here 20,000 neurons were grown on PDL–laminin-coated coverslips. Neurons were fixed at DIV28 in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA), 4% sucrose for 15 min. Primary antibodies used were mouse anti-TDP-43 (Abcam ab104223, 1:1,000), chicken anti-MAP2 (Abcam ab5392, 1:10,000), rabbit anti-CTIP2 (Abcam, ab18465, 1:200), rabbit anti-NKX2.1 (Abcam, ab76013, 1:200), chicken anti-PAX6 (Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank University of Iowa, 1:200), mouse anti-NeuN (Merck, MAB377, 1:1,000) and guinea pig anti-B3-Tubulin (Cosmo Bio, MSFR105980, 1:1,000), and were diluted in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C. Secondary antibodies used were goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-11029), goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 555 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), goat anti-guinea pig IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific A-21450) and goat anti-chicken IgY (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-21449), and were diluted in PBS 1:1,000 and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Cells were washed 3× in PBS, labelled with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) (1:1,000) for 5 min at room temperature and mounted in ProLong Gold mounting medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Roughly 500,000 neurons were grown on 50,000 primary rat astrocytes on PDL–laminin-coated coverslips. Neurons were fixed at DIV28 in 4% PFA for 10 min. Cells were then permeabilized in 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min. Primary antibodies used were guinea pig anti-Munc13-1 (Synaptic Systems 126 104) and mouse anti-Synapsin1 (Synaptic Systems 106 011), and were diluted in PBS at 1:500 and 1:1,000, respectively, and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were washed 3× in PBS. Secondary antibodies used were goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific A-11029) and goat anti-guinea pig IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific A-21450), and were diluted in PBS 1:1,000 and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Cells were washed 3× in PBS and mounted in Mowiol-4-88 (PolySciences) mounting medium containing 1:1,000 DAPI (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were imaged using a Zeiss 980 Airyscan confocal microscope using a ×63 objective with a 3× crop. Z-stacks of 7× 0.5-μm intervals were taken of synapses along a single neurite. Fiji (ImageJ) was used to analyse mean UNC13A intensity on the basis of manually selected synapsin-positive ROIs. Four Synapsin1 positive ROIs per neurite were manually selected on the basis of prominent size and intensity, while being blinded to the UNC13A channel. Selected ROIs were then used to measure the integrated density (IntDen) of the UNC13A channel. Selection of comparable Synapsin1 ROIs was confirmed through a separate comparison of ROI size (Control 0.405 s.e. ± 0.01, HaloPROTAC 0.419 s.e. ± 0.03, P = 0.68).

Recent findings suggest that immunostainings were made in iMNs mass cultures at DIV66. The neurons were washed twice with PBS and fixed by adding 4% PFA for 30 min at room temperature. The PFA was removed and leftover was quenched by adding 50 mM cold glycine for 10 min, followed by washing the neurons twice with PBS. The cells were either stored in PBS at 4 °C or immediately used for immunostaining. The cell membrane was permeabilized with cold 0.25% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min and rinsed once in pure PBS. To block non-specific binding sites, the cells were incubated in cold 0.3% NGS in PBS for 20 min. Here, 500,000 iNeurons were grown on 50,000 primary rat astrocytes on PDL–laminin-coated coverslips. Neurons were transfected after 3 weeks maturation on rat astrocytes with CAG::tdTomato, using Lipofectamine LTX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer’s protocol. After 5 weeks of maturation, neurons were fixed in 4% PFA for 10 min. Cells were then permeabilized in 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min and incubated in blocking solution (2% bovine serum albumin in PBS) for 1 h. Primary antibodies: mouse anti-Synapsin1 (Synaptic Systems, 106 011), rabbit anti-Homer1 (Synaptic Systems, 160 002) were diluted in blocking solution at 1:1,000 and 1:500, respectively, and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Neurons were washed 3× in PBS. Secondary antibodies, goat anti-mouse IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 488 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-11029) and goat anti-rabbit IgG (H+L) Alexa Fluor 647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-21245) were diluted in blocking solution at 1:1,000 with FluoTag-X4 anti-RFP nanobody conjugated to ATTO565 (NanoTag Biotechnologies, N0404) at 1:500 and incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Sources indicate that neurons expressing tdTomato were imaged on a Nikon AXR confocal microscope equipped with a ×60/1.40 numerical aperture oil-immersion objective, controlled by NIS-Elements software (Nikon). Excitation lasers were 488 nm, 561 nm and 640 nm and the same gain and power settings were used across all conditions for each culture. Then 2,048 × 2,048 images (pixel size 0.111 µm) were taken as sequential linescans, generating a z-stack with steps of 0.3 µm to cover the depth of the tdTomato-positive neuron. For one culture, 1,024 × 1,024 images were taken (pixel size 0.222 µm). Several z-stacks were taken to cover the entire dendritic arbour of each cell. The investigator was blinded to the treatment condition for synapse density imaging. Images were then analysed in Fiji (ImageJ) using custom-written macros. First, maximum projections of the tdTomato channel were used to trace dendrites using the NeuronJ plugin. Binary traces were dilated three times to generate a dendritic mask. Maximum projection images of the Synapsin1 (presynaptic) staining were filtered with a top hat filter of radius of two and an automated threshold using the Moments algorithm was applied, followed by watershed processing to separate merged puncta. Particles of size 0.08–2.5 µm2 were analysed to generate presynaptic ROIs. Maximum projections of the Homer1 (postsynaptic) staining were filtered using a top hat filter of radius 1 and underwent automated thresholding using the Renyi Entropy algorithm, followed by watershed processing and analysis of particles of size 0.00–1.2 µm2 to identify postsynaptic ROIs. Postsynaptic ROIs were enlarged by 1 pixel and analysed for overlap with both the dendrite masks and presynaptic ROIs. Synapses on dendrites that consisted of both a presynaptic and postsynaptic partner were counted and divided by the total area of the dendrite mask to calculate the synapse density for each cell.

In a recent development, around 10,000 HaloTDP iNeurons were plated on 5,000 primary rat astrocytes in 96-well imaging phenoplates (Revvity) and matured in synaptic media (BrainPhys, StemCell Technologies), with 1× N2-Max Supplement (R&D Systems), 1× N21-Max Supplement (R&D Systems), 10 ng ml−1 NT3 (StemCell Technologies), 20 ng ml−1 GDNF and BDNF (Peprotech), 2.5% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1× Non-Essential Amino Acids (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 0.2 mg ml−1 cAMP (Sigma-Aldrich), 1× GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 200 nM ascorbic acid (Sigma-Aldrich)54. HaloPROTAC (30 nM) was added at DIV14. Plates were longitudinally imaged and neuronal cell bodies automatically quantified by means of phase-contrast detection using the Incucyte S3 imaging platform. Subsequently, plates were fixed with PFA at weekly timepoints and stained for NeuN and DAPI (as above). NeuN automated imaging was carried out on an Opera Phenix high-content screening system (Revvity) and NeuN/DAPI counts quantified using Harmony v.4.9 Software.

Mouse C57BL/6J embryonic stem cells (B6.N6) were transfected with a targeting vector, designed to replace mouse intron 20 with the orthologous human sequence using an 817-bp 5′ homology arm and a 1,462-bp 3′ homology arm. Two risk allele SNPs for ALS and frontotemporal dementia (rs12973192 (G) and rs12608932 (C)) were present within the human intron sequence used to replace the endogenous mouse intron. Two CRISPR–Cas9 site-specific nucleases targeting the boundaries of intron 20 (5′-GGAGCCAGCTGTATGCGTCT-3′ and 5′-GTACCAAGGAGACGTGGCAT-3′) were cotransfected as pX459 (Addgene no. 62988) vectors. Following transient selection in 1.8 μg ml−1 puromycin for 48 h, applied 24 h after transfection, clones were grown, isolated and screened for homologous recombination events using primers 5′-LR-FWD1–REV1 and 3′-LR-FWD1–REV1 to amplify over the 5′ and 3′ homology arms, respectively. qPCR assays were designed against the mouse and human intron 20 and used to verify the loss of the mouse intronic sequence and the gain of the human intronic sequence. Recombinant embryonic stem cells were microinjected into albino C57BL/6J blastocysts and the resulting chimeras were bred with C57BL/6J mice. The offspring were genotyped for the presence of the targeted allele.

Industry observers note that an aberrantly targeted line of mice was generated in which the homologous recombination event had occurred, but with a tandem duplication of the vector that led to a portion of the vector backbone being integrated within intron 23. Despite the tandem duplication, the human intron was correctly positioned within the context of the murine Unc13a gene, which was expressed and appropriately spliced. We refer to this mouse line as a human UNC13A reporter mouse and it was used in subsequent in vivo studies.

In a recent development, mice were injected with an recombinant AAV (rAAV) (PHP.eB) that expresses a synthetic microRNA targeting the mouse Tardbp gene (PackGene BioTech; gift from Trace Neuroscience) along with UNC13A ASO (M21-4) or vehicle at 8 weeks of age (P56-62). rAAV-Tardbp-microRNA was diluted in sterile PBS and administered as a 150-µl tail-vein injection. A total dose of 1.4 × 1012 vg was delivered per mouse. Mice were subsequently exposed to 5% isoflurane for anaesthetic induction, before reducing the concentration to 1.5–2% for maintenance purposes. Analgesia was provided with 5 mg kg−1 oral Metacam administered in a custard carrier 60 min before surgery, followed by subcutaneous injections of 10 mg kg−1 meloxicam and 0.1 mg kg−1 buprenorphine. A subcutaneous injection of 2 mg kg−1 bupivacaine was given as an incisional block shortly after anaesthetization. Intracerebroventricular injections of 10 µl of ASO (30 mg ml−1 in artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) (Harvard Apparatus, 59-7316) supplemented with extra Mg2+ to achieve a 3:1 Mg2+:ASO ratio) or vehicle (0 mg ml−1 in ACSF + Mg2+) were performed using a Hamilton syringe at a rate of 1 µl min−1. Injection coordinates were set at −0.35 mm y, +1 mm x, −1.75 mm z relative to the line of best-fit bregma and brain surface. The incision was subsequently sutured closed, and animals were returned to their home cages. Mice were closely monitored for 3 days post-surgery and provided with 5 mg kg−1 Metacam in custard carrier every 24 h postsurgery for the duration. Injections were performed blinded to treatment group. Mice of both sexes were included, with n = 9 (6 females, 3 males) for ASO and n = 7 (5 females, 2 males) for ACSF vehicle. Three weeks post-injection (P77-83), thoracic spinal cord was dissected and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Sample size for the in vivo mouse experiment was based on a pilot study showing a large effect of TDP-43 knockdown in one humanized UNC13A mouse. Subsequently, all animals that could be generated during the experimental period were used. When injections spanned many days, equal numbers of mice from each group were injected on each day. Injections were not randomized.

It has been revealed that spinal cord samples were immersed in 0.5 ml of ice-cold QIAzol Lysis Reagent (Qiagen, 79306) in 2-ml tubes (Fisher 15545809). Two 1.4-mm ceramic beads (Omni International 19-645) were added to each tube and samples were homogenized at 4 °C using a Precellys 24 touch homogenizer (Bertin Technologies) at 6,500 r.p.m. for 30 s on, then 120 s off, four times. Samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 12,000g at room temperature and supernatants were transferred (400 μl) to latest tubes. Chloroform (100 μl) was added to each sample and then samples were vigorously shaken for 15 s followed by incubation at room temperature for 3 min. Samples were centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min at 4 °C and then the upper aqueous phase was transferred to new tubes (200 µl). Then 70% ethanol (200 μl) was added and samples were mixed by vortexing. RNA was purified from samples using the RNeasy (Qiagen) kit including the on-column DNase (Qiagen) digestion step. RNA was eluted with water and quantified using a NanoDrop (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Reverse transcription was performed as described above using the RevertAid first-strand cDNA synthesis kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For RT–qPCR the following reagents were used: Mouse Tardbp (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Mm01257504_g1) and Mouse Hprt1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Mm03024075_m1), custom UNC13A cryptic exon assay. For RT–PCR, Mouse Unc13a exon 20 forward and Mouse Unc13a exon 21 reverse primer were used (Supplementary Table 4).

Datasets were assessed for normality. For normally distributed data, t-tests were used for statistical comparison of two groups. One-way ANOVA tests with post-hoc multiple pairwise comparison of means was used for statistical analysis of three or more groups. For non-normally distributed data, non-parametric tests were used. For MEA analysis, log2[fold change] is presented in figures as a matter of clarity, but all analyses were performed on raw data, or on fold changes derived from raw data for rescue experiments, using paired ratio t-tests. Statistical tests were carried out using GraphPad Prism (v.10.6.1; GraphPad Software) or with the R statistical library. Sample size and P values are specified in figure legends.

It has been revealed that statistical analyses of pooled datasets from several experiments (electrophysiology and synaptic imaging) were performed in R (v.4.4.1) using the lme4 (ref. 72) and lmerTest73 packages. Data were log1p-normalized before fitting a Gaussian linear mixed-effects model (LMM) by restricted maximum likelihood with experimental batch as a random intercept to account for between-batch variability. The intraclass correlation coefficient for batch ranged from 0 to 0.4451 across datasets. Inclusion of batch as a random intercept was confirmed by a likelihood ratio test. Normality of model residuals was assessed by Shapiro–Wilk test and Q–Q plot inspection; W statistics ranged from 0.85 to 0.99 across datasets. For datasets in which residuals showed greater deviation from normality (W < 0.90), results were confirmed separately using a Gamma generalized LMM with log link (glmmTMB74), which yielded consistent conclusions in all cases, supporting the robustness of the primary LMM analysis. For experiments designed a priori to test cryptic exon deletion or ASO rescue of the TDP-43-knockdown phenotype, TDP-43 KD was set as the reference condition, with all comparisons made directly against this baseline. P values were derived from Satterthwaite degree-of-freedom-corrected t-tests. For experiments without a priori comparisons, Tukey’s test for multiple comparisons was used.

All iPS cell experiments used the established human iPS cell line WTC11 (GM25256), obtained from the NIGMS Human Genetic Cell Repository at the Coriell Institute for Medical Research. The line was originally derived from de-identified adult dermal fibroblast with informed consent and approval from the University of California, San Francisco Institutional Review Board. No fresh human tissue was collected; therefore, this work did not constitute human subjects research and did not require further ethics committee approval at University College London, King’s College London or Leibniz-FMP-Berlin. All procedures complied with relevant institutional guidelines for the use of human cell lines.

WT astrocytes were obtained from Wistar rat embryos (Charles River Laboratories) as described above. Animals were housed in individually ventilated cages with a 12-h light–12-h dark cycle, with ad libitum access to food and water. Facilities were maintained at 20–24 °C and 55 ± 10% relative humidity. Ethical review and approval was not required for this part of the study because only Schedule 1 procedures performed by a competent individual were used, which are exempt under the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986.

In a recent development, a, Amplicon sequencing of PCR products from Fig. 1a indicates correct HaloTag editing of TARDBP. b, Manhattan plots of low pass whole genome sequencing results from parental and HaloTDP WTC11 iPSC lines indicate no large chromosomal rearrangements are present. c, PCR from genomic DNA at CRISPR–Cas12 off target loci (n = 1). d, IGV plot of sequencing results from PCR products in (c) indicates no edits are present at off-target sites. e, HaloTDP iNeurons were untreated (NT) or treated with the indicated concentration of HaloPROTAC for 4 days and processed for western blot analysis indicating a dose response curve of HaloPROTAC on TDP-43 knockdown. f, Quantification of western blots in (e) n = 3 biological replicates. g, HaloTDP iNeurons were untreated (NT) or treated with 30 nM HaloPROTAC for 3 h in the presence of DMSO, proteasome inhibitor MG132, or NEDD8 E1 inhibitor MLN4924 (n = 2). h, Immunofluorescence analysis of HaloTDP iNeurons at DIV28 with the indicated neuronal markers indicates neurons have a cortical (CTIP2 ISL1+) glutamatergic (NKX2.1−) deep layer (PAX6−) identity. i, RT-PCR analysis of WT and HaloTDP iNeurons demonstrates the HaloTag induces a mild loss of TDP-43 function and can induce cryptic exon inclusion in the indicated transcripts (n = 2). Graphs for (f) and (h) represent mean ± s.e.m. Uncropped gels are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4.

a, RT-qPCR analysis of correctly spliced UNC13A at exon 20–21 junction n = 10 biological replicates from 3 experiments. b-f, Analysis of control and CRISPRi-mediated TDP-43 knockdown in DIV 28 iNeurons. (b) RT-PCR analysis of UNC13A splicing at exon junction 20–21 reveals the inclusion of a long and short cryptic exon after TDP-43 KD. (c) Quantification of results in (b) n = 6 from 3 experiments. PSI (Percentage Spliced-In). (d) RT-qPCR analysis shows a reduction in correctly spliced UNC13A at exon 20–21 junction following TDP-43 KD n = 12 from 3 experiments. (e) Western blot analysis indicates a dramatic decrease in UNC13A protein after TDP-43 KD. (f) Quantification of results in (e) n = 7 from 3 experiments. g, RT-qPCR analysis of DIV38 HaloTDP iNeuron cultures indicates similar expression of glutamate receptors in untreated (NT) and TDP-43 knockdown conditions. A cryptic exon in CamK2B and cryptic polyadenylation in STMN2 result in reduction of mRNA transcripts. n = 8 from 2 experiments. h, Representative western blot analysis of control and CRISPRi-mediated UNC13A knockdown in iNeurons n = 3. Graphs in (a) (c) (d) (f) and (g) represent mean ± s.e.m. Statistics for (c) and (d), two-sided Student’s t-test. Statistics for (f), two-sided paired t-test on log-transformed, loading control normalized values. Statistics for (g), two-sided Student’s t-test with additional Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. * P < 0.05; ** P < 0.01; *** P < 0.001; **** P < 0.0001; ns (not significant). Uncropped gels are shown in Supplementary Fig. 5.

a, AMPAR blockade using CNQX abolishes mEPSC activity. b, mEPSC amplitude from control (n = 12) and UNC13A depleted (n = 13) iNeurons pooled from 3 experiments. c, mEPSC amplitude from control (n = 20) and TDP-43 knockdown (n = 22) HaloTDP iNeurons from 3 experiments. d, Quantification of passive membrane properties for UNC13A knockdown iNeurons. e, Quantification of passive membrane properties for TDP-43 knockdown iNeurons. f, Representative MEA raster plots following AMPAR blockade using CNQX. Quantification shows CNQX treatment at DIV41 abolishes network synchrony on multi-electrode array recordings, with minimal effects on firing rate. 30 s shown. g, Quantification of additional MEA metrics following CNQX treatment, UNC13A knockdown and TDP-43 knockdown. Each dot represents a well in the CNQX plot, while in TDP-43 and UNC13A plots, each dot represents the area under the curve for a separate experiment. h, Phase contrast images showing cell coverage on multi-electrode array plates. Tech Report: When did Scotland last beat Switzerland? Full head to head record and last five games

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scotland’s Nations League campaign wraps up on Monday evening with a tough encounter against Switzerland as the side aims to snatch an unlikely promotion playoff spot in Group B1 from Slovenia.
  • Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli finally got his first home win with a 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday, and now his team will look to make it back-to-back wins for the first time under his management while hoping Slovenia slip up in the group’s other game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scotland’s Nations League campaign wraps up on Monday evening with a tough encounter against Switzerland as the side aims to snatch an unlikely promotion playoff spot in Group B1 from Slovenia.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli finally got his first home win with a 2-1 win over North Macedonia on Friday, and now his team will look to make it back-to-back wins for the first time under his management while hoping Slovenia slip up in the group’s other game.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, should Scotland fail to win in St Gallen, hopes of promotion back to League A will be extinguished. A third-place finish will also have ramifications for the upcoming Euro 2028 qualifiers, which are drawn in Belfast this December.

In a recent development, but when did Scotland last beat Switzerland? What is their head-to-head record, and when did they last meet? Here’s everything you need to know about Scotland’s record against Switzerland.

The teams have faced each other a total of 18 times, and have met twice in major tournament finals, with both encounters taking place in the group stage of the European Championships.

It has been revealed that they last faced each other just last month in the Nations League, where Switzerland ran out 3-0 winners after Jack Hendry was sent off early on at Hampden Park. Prior to that game, they drew 1-1 at Euro 2024 in Germany, with Scott McTominay opening the scoring early on for Scotland, before Xherdan Shaqiri equalised shortly afterwards.

Recent findings suggest that from their 18 games played, Scotland have eight wins, giving them a 33.3% win percentage. Switzerland have won a total of six times - a 22.22 per cent win percentage. A further four games have ended in a draw.

It has been revealed that despite having the better head to head record against the Swiss, the Scotland men’s national team have not tasted victory against them for over 30 years. Their most recent win came at Euro 1996 at Villa Park, Birmingham on 18 June, where they earned their first win a 1-0 win in their final group game at the tournament.

It has been revealed that the victory came via a fine strike from Ally McCoist in the 36th minute, but was not enough for Scotland to qualify for the knockout stages of the tournament, with the Netherlands finishing above them on goal difference. The Switzerland side that day included future Celtic defender Ramon Vega.

Scotland line up that night: Andy Goram, Tom Boyd, Colin Calderwood, Colin Hendry, Stuart McCall, Gary McAllister, John Collins, Tosh McKinlay (Scott Booth, 60), Craig Burley, Gordon Durie and Ally McCoist (John Spencer, 84).

29 September 2026: Scotland 0-3 Switzerland (Nations League).

19 June 2024: Scotland 1-1 Switzerland (Euro 2024).

1 March 2006: Scotland 1-3 Switzerland (Friendly).

18 June 1996: Scotland 1-0 Switzerland (Euro 1996).

8 September 1993: Scotland 1-1 Switzerland (World Cup 1994 Qualifier).

Worthing Women: Make Mackay-ne a double!

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nicole Mackay’s brace made it three goals in two games for her and a second successive win for Worthing Women, as they saw off Aylesford at the Sussex Transport Community Stadium.
  • After last week’s epic cup comeback at Camden, teenage starlet Hattie Rainey made her full debut while Ruby Murdock also came into the starting eleven; meaning that Skye Birkinshaw and Cristie Pritchard began on the bench.
  • Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nicole Mackay’s brace made it three goals in two games for her and a second successive win for Worthing Women, as they saw off Aylesford at the Sussex Transport Community Stadium.

After last week’s epic cup comeback at Camden, teenage starlet Hattie Rainey made her full debut while Ruby Murdock also came into the starting eleven; meaning that Skye Birkinshaw and Cristie Pritchard began on the bench.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Barely had supporters sat in their seats than the aforementioned Mackay got the home team off and running, just three minutes in.

Seizing on  a loose ball on the edge of the eighteen yard area, the in-form striker drilled low and hard into Aylesford ‘keeper Sade Rider’s bottom right-hand corner, to open the scoring in emphatic fashion.

Although a very different picture might have been painted had the Rebels's netminder Sian Woods not denied a clean through Leigha Bradding-Butler not once but twice, to deny the visitor’s top scorer a seventh strike of a prolific campaign.

Still inside the opening ten minutes, Mackay came the width of the crossbar away from extending the host’s advantage. Dusting herself down and stepping up to take a free-kick she herself had won, the ball cannoned back off the frame of the goal, with Jess Richardson landing the rebound on top of the net.

The game settled into a more even contest for some time after that, as Worthing pressed forward in search of a second before the break, with Aylesford looking dangerous on the counter-attack.

Approaching the half-time interval, an audible sigh of relief reverberated around Woodside Road via Immy Armstrong - a threat from her set-pieces - firing narrowly over the target from inside the penalty area.

The sun then broke through the clouds on a pleasant November afternoon; similar to the way in which Aliyah Sheridan did when gifted possession by the homester’s otherwise solid last line of defence. Woods redeemed herself via a strong parry to her left of Sheridan’s subsequent shot.

One final opportunity before the change of ends fell to visiting Skipper Ami Burnham, only for Woods to keep her out by way of another excellent stop.

It’s tight at the bottom of the London & South East Prem but it was the Reds who headed into the interval with a precious one-goal lead.

Worthing continued to probe and were rewarded just shy of the hour mark, thanks to the persistence of Mackay. Although it was centre-half Ella Terry who got the ball rolling, courtesy of a wonderful switch of play from the middle of the park out to the roving Richardson on the right flank. The winger then found a well-placed Mackay to test Rider in the travellers’ net, with the Kent club’s custodian unable to prevent the Rebel’s number nineteen from overtaking Amber Hazlewood as leading markswoman in a red (occasionally lilac) shirt.

Some fine build-up laid the foundations for a possible third not long afterwards, when a Hattie Rainey pass went from a central position to wide on the right again, releasing the rapid Richardson to, ultimately, find Mackay once more, with the forward teeing up Neve McEvaddy for a long-range piledriver which saw Rider pull off a terrific save.

Goalscorer nearly turned provider three-quarters of the way into the contest but neither Richardson nor Annie Gracey could apply the finishing  touch to a dangerous-looking delivery.

Almost instantly, the visiting Blues hit back via a neat move of their own, culminating in half-time substitute Kara Richardson forcing Woods to hold on.

Ten to go and another excellent long ball from Terry resulted in some equally impressive hold-up play by the recently-introduced Paige Baker-Carroll, providing Richardson with an opening that she couldn’t quite keep down.

Not over the line yet though, the home side were reminded of the threat carried by Aylesford when Bradding-Bulter’s corner eventually led to Kara Richardson drawing a one-handed stop out of Woods, at the (in)expense of another flag-kick.

Time was running out for the girls from the Garden of England and Armstrong was quick to pounce on Pritchard's pass to fellow replacement Megan Gates; although the final flourish from twenty yards failed to test Woods between the home posts.

Fittingly, Worthing’s brightly-clad netminder had the last word on proceedings, as she added to her collection of wonder saves by frustrating Sheridan with only a few short minutes of normal time to play.

That would, indeed, be that and three vital points stayed at the Sussex Transport Community Stadium to move the Rebels up to ninth in the table, ahead of another tough test at bottom-of-the-table and fellow Sussex side Eastbourne Borough next Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Tuesday night YM enjoyed a crucial away win, moving them off the bottom of the table by beating Midhurst and Easebourne comfortably 3-1.

YM joint manager Will Hendon told the County Times before Saturday’s clash with Billingshurst: “We’re very much looking forward to it, hoping that Tuesday’s result will build some confidence.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"It takes time to create a completely fresh team, but the application from the players has been brilliant.”.

Having purchased their Gorings Mead ground, received planning permission for an all-weather pitch, and welcomed new sponsor HSM Global, the future is bright at YM, Hendon adding: “Very exciting times ahead – we’ve just got to keep pushing up the league now.”.

And, on Saturday, YM duly responded with their best performance of the season securing a timely win over Billingshurst, with the three points moving them up to 17th – one below Billingshurst.

YM starting threateningly with a free kick pushed away for a corner by Hurst keeper Fraser Trigwell. Four more corners followed – two apiece – but the first half finished goalless after YM’s Etienne Frimpong was hospitalised with a dislocated shoulder.

Restarting, YM came close when Will O’Brien’s cross was headed just over by sub Ryan Riddles, Ash Mutongerwa also being too aerial ahead of a pair of YM corners.

Hurst replied with YM indebted by skipper Rojo Grant’s clearance, but they were promptly rewarded by an outstanding goal from Callum Dowdell, before Tom Lyons scored direct from a corner six minutes later.

Although Hurst kept scrapping they were unable to get the ball in the net, Hendon saying: “We targeted six points from the Midhurst and Billingshurst games and we’re very pleased to have achieved that.

"We’ve now got two away fixtures followed by four at home and are looking to continue the momentum from the back-to-back wins.” On Saturday YM go to upper-table Lingfield, who beat them 3-1 in September, while Billingshurst have a tough assignment with a visit from high flying Hassocks.

Industry News: Sonia Bompastor's side show their teeth as Chelsea sink the reigning champions to reclaim top spot in WSL title race: Chelsea 1-0 Man City
