Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status1.
  • Medical diagnoses typically define disease on the basis of objective signs of organ dysfunction2 (see https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/diagnosis).
  • The absence of a clinically grounded definition has impeded recognition of obesity as a distinct disease, contributing to gaps in care, inconsistent prevention, misallocated resources and persistent stigma6,7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 2025, a Lancet Commission proposed distinguishing clinical obesity, defined by adiposity-related organ dysfunction, from preclinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity with preserved function, and recommended using anthropometric measures beyond body mass index (BMI) to confirm obesity status1. Here we report the comparative performance of this framework versus conventional BMI-based classification using prevalence, incidence and mortality data from 844,108 adults across four cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain. Complementing BMI with waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio data showed that BMI alone overestimated obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimated it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. The combined anthropometric definition increased overall obesity prevalence by 3.3–7.4% relative to BMI-based classification. Clinical obesity accounted for 22.7–31.3% of total obesity, with an overall population prevalence of 5.6–10.9%. A large proportion of individuals (between 77.4% and 91.3%) with preclinical obesity at baseline showed no progression to clinical obesity over 10 years. Increased mortality risk was associated with the combined anthropometric definition of obesity, but not with BMI-only obesity. Clinical obesity was associated with substantially higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.69, 95% confidence interval 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity conferred only modest risk (1.19, 1.14–1.24). These findings support the global adoption of the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework to improve obesity care and policy.

Medical diagnoses typically define disease on the basis of objective signs of organ dysfunction2 (see https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/diagnosis). By contrast, the health impact of obesity has historically been assessed using body mass index (BMI)—a proxy for body size—alongside obesity-related comorbidities3,4,5. This approach provides an aggregate measure of ill health rather than a disease-specific diagnosis.

The absence of a clinically grounded definition has impeded recognition of obesity as a distinct disease, contributing to gaps in care, inconsistent prevention, misallocated resources and persistent stigma6,7.

In a recent development, to address this, in 2025, a Lancet Commission from The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology proposed a new diagnostic framework that distinguishes between two categories of obesity: clinical obesity, defined by excess adiposity impairing organ function or daily activities; and preclinical obesity, characterized by increased adiposity and increased health risks but with preserved organ and whole-body function1. The framework also recommends supplementing BMI with other anthropometric measures, such as waist circumference (WC), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) or fat quantification with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, when available, to improve the detection of excess adiposity. Although consistent conceptually with diagnostic principles in medicine, the clinical implications of this framework remain uncertain. It is unknown how substantially the recommended use of additional anthropometric measures changes the classification of obesity compared with BMI alone, or whether the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity captures meaningfully different health states. The natural history of preclinical obesity is also poorly characterized, including the extent to which it remains stable or progresses to clinical obesity over time. More broadly, whether these classifications show consistent associations with prognosis across populations and healthcare settings has yet to be established. We examined these questions using data from 844,108 adults from four large cohorts in China, the UK, the USA and Spain, aiming to evaluate the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework in terms of obesity classification, the distribution and longitudinal course of clinical and preclinical obesity and their associations with mortality.

Sources indicate that to assess whether incorporating other anthropometric measures (WC and WHtR) improves obesity detection beyond the use of BMI alone, we analysed data from four cohorts: the Kailuan Study (China, n = 137,795), the UK Biobank (UKB, n = 436,203), the All of Us Research Program (AoU; USA, n = 218,841) and the SIDIAP database (Spain, n = 51,269). The characteristics of the study populations are shown in Supplementary Table 1, selection of study participants from each cohort is shown in Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and the details of study design of each cohort are presented in the Methods and Supplementary Methods. Following the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic criteria1, obesity confirmation required any of the following three components: (1) BMI ≥ 40.0 kg m−2; (2) BMI ≥ 30.0 kg m−2 (≥28.0 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals) plus elevated WC or elevated WHtR; or (3) BMI 25.0–29.9 kg m−2 (24.0–27.9 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals) plus both elevated WC and elevated WHtR. Elevated WC was defined as ≥102 cm for male and ≥88 cm for female individuals (≥90/85 cm (male/female) for Chinese individuals)8,9, and WHtR thresholds varied by ethnicity (non-Hispanic white: male/female ≥0.57/0.58; non-Hispanic Black: ≥0.55/0.57; Hispanic: ≥0.57/0.59; Asian: ≥0.56/0.59; others: ≥0.50)10.

It has been revealed that classification based on BMI alone resulted in both over- and under-identification of obesity across all four cohorts (Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1). The proportions classified as obese by BMI but without elevated WC or WHtR were 3.1% in the Kailuan Study, 1.9% in the UKB, 1.9% in the AoU and 1.2% in the SIDIAP, whereas 6.6%, 5.2%, 7.5% and 8.6%, respectively, of individuals with BMI-defined overweight met both WC and WHtR criteria for obesity-level adiposity. With the Lancet Commission’s recommended multi-criteria definition, hereafter referred to as the combined anthropometric definition of obesity (CAD-obesity), overall obesity prevalence increased from 17.8% to 21.3% in the Kailuan Study, 24.0% to 27.3% in the UKB, 42.5% to 48.1% in the AoU and 18.7% to 26.1% in the SIDIAP. Overall, CAD-obesity yielded a modest net increase in obesity prevalence of 3.5% in China, 3.3% in the UK, 5.6% in the USA and 7.4% in Spain.

Definitions of BMI-based obesity, WC-based obesity, WHtR-based obesity and CAD-obesity are provided in the Methods. The analyses included 137,795 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants from the All of Us (AoU) Research Program and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Prevalence estimates are presented as percentages. a, Prevalence of obesity defined separately by BMI, WC and WHtR. b, Reclassification of obesity status across BMI-defined categories after applying CAD-obesity criteria. Colours indicate the corresponding reclassification categories as defined in the figure.

Clinical obesity was defined as CAD-obesity accompanied by at least one of the 18 adult diagnostic criteria specified by the Lancet Commission. These criteria represent obesity-related organ dysfunction or functional impairment across several systems, including cardiovascular (for example, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, thromboembolic disease and hypertension), respiratory (obstructive sleep apnoea and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), metabolic (combined dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia), hepatic (MASLD with fibrosis), renal (chronic kidney disease), neurological (intracranial hypertension), musculoskeletal (hip or knee osteoarthritis), reproductive (infertility), urological (urinary incontinence) and lymphatic dysfunctions, together with limitations in daily activities. Criteria for clinical obesity were operationalized using predefined clinical, laboratory, imaging or diagnostic criteria adapted to the variables available in each cohort. Detailed definitions and cohort-specific assessment methods are provided in the Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 2.

However, not all organ dysfunction that coexists with CAD-obesity can be assumed to be attributable to obesity. We therefore applied an attributable fraction (AF) approach to provide a population-level estimate of attribution and to adjust subsequent estimates accordingly11. The AF was calculated as: \({\rm{AF}}=\frac{{\rm{HR}}-1}{{\rm{HR}}}\), where HR denotes the hazard ratio for the association between CAD-obesity and risk of incident organ dysfunction with adjustment for relevant confounders using Cox proportional hazards models. The cohort-specific HRs used to derive the AF estimates were 1.62 (95% confidence interval (CI), 1.58–1.66) in the Kailuan Study, 1.68 (1.64–1.72) in the UKB, 1.67 (1.61–1.73) in the AoU and 2.07 (1.97–2.18) in the SIDIAP (Extended Data Table 2), corresponding to AF values of 0.383, 0.405, 0.401 and 0.517, respectively.

Sources indicate that because the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity depends on the presence of organ dysfunction among individuals with CAD-obesity, we first quantified the observed crude prevalence of organ dysfunction and then applied the cohort-specific AF estimates to account for the proportion plausibly attributable to obesity at the population level. The crude prevalence of organ dysfunction among people with CAD-obesity ranged from 56.7% in the AoU to 75.3% in the UKB (Fig. 2; Extended Data Table 3). AF-adjusted clinical obesity accounted for 26.3% (95% CI: 25.2–27.3) of total obesity in the Kailuan Study, 30.5% (29.4–31.6) in the UKB, 22.7% (21.5–24.0) in the AoU, and 31.3% (30.9–31.8) in the SIDIAP (Fig. 2; Extended Data Table 3). Accordingly, the proportion of individuals with CAD-obesity but without any detectable organ dysfunction—representing the minimum estimate of preclinical obesity—ranged from 24.7% in the UKB to 43.3% in the AoU, and the maximum estimate of preclinical obesity (1 minus the AF-adjusted prevalence of clinical obesity) ranged from 68.7% in the SIDIAP to 77.3% in the AoU (Extended Data Table 3).

It has been revealed that definitions of CAD-obesity, preclinical obesity and clinical obesity are provided in the Methods. The analyses included 137,795 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants from the All of Us Research Program and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Grey segments represent individuals without CAD-obesity. Orange segments represent the estimated AF-adjusted prevalence component of clinical obesity, corresponding to CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction statistically attributable to CAD-obesity at the population level. Green segments represent individuals with CAD-obesity but without evidence of organ dysfunction. Segments with a colour gradient represent the estimated non-attributable prevalence component among participants with CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction after application of the AF adjustment. Together, the green and gradient segments represent the estimated AF-adjusted prevalence of preclinical obesity.

Industry observers note that the overall prevalence of AF-adjusted clinical obesity in the full population was 5.6% (95% CI: 5.4–5.8) in the Kailuan Study, 8.3% (8.0–8.6) in the UKB, 10.9% (10.4–11.5) in the AoU and 8.2% (8.1–8.3) in the SIDIAP (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 3).

Recent findings suggest that sensitivity analyses restricting to the nine organ dysfunction indicators available across all datasets yielded results that were highly consistent with the primary analyses. Prevalence estimates changed minimally under the restricted definition, indicating that additional cohort-specific indicators contributed little to classification (Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Indicators that were not universally available were individually rare, and most participants presenting them also had at least one of the nine common indicators, supporting the robustness and comparability of the classification across cohorts (Supplementary Table 5).

To assess the progression from preclinical to clinical obesity, we performed an analysis among individuals with CAD-obesity but without any organ dysfunction at baseline. The AF-adjusted 10-year incidence of clinical obesity was 21.2% in the Kailuan Study, 8.7% in the UKB and 22.6% in the SIDIAP; because of a shorter follow-up in the AoU cohort, only an AF-adjusted 4-year incidence was calculated and an incidence of 8.5% was found (Fig. 3). Thus, approximately 70–90% of individuals with preclinical obesity remained stable over a decade. The incidence rates were similar between male and female individuals (Supplementary Fig. 5), and sensitivity analysis restricting to the nine organ dysfunction indicators yielded similar results (Kailuan Study: 21.4%; UK Biobank: 8.8%).

In a recent development, the analyses included 8,009 participants from the Kailuan Study, 29,338 participants from the UK Biobank, 54,535 participants from the All of Us Research Program and 5,273 participants from the SIDIAP database, all of whom had preclinical obesity at baseline. Solid lines represent the estimated cumulative incidence of clinical obesity, calculated by applying AF-based estimates to the observed incidence of organ dysfunction among individuals with preclinical obesity. Dashed lines represent the observed cumulative incidence of incident organ dysfunction. Shaded areas represent the corresponding 95% CIs. Cumulative incidence curves were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods and were generated from baseline until incident organ dysfunction, death or the end of follow-up, whichever occurred first. AF estimates were calculated from HRs derived using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for cohort-specific covariates, as described in the Supplementary Methods.

Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations of BMI-based obesity and CAD-obesity with all-cause mortality, adjusting for sociodemographic covariates. The AoU cohort was excluded because of limited follow-up. Median follow-up was 15.3 years in the Kailuan Study (17,642 deaths), 13.8 years in the UKB (31,812 deaths) and 11.2 years in the SIDIAP (2,338 deaths).

Compared with individuals with no overweight or obesity, participants with BMI-defined overweight or obesity but without CAD-obesity had a lower all-cause mortality risk (pooled HR 0.88 [95% CI: 0.86–0.90] and 0.93 [0.86–0.99], respectively). By contrast, individuals with CAD-obesity, regardless of whether their BMI was in the overweight or obese range, had a significantly higher, albeit modest, mortality risk (pooled HR 1.06 [1.03–1.10] and 1.07 [1.05–1.10], respectively; Fig. 4a and Extended Data Table 4).

It has been revealed that the analyses included 137,792 participants from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants from the UK Biobank and 51,269 participants from the SIDIAP database. Each panel presents Kaplan–Meier survival curves and adjusted HRs with 95% CIs for all-cause mortality, with cohort-specific survival curves shown on the left and pooled HR estimates from Cox proportional hazards models shown on the right. Solid lines in Kaplan–Meier plots represent survival probability estimates for each obesity classification group, with colours indicating the categories defined in each panel. Shaded areas around survival curves indicate 95% CIs. In forest plots, points represent HR point estimates and horizontal lines represent corresponding 95% CIs. The x axes of the forest plots are presented on a logarithmic scale. Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for cohort-specific covariates as specified in the Supplementary Methods, and pooled HR estimates were obtained using fixed-effects models. All statistical tests were two-sided, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed. a, Mortality risk according to BMI-based overweight or obesity and CAD-obesity status. Colours indicate BMI-based categories combined with CAD-obesity status: no overweight or obesity; overweight BMI without CAD-obesity; BMI-based obesity without CAD-obesity; overweight BMI with CAD-obesity; and BMI-based obesity with CAD-obesity. b, Mortality risk according to obesity stage defined by CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction, including preclinical and clinical obesity. Colours indicate four groups: no CAD-obesity and no organ dysfunction; no CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction; CAD-obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); and CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity).

Further cause-specific mortality analyses were done in the UK Biobank (the only cohort with available cause-specific mortality data), including cardiovascular mortality, obesity-related cancer mortality and their combination (Supplementary Table 6). After multivariable adjustment, BMI-defined overweight or obesity without CAD-obesity was not associated with increased risks of these cause-specific mortality outcomes. By contrast, CAD-obesity was associated with higher risks, including among individuals in the BMI-defined overweight range.

In further sensitivity analyses, exclusion of deaths occurring within the first 5 years of follow-up did not materially alter the associations, arguing against reverse causation as a major explanation for the findings (Supplementary Table 7). The proportion of missingness was low across all cohorts, with no variable exceeding 20% (Supplementary Table 8), and a sensitivity analysis restricted to participants without missing variables also yielded robust results (Supplementary Table 9). Stratified analyses by smoking status confirmed that smoking was a strong effect modifier; however, among never-smokers, CAD-obesity remained consistently associated with higher mortality risk, whereas BMI-defined overweight and obesity in the absence of CAD-obesity showed no or modest mortality risk after multivariable adjustment (Supplementary Table 10).

We evaluated the association between clinical obesity and mortality risk. Participants were first categorized into four baseline groups: (1) no CAD-obesity and no organ dysfunction (reference group); (2) no CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction; (3) CAD-obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); and (4) CAD-obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity). Clinical obesity was associated with a substantially higher mortality risk (pooled HR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.64–1.73), whereas preclinical obesity showed a modest association (pooled HR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.14–1.24; Fig. 4b and Extended Data Table 5). Cohort-specific estimates were directionally consistent.

Sources indicate that sensitivity analyses by excluding deaths occurring within the first 2 or 5 years of follow-up or by incorporating waist-to-hip ratio into the diagnostic indicators did not materially alter the associations (Extended Data Table 6). The association between clinical obesity and mortality was stronger in female individuals and in those aged younger than 60 years (P < 0.001 for interactions; Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 11). In the age-stratified analysis, sensitivity analyses by further excluding deaths occurring within the first 5 years or restricting participants without missing variables yielded similar results to those of the primary analysis (Supplementary Tables 12 and 13), providing further reassurance against reverse causation and selection biases.

To disentangle the relative contributions of BMI-defined obesity, CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction to mortality risk, participants were further classified into eight groups according to the presence or absence of each component. In groups defined by organ dysfunction and CAD-obesity, BMI-defined obesity conferred little additional risk, when compared with the BMI-defined non-obese status. On the other hand, CAD-obesity highlighted a consistently higher mortality risk, and the highest mortality risks were observed among participants with both CAD-obesity and organ dysfunction (that is, clinical obesity) (Extended Data Table 7).

Separate cause-specific mortality analyses of clinical and preclinical obesity in the UK Biobank dataset revealed that clinical obesity was consistently associated with substantially higher risks, with effect sizes generally stronger than those observed for all-cause mortality, whereas preclinical obesity showed elevated but consistently lower risks (Supplementary Table 14).

We performed further complementary analyses to examine the appropriateness of the ethnicity-specific WHtR thresholds used to confirm obesity status. First, the relationship between BMI and WHtR was broadly consistent across cohorts (Pearson r ≥ 0.64; Extended Data Fig. 2). On the basis of fitted linear regression models, the conventional WHtR cut-off of 0.50 corresponded approximately to the BMI-defined overweight threshold, whereas WHtR values corresponding to the BMI-defined obesity threshold were generally higher than 0.55 (from 0.55 to 0.60 across the four cohorts).

Mortality analyses showed a similar pattern. Restricted cubic spline models indicated that mortality risk began to increase at WHtR values around 0.55 (Extended Data Fig. 3). Consistently, participants with a WHtR between 0.50 and the ethnicity-specific thresholds had no excess mortality risk (pooled HR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.97–1.02), whereas those with a WHtR above the ethnicity-specific threshold had a higher risk (pooled HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.18–1.24; Supplementary Table 15).

In a recent development, using 0.50 instead of the ethnicity-specific thresholds substantially increased the proportion of participants defined as having obesity by meeting the WHtR criterion across all four cohorts (Kailuan, 59.2% versus 18.3%; UKB, 66.7% versus 27.2%; AoU, 74.3% versus 48.8%; SIDIAP, 71.1% versus 33.3%). When these thresholds were incorporated into the definition of confirmed obesity, the same risk pattern was observed: participants classified only by the 0.50 threshold highlighted no excess mortality (pooled HR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.96–1.03), whereas those meeting the ethnicity-specific thresholds had a higher mortality risk (pooled HR, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.18–1.22; Supplementary Table 16).

To our knowledge, this is the first large-scale, multinational study to comprehensively evaluate the Lancet Commission diagnostic framework1 against the widely used BMI-based classification. Previous studies have examined individual components of the framework—such as expanded anthropometric criteria or prevalence estimates of clinical obesity—but have lacked integrated assessment or longitudinal follow-up12,13,14,15,16. This study evaluated several interrelated elements of the new diagnostic framework: the implications of using combined anthropometric criteria to confirm obesity; their effects on prevalence and risk stratification compared with BMI alone; the importance of selecting appropriate anthropometric cut-offs; and the prognostic implications of distinguishing clinical from preclinical obesity.

Industry observers note that with regard to anthropometric classification, our findings show that BMI alone both over- and under-identifies obesity and does not reliably distinguish individuals who have an increased mortality risk. These results support the Commission framework’s use of complementary anthropometric measures alongside BMI to improve obesity classification and risk stratification. Although WC and WHtR are, like BMI, indirect measures of adiposity, increased values for these measures are (for anatomical and physiological reasons) more likely to reflect fat-mass expansion, whereas a higher BMI might also reflect greater lean mass. Their correlation with direct body-composition measurements10 supports their use as a pragmatic means of detecting excess adiposity where direct measurement is impractical. Future studies should determine whether direct measurement of fat adds meaningful precision and could ultimately replace combined anthropometry if reliable bedside technologies become widely available.

According to recent reports, we observed substantial discordance between BMI-based classification and CAD-obesity, with BMI overestimating obesity in 1.2–3.1% and underestimating it in 5.2–8.6% of participants across cohorts. When considered against national obesity estimates from the 2025 World Obesity Atlas17, these proportions suggest that BMI misclassification affects tens of millions of individuals in countries with large populations, underscoring the potential public-health implications of seemingly modest differences in classification.

Industry observers note that however, the effects of using a combined anthropometric definition of obesity depend, crucially, on how the Commission’s recommendations are operationalized. Unlike our findings, previous studies in US cohorts reported that applying the Lancet Commission framework substantially increased overall obesity prevalence12,13,14,15,16. These discrepancies mainly reflect methodological differences, particularly the choice of anthropometric cut-offs and incomplete adherence to the framework’s recommendations. In one study14, higher prevalence estimates were driven by the use of a single low WHtR cut-off of 0.50 across populations, potentially classifying individuals with milder increases in adiposity and associated risk as having obesity. Another study16 reported an overall obesity prevalence of 60% in the AoU cohort, compared with 48.1% in our analysis. In addition to using a single WHtR cut-off of 0.50, the study applied the cut-off across the full BMI range, including individuals with a normal BMI. This approach diverges from the Commission’s recommendation that anthropometric confirmation be used mainly in individuals with BMI values below—but near —the BMI obesity threshold1. Applying anthropometric criteria outside this context risks classifying individuals with normal body weight and localized abdominal adiposity—such as those with lipodystrophy or related conditions, which are biologically and clinically distinct—as having obesity. For this reason, the Commission retained BMI as the initial screening tool1, and we limited the assessment of obesity to participants within the conventional BMI-defined overweight and obesity ranges.

It has been revealed that in closer alignment with the Commission’s guidance, we applied obesity-level, ethnicity-specific thresholds for WC and WHtR. In our data, the conventional WHtR cut-off of 0.50 corresponded approximately to the BMI-defined overweight threshold, whereas WHtR values corresponding to the BMI-defined obesity threshold and increasing mortality risk were generally observed around or above 0.55. This convergence between anthropometric and mortality analyses supports the use of higher WHtR thresholds for obesity classification and is consistent with the previously proposed cut-off of 0.55–0.59 (ref. 10). Further prospective evaluation will be required to refine population-specific thresholds.

The application of obesity-level thresholds for WC and WHtR further illustrates the limitations of BMI-based classification. Although these measures remain indirect proxies of body fat, the reclassified groups had distinct mortality profiles, showing that conventional BMI categories encompass individuals with heterogeneous risk and that additional measures provide clinically relevant stratification beyond BMI alone. This is particularly consequential for the overweight category. The Lancet Commission framework intentionally does not retain overweight as a separate intermediate-risk category; instead, it extends the definition of obesity to individuals with a BMI classified as overweight who meet additional anthropometric criteria indicating obesity-level adiposity. Our data support this approach: individuals with a BMI in the overweight range who met CAD-obesity criteria had a mortality risk comparable with that of individuals with a BMI in the obesity range who also met CAD-obesity criteria. By contrast, those with a BMI classified as overweight who did not meet CAD-obesity criteria had no excess risk and, in several analyses, had a lower risk than did individuals with a normal BMI. The CAD-obesity criteria therefore identify adiposity-related risk that would otherwise remain obscured within the conventional overweight range.

According to recent reports, the implications are substantial. An estimated 1.5 billion adults worldwide are classified as overweight by BMI17, yet our findings indicate that individuals in this population should not all be regarded as being at increased risk. Our data suggest that combining BMI with WC and appropriately calibrated WHtR cut-offs, such as those evaluated here, can identify higher-risk individuals without substantially increasing overall obesity prevalence. This selective reclassification provides a clinically meaningful basis to inform individual care, health policy and resource allocation.

Anthropometric confirmation improves the identification of mortality risk associated with excess adiposity. However, because clinical obesity denotes an active disease state, its diagnosis requires a further step: establishing the presence of organ dysfunction that can plausibly be attributed to that adiposity. This requirement reflects a fundamental principle of disease definition: because similar alterations in organ function can arise from different disease processes, causality cannot be inferred from coexistence alone. For example, not all joint inflammation is caused by rheumatoid arthritis, nor is all heart failure attributable to the same underlying heart disease. In clinical practice, differential diagnosis addresses this uncertainty by considering alternative causes and, where possible, excluding them; it is therefore essential to diagnostic specificity. For this reason, organ dysfunction coexisting with obesity cannot automatically be considered obesity-related; doing so could overattribute dysfunction to obesity and substantially inflate estimates of clinical-obesity prevalence and incidence. Most previous applications of the framework classified all coexisting organ dysfunction as obesity-related without accounting for alternative causes13,14,15,16, and might therefore have overestimated the prevalence of clinical obesity.

In a recent development, to mitigate this problem, we applied the AF method at the population level to estimate the proportion of organ dysfunction that is statistically attributable to CAD-obesity, and adjusted the prevalence and incidence estimates accordingly. Although this adjustment cannot establish causality in individual participants, it mitigates the risk of attributing organ dysfunction to obesity when other causes could be responsible, thereby reducing systematic overattribution and improving population-level estimates of the prevalence and incidence of clinical obesity. Notably, an earlier US study12 using a different adjustment approach estimated the clinical-obesity prevalence as 9.7%, close to the 10.9% that was observed in the AoU cohort after AF adjustment. This concordance between studies using different population-level methods to account for plausible attribution provides some reassurance about the robustness of our estimates.

In a recent development, our longitudinal and mortality analyses provide evidence supporting the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity. Despite variation across cohorts, 70–90% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over 10 years. Clinical obesity was also associated with substantially higher all-cause and obesity-related mortality, whereas preclinical obesity showed only a modest excess mortality risk. The observed patterns of progression and differences in mortality risk show that these health states differ not only in their defining clinical characteristics but also in their prognostic implications. The distinct clinical and prognostic profiles of clinical and preclinical obesity provide a foundation for personalized, proportionate care. Preclinical obesity warrants a mostly preventive approach aimed at reducing future risk, with the nature and intensity of intervention guided by the individual’s risk of progression and the presence of relevant comorbidities. By contrast, established functional impairment and higher mortality risk in clinical obesity justify greater urgency and, where appropriate, more intensive treatment and prioritized access. The distinction can therefore guide the purpose, timing and intensity of individual care and support evidence-based decisions on treatment prioritization, coverage and resource allocation.

It has been revealed that notably, using this distinction to guide proportionate care does not imply withholding treatment from people with preclinical obesity. One criticism of the Lancet Commission framework is that distinguishing preclinical from clinical obesity could encourage ‘watchful waiting’ or restrict access to treatment18,19,20. However, this concern seems to conflate diagnostic classification with treatment eligibility. Like any diagnosis, the distinction between clinical and preclinical obesity provides a snapshot of an individual’s current health status; it does not prescribe inaction or determine eligibility for treatment by itself. Analogous distinctions—such as those between prediabetes and diabetes or adenomatous polyps and carcinoma—guide the purpose, urgency and intensity of intervention without precluding care for prediabetes or adenomatous polyps21. Accordingly, preclinical obesity might warrant active preventive treatment, including lifestyle, pharmacological or, in selected cases, surgical interventions, depending on progression risk and comorbidities that could benefit from weight reduction. Treatment decisions should therefore be informed by diagnosis but not reduced to diagnostic category alone.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The retrospective design of our study and its reliance on electronic health record (EHR) data could limit diagnostic precision and introduce inter-cohort variability. Organ dysfunction was identified using administrative codes rather than standardized clinical assessments, and not all 18 dysfunction indicators were available in every cohort, potentially leading to the underestimation or misclassification of specific organ disease subtypes. This limitation is highlighted by the Kailuan cohort, in which the higher observed incidence of clinical obesity might reflect more frequent (biennial) clinical evaluations. However, sensitivity analyses showed that the additional indicators contributed minimally to classification, supporting the conclusion that differences in the number of available organ-dysfunction indicators are unlikely to be a major driver of the inter-cohort variability observed in the primary analyses. Finally, the AF method cannot determine attribution at the individual level, and future prospective studies using clinically adjudicated diagnoses of clinical and preclinical obesity will be essential to refine estimates of disease burden and progression. Nonetheless, the consistency of findings across geographically and demographically diverse cohorts strengthens the robustness, generalizability and clinical relevance of the proposed diagnostic framework.

Industry observers note that in summary, BMI alone misclassifies obesity in a substantial proportion of individuals, both overestimating and underestimating the clinical relevance of excess adiposity, and does not meaningfully discriminate higher mortality risk. Integrating other anthropometric measures (such as WHtR and WC) and clinical criteria reflecting organ function into a multi-criteria framework improves obesity detection and aligns diagnosis more closely with true disease status. Clinical and preclinical obesity represent distinct and prevalent subgroups, with markedly different mortality risks. This study demonstrates the clinical utility and prognostic importance of distinguishing between clinical and preclinical obesity, and supports the global applicability of this classification scheme for guiding care and informing health policy.

Recent findings suggest that this population-based multinational study analysed data from four large and well-characterized adult cohorts: the Kailuan Study (China), the UK Biobank (UKB; UK), the All of Us Research Program (AoU; USA), and the Information System for the Development of Research in Primary Care (SIDIAP, Spain). The Kailuan Study is an ongoing prospective cohort initiated between 2006 and 2007 among more than 100,000 employees of the Kailuan Group, with biennial follow-up examinations thereafter22. The UK Biobank enrolled around 500,000 individuals aged 37–73 years from 2006 to 2010 with questionnaires, physical examinations and biomarker assessments23. The All of Us Research Program is a US precision-medicine initiative aimed at building a diverse biomedical database to study the biological, clinical, social and environmental determinants of health24. The SIDIAP database includes pseudonymized EHRs from more than eight million individuals in Catalonia since 2006, with approximately 75% of the regional population represented25.

Recent findings suggest that the Kailuan Study was approved by the ethics committee of the Kailuan Medical Group. The UK Biobank received ethical approval from the North West Multi-Centre Research Ethics Committee. The All of Us Research Program is overseen by the All of Us institutional review board. The SIDIAP analysis was approved by the IDIAP Jordi Gol ethics committee (20/204-P). All studies followed the Declaration of Helsinki, and all participants gave their written informed consent. No additional ethical approval was required for the current study because no new data were collected and all analyses were performed using previously collected data.

Industry observers note that participants aged 18–74 years who were free from stroke, myocardial infarction and cancer at baseline and for whom anthropometric (BMI, WC and WHtR) and organ-dysfunction data were available were included. The final numbers included in the prevalence estimates were 137,795 from the Kailuan Study, 436,203 from the UKB, 218,841 from the AoU and 51,269 from the SIDIAP. The progression from preclinical obesity to clinical obesity was estimated among those with CAD-confirmed obesity but without any organ dysfunction, and the sample size was 8,009, 29,338, 54,535 and 5,273, respectively. For the mortality analysis, the AoU study was excluded owing to its relatively short follow-up duration; for the other three cohorts, the sample size was generally the same as that in the prevalence analysis, except for the Kailuan Study, in which three participants without valid mortality data were further excluded. Details of the study design for each cohort can be found in the Supplementary Methods, and the selection of study participants is in Supplementary Figs. 1–4.

Following criteria from the Lancet Commission1, clinical obesity was defined as excess adiposity plus at least one sign of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. Preclinical obesity was defined as excess adiposity without such dysfunction.

It has been revealed that excess adiposity was defined by any of the following criteria, to be consistent with the proposed framework: (1) BMI ≥ 40 kg m−2; (2) BMI ≥ 30 kg m−2 (≥28 for Chinese individuals) plus elevated WC or WHtR; or (3) BMI 25–30 kg m−2 (24–28 for Chinese individuals) plus both elevated WC and WHtR. The thresholds for population-specific WC-defined adiposity are ≥102 cm for male and ≥88 cm for female individuals in the Western population, and ≥90 cm for male and ≥85 cm for female individuals in the Chinese population8,9. The thresholds for race- and sex-specific WHtR-defined adiposity are 0.57 (male) and 0.58 (female) for non-Hispanic white individuals; 0.55 (male) and 0.57 (female) for non-Hispanic Black individuals; 0.57 (male) and 0.59 (female) for Hispanic individuals; 0.56 (male) and 0.59 (female) for Asian individuals; and 0.50 for others10. To illustrate that the commonly used WHtR cut-off of 0.50 (ref. 26) is not an appropriate measure for central obesity, the bivariate scatter plots between BMI and WHtR were generated with fitted linear regression lines. The optimal cut-off values for WHtR that correspond to established BMI thresholds of obesity (28 kg m−2 for Chinese individuals and 30 for others) were derived from the linear regression lines given the very high Pearson correlation coefficients in the four cohorts (r ≥ 0.64).

Sources indicate that organ dysfunction was defined as the presence of at least one of 18 clinical indicators listed in the Commission report. Notably, in line with the Commission’s recommendations, the metabolic cluster criterion for clinical obesity (hyperglycaemia together with low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and high triglycerides) was considered to be met only when diabetes and dyslipidaemia occurred together, and not when either condition occurred alone. Data availability about organ dysfunction ranged from 9 (SIDIAP) to 18 (UKB) indicators. Case ascertainment was based on medical records, self-reports and health assessments (Supplementary Table 2).

Socio-demographic and lifestyle data were collected for each cohort; details can be found in the Supplementary Methods.

Organ dysfunction and death events were identified through self-reports, clinical exams, medical records and provincial death certificates in the Kailuan Study. In the UKB, events were ascertained through linkages with hospital records and death registries. Incident organ dysfunctions were obtained through EHRs in the AoU study, with measurements recorded at different time points and clinic visits. Outcomes in the SIDIAP were identified through linkage to primary care and hospital EHRs.

Industry observers note that given the challenges in establishing causality between obesity and coexisting organ dysfunction at the individual level, we applied the AF approach at the population level to quantify the proportion of organ dysfunction cases attributable to obesity among individuals with obesity11. The AF was calculated as: \({\rm{AF}}=\frac{{\rm{HR}}-1}{{\rm{HR}}}\), where HR denotes the hazard ratio for the association between obesity and risk of incident organ dysfunction with adjustment for relevant confounders using Cox proportional hazards models. Details are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Descriptive statistics were reported as mean (s.d.), median (interquartile range) or percentages, as appropriate. Multiple imputations using chained equations (linear and logistic regression) were used to impute the missing data (mice package in R, v.3.19.0). Prevalence estimates and 95% CIs were calculated using the epi.conf function from the epiR package in R (v.2.0.95). To quantify the misclassification of obesity by BMI alone, we estimated the prevalence of abdominal obesity (based on WC and/or WHtR) in each BMI category. We further estimated the prevalence of clinical obesity among people with obesity, as well as among the total population, with adjustment using the AF method. The AF-adjusted prevalence of clinical obesity was estimated by multiplying the crude prevalence of clinical obesity and the corresponding AF values in each cohort. The unadjusted prevalence (that is, the observed prevalence) was considered as the maximum of the prevalence of clinical obesity.

Using longitudinal data from all four cohorts, we estimated the cumulative incidence of incident organ dysfunction among individuals with preclinical obesity. Follow-up time was calculated from baseline until the first occurrence of incident organ dysfunction, death or end of follow-up. Cumulative incidence curves were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods implemented in the survival package in R (v.3.8.6), with cumulative incidence calculated as 1 minus the survival probability. The AF-adjusted cumulative incidence of clinical obesity was estimated by multiplying the observed cumulative incidence of organ dysfunction by the corresponding AF estimates in each cohort.

For mortality risk analysis, participants were categorized into four groups: (1) no confirmed obesity and no organ dysfunction (reference group); (2) no confirmed obesity but with organ dysfunction; (3) confirmed obesity without organ dysfunction (preclinical obesity); or (4) confirmed obesity with organ dysfunction (clinical obesity). To evaluate whether the composite anthropometric criteria could detect high-risk individuals misclassified by BMI alone, we conducted the analysis of the association between obesity status and mortality in the following five groups: (1) no overweight or obesity (BMI < 24/25; reference group); (2) BMI-based overweight without CAD-obesity; (3) BMI-based overweight with CAD-obesity (that is, both elevated WC and elevated WHtR; this group can be viewed as the underdiagnosis of obesity by BMI alone); (4) BMI-based obesity without CAD-obesity (this group can be viewed as the overdiagnosis of obesity by BMI alone); and (5) BMI-based obesity with CAD-obesity. To further evaluate the effects of composite anthropometric criteria for excessive adiposity, participants were categorized into eight groups based on BMI-defined obesity status (yes, no), CAD-obesity status (yes, no) and presence of organ dysfunction (yes, no) at baseline.

The association between obesity subtypes and mortality was estimated using the Cox proportional hazards models implemented in the survival package in R (v.3.8-6). Study-specific HRs and 95% CIs were pooled using fixed-effects meta-analysis implemented in the meta package in R (v.8.5.0). Time-at-risk extended from baseline to death or administrative censoring (31 December 2023 for the Kailuan Study, 19 December 2022 for the UKB and 31 December 2021 for the SIDIAP). Proportional hazards assumptions were verified using log–log survival plots. We performed several robustness checks, such as excluding deaths occurring within the first 2 or 5 years after baseline or including waist-to-hip ratio (≥0.90 for male and ≥0.85 for female individuals) as an additional criterion for central obesity. Stratified analyses by age groups (<60 and ≥60 years old), sex (male and female) and smoking status (never, former and current) were further performed to test the robustness of the results across subgroups of the participants.

All analyses were performed using SAS v.9.4 and R v.4.4.2. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05 (two-sided).

It has been revealed that results are shown as HRs and 95% CIs from the Cox proportional hazards model. The analyses included 137,792 participants with 17,642 deaths in the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants with 31,812 deaths in the UK Biobank and 51,269 participants with 2,338 deaths in the SIDIAP database. Points indicate HR point estimates and horizontal lines indicate 95% CIs. Models were adjusted for demographic factors (age and sex in all studies and, in addition, ethnicity in the UK Biobank), socio-economic status (marital status, educational level and household income in the Kailuan Study; employment, education and Townsend deprivation index in the UK Biobank; and MEDEA deprivation index in the SIDIAP) and lifestyle factors (smoking and alcohol consumption in all studies; physical activity in the Kailuan Study; and physical activity, diet quality and sleep duration in the UK Biobank). Interactions of obesity status with sex and age group were evaluated using joint Wald tests of the corresponding interaction terms; all Pinteraction values were <0.001. Pooled estimates were obtained using a fixed-effect meta-analysis model. All statistical tests were two-sided. In panel a, blue and orange represent men and female, respectively. In panel b, green and purple represent participants aged <60 years and ≥60 years, respectively. a, Sex-stratified analyses. b, Age-stratified analyses.

Sources indicate that scatter plots showing the association between BMI and WHtR among 137,795 participants in the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants in the UK Biobank, 218,841 participants in the All of Us Research Program and 51,269 participants in the SIDIAP database. Each point represents one participant. Points are coloured according to log-transformed point density. The solid line represents the fitted linear regression relationship between BMI and WHtR. Dashed vertical lines indicate BMI thresholds for overweight and obesity, defined as 24 and 28 kg/m² in the Kailuan Study and 25 and 30 kg/m² in the other cohorts. Dashed horizontal lines indicate the predicted WHtR values corresponding to these BMI thresholds based on the fitted linear regression models. Pearson correlation coefficients (r) between BMI and WHtR are shown within each panel. Pearson correlation tests were two-sided and statistically significant (P < 0.001). BMI was expressed as kg m−2, and WHtR was calculated as WC divided by height.

It has been revealed that restricted cubic spline curves showing the associations between WHtR and all-cause mortality among 137,792 participants with 17,642 deaths in the Kailuan Study, 436,203 participants with 31,812 deaths in the UK Biobank and 51,269 participants with 2,338 deaths in the SIDIAP database. HRs and 95% CIs were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic factors, socio-economic status and lifestyle factors. The solid red lines indicate HRs, and the shaded areas indicate 95% CIs. The horizontal dashed line represents a HR of 1.0. Green dots indicate the reference values of WHtR in each cohort. Blue dashed curves indicate the density distribution of WHtR. Overall and nonlinear associations were assessed using two-sided Wald chi-square tests, with corresponding P values shown within each panel (Kailuan: Poverall = 5.99 × 10−29, Pnonlinear = 5.01 × 10−05; UK Biobank: Poverall = 4.75 × 10−253, Pnonlinear = 2.58 × 10−87; SIDIAP: Poverall = 9.47 × 10−20, Pnonlinear = 2.90 × 10−12).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Declan Rice has claimed England “knew” they would beat world champions Spain.

The Three Lions finished top of their Nations League group ahead of the Spanish on Sunday with a stunning 3-2 win over the world champions.

According to recent reports, after goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White put the visitors three goals up, Elliot Anderson was sent off and the hosts made their way back to within one. But England held on for victory to overtake their hosts in the group.

Following the game, the Arsenal midfielder spoke about the confidence his side will take from their victory and claimed Thomas Tuchel’s team knew they were going to claim all three points in Madrid.

“We knew we were going to beat them tonight,” Rice told ITV.

“The message from the manager after the Croatia game has been so positive. The first 10 minutes was the best we’ve played. Pressure, pressure. Overall, 10 men for half an hour, winning 3-2 against a team unbeaten in 43 [matches] is massive.”.

Industry observers note that rice added: “Argentina that day [in the World Cup semi-finals] wasn’t meant to be. That’s football.

Recent findings suggest that “When they [Spain] got a second [goal], maybe it could have gone another way. It’s a massive win. Everything happened so quickly [at the end], so for him [James Trafford] to make two in the space of two seconds is massive.”.

England, as group winners, will have a favourable draw for the quarter-finals of the Nations League, and they will find out their opponents on Friday.

They will face a runner-up from one of the other three ‘Group A’ tables.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eighteen years ago, Bournemouth were minutes away from being liquidated and playing in the fourth tier. On Thursday night, Bournemouth not only welcomed AC Milan in Europe; they did so as favourites, and then pummelled them.

When Amine Adli curled in an 84-minute free-kick with his left foot at the Vitality Stadium, it put the seal on the most extraordinary evening in Bournemouth’s history. On a brutally windy and wet night, Bournemouth trounced AC Milan 3-0.

Amine Adli with a SUPERB free-kick to give Bournemouth a 3-0 lead vs AC Milan 🚀 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/KX5i5oM3TG.

Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the fresh European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

It has been revealed that “It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, noted. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”.

Sources indicate that evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench indicated the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

Thirty-one years ago, Patrick Kluivert scored against AC Milan in Europe. If his son Justin’s eighth-minute penalty will not receive the acclaim of Patrick’s winner for Ajax in the 1995 Champions League final, the goal will be etched in Bournemouth’s hearts.

According to recent reports, after Evanilson’s header from a corner struck Koni De Winter’s hand, a VAR review led to Bournemouth being awarded a penalty. Kluivert eyed up Mike Maignan, and waited for the goalkeeper to dive before nonchalantly stroking the ball into the unguarded left corner.

Bournemouth lead against AC Milan in a European competition! 🍒 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1BQt3wKSr9.

And so Bournemouth were beating AC Milan, a scenario that would have seemed unfathomable for vast swathes of these two clubs’ existence. Even more extraordinary was how deserved the goal was: both Kluivert and Evanilson had already spurned opportunities, with Milan seeming overwhelmed by Bournemouth’s intensity.

Watching his side lack any coherence in their passing, Ruben Amorim rapidly came to look as ghoulish as in his last days at Old Trafford. Or, indeed, Michael Carrick in Como 24 hours earlier.

Sources indicate that amorim swiftly had cause to become more irate. Just as Milan had threatened to regain a semblance of control, Maignan inexplicably pushed Tyler Adams in the face when Bournemouth had a corner. VAR had no reason to give Maignan a reprieve from his red card, and Bournemouth’s ensuing penalty.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Unmissable 🍿 https://t.co/Ag1pyu5r6f.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ukraine welcome Georgia to Kosicka futbalova arena on Tuesday night for a matchday six clash in UEFA Nations League B Group 2.
  • The hosts are third in the standings and two points ahead of their bottom-placed visitors, leaving both teams fighting to confirm their survival in League B.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ellis Stevens | 15 Nov 2026 16:54.

Ukraine welcome Georgia to Kosicka futbalova arena on Tuesday night for a matchday six clash in UEFA Nations League B Group 2.

The hosts are third in the standings and two points ahead of their bottom-placed visitors, leaving both teams fighting to confirm their survival in League B.

Ukraine got their 2026-27 Nations League campaign underway with an encouraging 1-0 victory over Hungary, with Danylo Sikan scoring the only goal just before half-time.

After following that result up with a 0-0 draw against Georgia, Ukraine have subsequently fallen to three consecutive defeats, losing 3-0 and 1-0 to Northern Ireland and 2-1 to Hungary.

Andrea Maldera's side, as a result, sit third in Nations League B Group 2 with four points from five matches, and with just one game remaining, Ukraine are unable to climb into the promotion playoff places.

However, Ukraine are still fighting to ensure their survival in League B, as they lead visitors Georgia by only two points, meaning defeat on Tuesday would consign Maldera's men to a relegation playoff fixture.

Ukraine will secure their League B status with at least a draw, and they will, therefore, be hoping to replicate or improve upon their 0-0 stalemate with Georgia in the reverse fixture.

Georgia have failed to win any of their five League B matches, recording two draws and suffering three defeats during that time.

Despite boasting the likes of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Georges Mikautadze in attack, Georgia have also failed to find the back of the net in any of their five matches, while they have conceded four times.

Georgia will be hoping to end their goalless streak when they come up against Ukraine, who have conceded more than any other team in the group (six conceded).

However, Georgia's attack has been weakened by the long-term injury to Kvaratskhelia, who scored the nation's last goal in their 2-0 victory over Bahrain in a friendly in June.

Georgia will also have to overcome a miserable record in meetings with Ukraine, having failed to defeat Tuesday's opponents in any of their 12 meetings - losing seven and drawing five.

Ukraine form (all competitions):.

Georgia form (all competitions):.

Ukraine failed to find the net for the third time in Group 2 as they lost 1-0 to Northern Ireland last time out, and Maldera may opt to make changes in attack as a result, meaning the likes of Artem Dovbyk could start.

At the opposite end, captain Mykola Matvienko could start alongside Ilya Zabarnyi, with Illia Krupskyi introduced at right-back.

Meanwhile, Georgia will be without superstar Kvaratskhelia due to a long-term injury, meaning much of the attacking responsibility will rest on Mikautadze's shoulders.

The striker should be supported by Zuriko Davitashvili, Nika Gagnidze and Giorgi Kvernadze, with Anzor Mekvabishvili and Giorgi Chakvetadze in midfield.

Ukraine possible starting lineup:.

Trubin; Krupskyi, Zabarnyi, Matvienko, Mykolenko; Andriyevskiy, Yarmoliuk, Ocheretko, Sudakov; Dovbyk, Krasnopir.

Georgia possible starting lineup:.

Mamardashvili; Kakabadze, Goglichidze, Dvali, Lochoshvili; Chakvetadze, Mekvabishvili; Kvernadze, Gagnidze, Davitashvili; Mikautadze.

Georgia have failed to score in any of their five matches and are further weakened by Kvaratskhelia's absence, and with Ukraine boasting the home advantage, we are predicting a win for the hosts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Thomas Tuchel and his England coaching staff come to reflect on England’s sensational victory in Spain, they will come to the conclusion it could scarcely have gone better.

Such a statement may feel bizarre given the visitors were at one stage 3-0 up with cruise control applied, before another Jarell Quansah error led to an Elliot Anderson red card, a penalty converted, and then a second goal back for a Spain team totally rejuvenated.

The reality, though, is that if England’s canter to a one-sided victory had continued as it was doing, Tuchel and his team would have far less to pore over as they unpick the headers and volleys at the end of this calendar year and the learning they can take from what still finished - by getting over the line 3-2 and topping the group - a hugely successful international break.

Tuchel had repeatedly described this affair as “a final” in the days leading up, but just as important as finishing top of the group and the potentially easier quarter-final opponent it could secure them in March was delivering a performance to provide encouragement that the Three Lions can indeed go toe-to-toe with the very best and avoid unforced errors in the process.

In a recent development, OK, there was one such mistake: Quansah, at fault for Croatia’s goal at Wembley on Thursday, dawdling on the ball and conceding possession cheaply. England’s magnificent earlier work threatened to unravel at that point as the dominoes of the resultant red card, goal and second strike fell.

But then came the memories of the cavalry this summer, their resolute World Cup closing-it-out jobs against Mexico and then Norway and then the ugly attempt to do it all over again at the semi-final against Argentina. Instinct kicked in.

James Trafford getting the nod ahead of Jordan Pickford in the Spanish capital was a bold call, as was Ben White starting at right-back and Lewis Hall on the left, but all three were superb, as the head coach’s major decisions were wholly vindicated. The world champions’ unbeaten run was ended by England, the Spanish tasting defeat in Madrid for the first time in 39 years, since a certain Gary Lineker netted all four in a 4-2 England win.

Recent findings suggest that lamine Yamal posed England all sorts of questions from the right wing - a fabulous player - but did he cause them a wealth of problems? Aside from a simple assist for Spain’s second, no, not really. Hall was sturdy at left-back, just as England were all over the pitch.

Their first-half display, after which point they led 1-0 through a Harry Kane penalty, was described by Roy Keane in ITV’s coverage as “perfect”. They had certainly all been on the same wavelength, their passing sequences all crisp. And in the second half, after those two quickfire goals shipped, the defensive equivalent of that joined-up thinking was visible from a team that looked like one.

Sources indicate that the players involved in this Nations League group game represent many of the Champions League powerhouses and yet there was no hint of this being an unwanted match that disrupts the club football juggernaut and where there is a needless risk of injury. Not a bit of that. When Jude Bellingham’s number came up and he was substituted in the 83rd minute, presumably to keep Real Madrid happy, he looked angered not to be carrying on in a game that had just about everything. What’s more: it had the result that England craved. And expected.

Divock Origi has discussed what went wrong during his time at AC Milan, from the injuries to the Rossoneri’s decision to exclude him.

Origi joined Milan after the Scudetto season, i.e. the summer of 2022, and the idea was that he would be able to alternate with Olivier Giroud. However, a couple of injuries made his start difficult and it only went downhill from there.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Despite making 36 appearances in his first season, he got just two goals and was thus sent out on loan for the next season, joining Nottingham Forest. One goal and one assist later, he returned to Milan, where it was quickly decided that he was no longer part of the project.

Instead of taking the opportunity to continue his career elsewhere, Origi decided to stay and train on his own. His hefty salary of €4m net (€5.24m gross) frustrated Milan and in December 2025, they finally got the striker to terminate his contract six months earlier than its expiration.

In short, it was a costly deal for Milan and for Origi, the move effectively killed his career. Speaking to the Belgian outlet HLN.be, as cited by MilanPress, the former striker explained what happened and why he then decided to retire (in the summer of 2026).

Recent findings suggest that “At 27, my time at Liverpool was over. Sometimes you need to step out of your comfort zone and take on a upcoming challenge. It’s the only way to grow as a person. AC Milan was a very interesting project.

“Paolo Maldini signed me and I felt he truly believed in me. It’s just that I got injured. Usually, I work on my preparation with my personal trainer, but this time it didn’t work. I lost much of my basic fitness; it was difficult.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t take it personally. It was a professional decision. Was I happy about it? Obviously not. But can I understand it? Yes. I was left out of the squad for a while and wasn’t allowed to train with the first team.

Recent findings suggest that “There was the option of joining the youth team. I can’t say too much about some things for contractual reasons… Let’s just say we weren’t on the same page about it. My experience helped me keep a clear head.

“I was convinced that if you have the right intentions, everything will work out for the best in the end.”.

“I had options in football, but for me it was also a time when I was starting to think about my future away from the sport. Don’t get me wrong, I’ve always dedicated myself body and soul to football. It was my great passion, ” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • England and Spain have confirmed their starting lineups for Sunday's UEFA Nations League showdown at the Metropolitano Stadium.
  • Thomas Tuchel's men must beat the world and European champions to win League A Group 3, although both sides have already sealed their spots in the quarter-finals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 18:34, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 18:46.

England and Spain have confirmed their starting lineups for Sunday's UEFA Nations League showdown at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Thomas Tuchel's men must beat the world and European champions to win League A Group 3, although both sides have already sealed their spots in the quarter-finals.

The Three Lions have made three changes for their reunion with La Roja, all of which come in defence, including the already-known switch in goal between James Trafford and Jordan Pickford.

Tuchel has also brought Ben White - who was once again booed by England fans against Croatia on Thursday - back into the starting XI, at the expense of Trent Alexander-Arnold.

Fellow Arsenal man Ezri Konsa is also restored to the starting lineup after missing the midweek victory through injury, taking Dan Burn's place in the heart of defence.

Djed Spence and Myles Lewis-Skelly must make do with spots on the bench following their returns from injury and suspension respectively, as Tuchel sticks with an unchanged midfield and attacking selection.

As for Spain, head coach Luis de la Fuente has made five changes to the side that bested the Czech Republic 2-0 last time out, including expected recalls for Lamine Yamal and Mikel Oyarzabal.

The pair both missed Spain's penultimate group game as a precautionary measure, but they have unsurprisingly been selected over Yeremy Pino and Ferran Torres this time around.

De la Fuente has also made a bold call in the number 10 role, demoting Fermin Lopez in favour of Mikel Merino, but Alex Baena hold his spot on the left over Nico Williams - now fully fit again following illness.

Merino's Arsenal teammate Martin Zubimendi is also retained in midfield over Pedri, despite concerns over fatigue having played the full 90 against the Czech Republic amid a lack of game time at club level.

De la Fuente has made two changes to his backline foe the final matchday, as Marc Pubill replaces Pedro Porro at right-back, and Aymeric Laporte is in for Dean Huijsen in central defence.

England XI: Trafford; White, Konsa, Quansah, Hall; Anderson, Rice; Rogers, Ju. Bellingham, Gordon; Kane.

Subs: Pickford, Alexander-Arnold, Steele, Gibbs-White, Spence, Burn, Jo. Bellingham, Hill, Calvert-Lewin, Ngumoha, Eze, Lewis-Skelly.

Spain XI: Simon; Pubill, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Zubimendi, Ruiz; Yamal, Merino, Baena; Oyarzabal.

Subs: Raya, Garcia, Roca, Huijsen, Torres. Lopez, Pino, Porro, Barrios, Munoz, Williams, Pedri.

Arsenal have been dealt an injury concern over the international break after Martin Zubimendi hobbled off during Spain’s 3-2 defeat by England in the Nations League.

The world champions were initially blown away by the Three Lions at the Estadio Metropolitano, with the visitors going three up in Madrid thanks to strikes from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

But while there was elation for those two Arsenal stars, one of their club-mates’ evenings went from bad to worse, with Zubimendi injuring his hamstring in the second half in Madrid.

The midfielder was forced off, with Spain boss Luis de la Fuente replacing him with Nico Williams.

The Athletic Club winger, previously reported as a transfer target for Mikel Arteta’s side, scored the second goal for the hosts in a rollercoaster encounter, as the European champions threatened an unlikely comeback after Elliot Anderson’s red card for denying Lamine Yamal a goalscoring opportunity.

Zubimendi’s injury will come as a blow for the Gunners, despite the Spaniard struggling for game time at the Emirates Stadium after the summer arrival of Bruno Guimaraes and the form of Declan Rice, who starred for his country once more on Sunday evening.

It remains to be seen how long Zubimendi will be sidelined for, but should he be out for an elongated period, he could well miss the Premier League champions’ trip to Newcastle, Champions League clash with Borussia Dortmund and home encounter with Manchester City before the end of the month.

Thomas Tuchel has explained why England’s 3-2 win over Spain was the best performance of his tenure.

The German has been in charge of the Three Lions since January 2025 and guided them to third place at the World Cup in the summer, their highest finish in the competition since their only title in 1966.

Sources indicate that that included memorable wins against Croatia, DR Congo and Mexico. Last month, in the Nations League, England inflicted upon Croatia the heaviest defeat in their history as they thrashed Slaven Bilic’s side 7-0 in Rijeka.

But Tuchel admitted he views Sunday’s 10-man victory over the world champions in Madrid as the finest performance during his time at the helm.

In a recent development, harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored for the Three Lions as they ended the world champions’ 43-game unbeaten streak despite conceding twice in the second half. It secured England top spot in their Nations League group ahead of Spain.

“Brilliant performance,” Tuchel told ITV after the game. “A well deserved win. Overall we were the better team. Fantastic performance from start to finish.

Sources indicate that “It was a complete performance. We brought everything to the table. We were brave. Spirit-wise, energy-wise and also football quality was highest level.

Recent findings suggest that “We deserved it. We focused on our performance and attitude. I can’t praise the team high enough for what they put out there.”.

Speaking about how England dug in defensively once Spain had scored their second goal, Tuchel said: “Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]. That’s the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners.”.

In a recent development, asked what England revealed, he replied: “What we are made of and what we can do. We are always ready to push our limits. We had our best result in 60 years [at the World Cup] and we weren’t happy with it. It’s impressive what we did in the last two camps.”.

AC Milan proved that they are willing to spend money on talent in the summer and in January, it’ll seemingly be no different.

According to recent reports, there was a shift in the works at Milan in the summer. No longer were the club going to focus solely on buying quantity over quality, hoping for a gem. Instead, they were going to buy quality and so far, it’s largely paying off.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Now, the roadmap is there to do the same again in a few months.

According to Gazzetta dello Sport, as seen below, Cardinale is ready to invest around €70 million. After the €150m spent in the summer, it represents a substantial season of investment from the American and it seems this will be the trend moving forward.

There are currently decisions being made about who arrives, but it seems more likely that a new striker will be chosen and there are two standout names for the Rossoneri; both aren’t unfamiliar, too.

On one hand, you have Endrick and the other, you have Nicolo Tresoldi.

Sources indicate that starting with the former, the relationship between Roc Nation and Cardinale is strong, which could help negotiations. Of course, the American was also very keen to sign him in the summer mercato, so this interest stretches back.

They will have to compete with Roma, but to help give them the upper hand, they have involved Kaka in the process. The Brazilian – also an evangelical Christian – could do with Endrick ‘what Leonardo did with him’.

Cardinale prepares to offer a loan with a buy clause to help sweeten the deal, and this could be worth €60m, plus bonuses. Importantly, he’d also be willing to offer Real Madrid a buy-back clause, similar to the Nico Paz situation.

With Tresoldi, things aren’t as simple. Their admiration is well known – as is the striker’s for the Diavolo – but they are not alone in their interest. His future lies away from Belgium, but the path is difficult to know.

Ideally, they wouldn’t sell him in January, but if a compelling offer arrives, he could well leave the club in the Newly introduced Year. It may also be problematic if Premier League clubs become involved; they are desperate to avoid an auction.

On Tuesday, the USA aim to give their manager a fitting send-off when they host Haiti in the second leg of that quarter-final CONCACAF Nations League tie at TQL Stadium in Cincinnati.

It would require an epic collapse for the Yanks to be eliminated from this tournament on Tuesday, having beaten the Haitians 6-0 in leg one.

For the final time, Mauricio Pochettino will be on the US sidelines Tuesday, hoping to end his tenure on a positive note before heading to Old Trafford to join Manchester United.

While he leaves the national team program without a trophy, the Argentine coach has seen this team flourish since the World Cup concluded, and they are presently on a five-match winning run across all competitions.

Pochettino’s men have been near-flawless since the fall, posting three successive clean sheets while netting three or more goals in four of their last five encounters.

The US have only lost three Nations League knockout matches, boasting a 100% home record in quarter-final outings.

Tuesday will mark their fifth international at TQL Stadium, with the Yanks undefeated at the venue, including two wins.

They are unbeaten in their last 11 internationals against Haiti, winning those last four meetings by a combined margin of 10-1.

David Badia’s men have lost their last two matches by a combined margin of 8-0 after winning their first three Nations League group outings.

The Haitians have not won a quarter-final contest in a CONCACAF competition since the 2019 Gold Cup when they were down 2-0 and stunned Canada 3-2.

They have not lost a League A encounter in this tournament when netting the opening goal since the 2023 group stage when Jamaica beat them 3-2.

Les Grenadiers can claim their first victory over the US on American soil Tuesday since 1969, when they beat them 1-0 in a World Cup qualifier in San Diego.

There are two Haitian players without a cap to their name, including goalkeeper Jonah Mednard and midfielder Miguel Joseph.
