By MATT BARLOW, FOOTBALL WRITER.

Published: 02:01 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 14:00 EST, 15 November 2026.

Clive Tyldesley reaches for his glasses as he rummages through the commentary charts crammed into an old filing cabinet, jokes about his fading eyesight and supposes one day he will no longer be able to identify footballers from the gantry.

Fortunately, we are still far from that point. At 72, Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever. His eyes are perfectly good when bespectacled, his mind nimble enough to keep up with play and his soothingly familiar voice strong and authoritative with a gentle tendency towards self-deprecation.

This much was evident as Manchester United roared back to beat Roma in the Champions League and a clip of his spine-tingling commentary from the live CBS broadcast circulated on social media and found an appreciative audience in Europe.

'I don't know if there's an element of nostalgia in hearing my voice again,' states Tyldesley. 'If I'm honest, I've dodged the worst of the public's ire with everything including commentators because I haven't been around for the last few years.

According to recent reports, 'Absence has made a few hearts grow a little fonder towards me and maybe if I'd been on Sky every week for the last six years, I'd be no less unpopular than anybody else out there. So, I can't pretend it's not nice to get some engagement with an audience I used to commentate to on a regular basis, but I'm very happy where I am.'.

Tyldesley has been the lead commentator for the CBS coverage of the Champions League since 2020, converting transfer fees into US dollars and keeping his measurements imperial for a North American audience but otherwise approaching the job as he always did.

Clive Tyldesley is calling the game as accurately as ever at 72 and is 'very happy' in his role as the lead commentator of CBS coverage of the Champions League.

Tyldesley's commentary of Man United's comeback against Roma circulated on social media and received an appreciative audience in Europe.

The 72-year-old wonders whether there was an element of nostalgia to the reaction, with Tyldesley's work for CBS meaning his commentary cannot be shown in Europe.

Clips of the studio panel featuring Thierry Henry, Micah Richards, Jamie Carragher and presenter Kate Scott are popular on social media but live action featuring Tyldesley's commentary is governed by broadcasting rights deals and cannot be shown in Europe.

The one from Old Trafford of Matheus Cunha's winning goal in the 86th minute slipped through the net on X and reminded everyone his passion for football is undimmed, and his voice can still stand hairs on attention.

Recent findings suggest that 'I don't think I've seen a better game than the first leg of the Paris Saint-Germain v Bayern Munich Champions League semi-final,' says Tyldesley on the rare quality of Europe's elite competition. 'I listened to people with hundreds more England caps than me saying it was bad defending, but I watched the whole game back the next day and it wasn't.

'I'm sorry but it was wonderful attacking and a show of intent by two coaches who trusted defenders to defend one-on-one and attackers to score more than the opposition. Rob Green was my co-commentator and at the end we just put our microphones down and looked at each other and mentioned, "Wow.".

'I've not forgotten muddy pitches and assassin centre backs. You only need to look on YouTube to see football was different, but you can't pretend it was better. I see terrible games today just as I did then, but particularly in the Champions League, I regularly stumble upon football that gets me off my seat.'.

His exit from ITV, first displaced by Sam Matterface as lead commentator in 2020 and then released entirely after Euro 2024 clearly smarted but Tyldesley is comfortable as the veteran in the fast-changing media landscape.

'Most of the principles I picked up from watching John Motson, Barry Davies and Brian Moore in their pomp are applicable to commentary in 2026,' he says. 'There's no need to reinvent that particular wheel.

In a recent development, 'You can offer alternatives such as fan zones and screaming watchalongs for people to view it in a different way. I make it my business to look at J_Tekkz or LDN Movements or whatever is pulling in millions on YouTube.

Tyldesley believes he has not seen a better game than the first leg of PSG's Champions League semi-final with Bayern Munich last year.

The veteran commentator believes most of the principles he learned starting out still apply, but admits to having watched popular new voices to see if anything could apply to his commentary.

Tyldesley also works as a guest lecturer and commentates for blockbuster computer games, as well as selling framed prints of his commentary charts.

'I sample a bit of Mark Goldbridge to see why he's prominent but I'm hearing nothing in those guys applicable to the way I call a football match so I carry on with the same focus I've always had on what constitutes good commentary.'.

The central principle being that the game is bigger than the individuals in it, he points out, with viewers tuning in for the football not the commentator.

'The biggest challenge for a television commentator is to find the right words at the major moments, to go beyond "amazing," "brilliant", "incredible" and try to add some editorial context,' states Tyldesley.

'Every goal is unique. The words following a goal that is going to be remembered for years should be unique and specific to that goal, but that's difficult to do. It's unscripted performance and difficult to master and capture.

'I am concentrating hardest for the 10-15 seconds after a big goal because I'm searching for words which will become a small part of people's memories. That's very different to consciously trying to provide 45-second soundbites to amplify one's own personality and standing on social media.

'There's a danger of media leaning that way as it develops such an emphasis on the bitesize.'.

Among other things, Tyldesley is a guest lecturer for media students at the University of Salford, still doing commentaries for blockbuster computer games and selling framed prints of his commentary charts, something that started as 'a silly idea in lockdown'.

Sources indicate that his wife Susan bought a dozen frames to see how it went. Originally, he offered three Champions League finals won by English clubs in 1999, 2005 and 2012. He sent one each to Gary Neville who played for Manchester United in 1999 and Jamie Carragher who played for Liverpool in 2005. They both posted images online and demand skyrocketed.

Recent findings suggest that 'Two good friends,' smiles Tyldesley. 'I probably got about half a million pounds of free advertising out of them.' Sales have soared beyond 50,000. There's a Celtic chart on the gym in Rod Stewart's house. Ant and Dec have bought signed Newcastle charts.

His own venture into podcasting was short-lived and he politely declines between five and ten invitations each week to appear on others.

In a recent development, 'I've tried to step back from that kind of thing,' indicates Tyldesley. 'So much content I hear on football is empty, verbose and repetitive. Really, there are only so many things you can say about Alexander Isak having his shirt pulled in mid-air and Gary Neville probably remarked most of them in the 30 seconds following the incident.

Tyldesley has no intends to retire and Paramount, the owners of his employers CBS - and soon to be the owners of TNT Sports - will have the UK rights for the Champions League.

Sales of his framed commentary charts, something that started during lockdown, have soared beyond 50,000.

'There are so many brutally judgmental loud voices in and around football attracting attention that I want to be as far away from as possible, so that's what I do. Unless I sense an opportunity to talk about communication and broadcasting rather than whether club A, B or C should replace their manager. That's not for me Clive.'.

Sources indicate that so, there's a little less Tyldesley out there than there was. He was content to stay at home and watch the World Cup from his sofa this summer for the first time since 1990.

Recent findings suggest that but there are no intends to retire. And who knows what might change next season when Paramount, the owners of CBS – and soon to be the owners of current rights holders TNT Sports – have the UK rights for the Champions League.

There might be a familiar voice beamed into our living rooms once again.

When I saw the Dear England play, I was the only person in the theatre who didn't enjoy it, and that was because I hated the portrayal of Harry Kane.

Sources indicate that he was written as an uneducated numbskull. Written to laugh at and the theatre laughed at him. He was stupid and gullible, another thick footballer.

And anyone who has spent time with footballers will know they might lack for an Eton College education but are streetwise and invariably smart with a razor sharp sense of humour.

Kane is a leader of those men. There's not a single thing about the person Kane has made himself to laugh or sneer at and I wanted to stand up in the theatre that afternoon and shout at everyone.

Oddly, I was introduced to the playwright James Graham at a function a few weeks later and he kind of pushed me for my opinion of Dear England.

I tried to be diplomatic, but I felt so strongly I ended up scolding him for writing a character called Harry Kane who was nothing like Harry Kane.

It has been revealed that so, that was the end of a beautiful friendship before it began. And I'm so thrilled now there's a better appreciation of the person Harry is.

Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 52 min read (10317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase1,2.
  • DNA lesion bypass by leading-strand repriming was demonstrated for the core Escherichia coli replisome, in which primer synthesis is performed by the primase also responsible for lagging-strand replication12,13.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disruptions to leading-strand synthesis impair and stall replication forks because DNA synthesis by the leading-strand polymerase, Pol ε, is essential for optimal template unwinding by the replicative CMG (CDC45–MCM–GINS) helicase1,2. Failure to efficiently restart and/or protect stalled replication forks is a major source of genomic instability3,4,5,6. Stalled forks can be restarted by a variety of mechanisms, including repriming downstream of the impediment4. In human cells, the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL promotes fork progression during replication stress7,8,9,10, but how its activity is coordinated by the replisome is unresolved. Here, by reconstituting replication fork stalling and restart with purified human proteins, we show that the CMG helicase directs PRIMPOL for efficient replication fork restart. Unexpectedly, the interaction between PRIMPOL and replication protein A9,11 is not critical for fork restart in this system. We show that PRIMPOL binds directly to CMG, and a cryo-electron microscopy structure illustrates how this targets PRIMPOL specifically for leading-strand priming to minimize the size of post-replicative gaps. Ablating the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction abolishes fork restart in vitro and PRIMPOL-dependent DNA damage tolerance in human cells. Our work establishes PRIMPOL as an integrated component of the human replisome dedicated to leading-strand priming.

DNA lesion bypass by leading-strand repriming was demonstrated for the core Escherichia coli replisome, in which primer synthesis is performed by the primase also responsible for lagging-strand replication12,13. By contrast, eukaryotic replisomes reconstituted from purified Saccharomyces cerevisiae proteins cannot efficiently resume synthesis downstream of leading-strand lesions1 because the Pol α–primase complex that is responsible for priming each Okazaki fragment is targeted to the lagging-strand template14. This targeting mechanism is conserved in the human replisome14, indicating that inefficient priming on the leading strand by Pol α–primase is a universal feature of eukaryotic replisomes.

In a recent development, unlike S. cerevisiae, humans have an additional primase called PRIMPOL7,8,9. PRIMPOL is a 560-amino-acid (aa) monomeric enzyme comprising a 21-aa amino-terminal helix of unknown function, an archaeo-eukaryotic primase (AEP) domain, a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding zinc-finger (ZnF) and two C-terminal replication protein A (RPA) binding motifs (RBMs)6,15. Extensive evidence from human, mouse and chicken cell lines shows that PRIMPOL promotes replication fork progression under conditions that stall replicative DNA polymerases8,9,10 and that this requires PRIMPOL primase activity10,16,17,18, leading to the formation of daughter-strand gaps5,19. Current models indicate that PRIMPOL is recruited to replication forks through a direct interaction with RPA9,11,16. However, because RPA is constitutively associated with the lagging-strand template, it is unclear whether this mode of recruitment is sufficient for efficient PRIMPOL priming on the leading strand, or whether an additional mechanism directs PRIMPOL specifically to the leading-strand template to rescue stalled replication forks.

To investigate leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the replisome, we leveraged a system that we recently developed to assemble fast and efficient human replisomes from purified proteins20. In this approach, CMG is first loaded onto the forked end of a 9.7-kb DNA template before additional proteins are added to assemble replisomes that perform robust leading- and lagging-strand DNA replication (Fig. 1a). Pol ε performs the bulk of leading-strand synthesis, whereas Pol α–primase and Pol δ replicate the lagging strand. RFC and CTF18-RFC load the polymerase processivity factor PCNA onto the lagging and leading strands, respectively, and TIMELESS (TIM)–TIPIN, CLASPIN and AND1 associate with CMG to promote rapid replisome progression20. To monitor fork stalling and restart, a single cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD)—an vital ultraviolet (UV)-induced DNA lesion and a potent block to replicative polymerases—was introduced to the leading-strand template 3.5 kb from the forked end1,20.

Sources indicate that a, Schematic of the forked-DNA replication assay with a template containing a leading-strand CPD lesion. b, Time course of a replication assay on the leading-strand CPD template in the absence or presence of PRIMPOL. c, Two-dimensional gel analysis of a 30-min replication reaction in the presence of PRIMPOL.

Sources indicate that figure 1b indicates that the CPD is a potent block to leading-strand DNA synthesis (3.5-kb stall lead product in denaturing gel), which causes replication forks to stall, as visualized by the slowly migrating species in the native gel (stalled fork). Similar replisome behaviour was observed when the CPD was substituted for a tetrahydrofuran abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Addition of PRIMPOL caused a reduction in the stalled fork population and the accumulation of full-length products in the native gel, concomitant with the appearance of an approximately 6.2-kb product in the denaturing gel (Fig. 1b, lanes 5–8, restart lead product). This result strongly indicated that PRIMPOL was promoting fork restart by leading-strand repriming. To confirm that the 6.2-kb products resulted from leading-strand repriming, products were analysed by two-dimensional gel electrophoresis (Fig. 1c). This indicated that the 6.2-kb products were exclusively associated with the full-length product in the native gel and were roughly twice as intense as the 3.5-kb stall leading-strand product, as expected for bona fide restart products. Moreover, replication of the CPD template in the presence of a primase-defective PRIMPOL mutant (ZnFD2A)10 generated only stalled leading strands and Okazaki fragments (Extended Data Fig. 1b). These data illustrate the successful reconstitution of replication fork restart by leading-strand repriming using purified human proteins.

In a recent development, replication fork restart also occurred efficiently after polymerase stalling at an abasic site (Extended Data Fig. 1c), suggesting that the mechanism of repriming is agnostic to the chemical nature of the initial blocking lesion. Restart also occurred independently of Pol δ (Extended Data Fig. 1d) and Pol α–primase (Extended Data Fig. 1c), illustrating that only Pol ε is required to extend the primer made by PRIMPOL in this system. Therefore, unless stated, Pol δ is omitted from subsequent experiments to avoid complications from strand-displacement synthesis.

Recent findings suggest that unlike Pol α–primase, which has a strong preference for rNTPs for primer synthesis21, following the 5′ rNTP, PRIMPOL incorporates dNTPs with a much higher efficiency than rNTPs owing to a sugar discrimination mechanism7,8,22. Consistent with these properties, omitting GTP, CTP and UTP did not compromise leading-strand restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e, compare lanes 7 and 8), indicating that ATP is sufficient for primer initiation in these assays. However, despite previous reports that manganese stimulates PRIMPOL priming activity in vitro8, its addition did not enhance the efficiency of restart (Extended Data Fig. 1f).

The observation that restart products were close to their maximum possible length (6.2 kb) indicated that they were initiated a very short distance from the lesion. To obtain a high-resolution view of leading-strand restart, we devised a strategy to map priming sites at near single-nucleotide resolution (Fig. 2a). To do so, products were post-replicatively digested with restriction enzymes that cut upstream and downstream of the lesion to liberate fragments that could be resolved in polyacrylamide sequencing gels. Figure 2b demonstrates that, apart from the stalled leading strand and a minor population of read-through products, a ladder of products was generated upon digestion of the PRIMPOL-containing reaction (lane 4). We conclude that each band in the ladder corresponds to a unique leading-strand repriming site. Notably, most of the PRIMPOL-dependent primers used to restart replication were synthesized within 50 nucleotides of the CPD, even when the PRIMPOL concentration was reduced to 5 nM (Extended Data Fig. 2a). An indistinguishable ladder pattern was observed following replication of the abasic site template (Extended Data Fig. 2b), showing that the chemical nature of the DNA lesion plays no part in priming site specification. Because CMG is likely to continue slowly unwinding DNA after polymerase stalling1,2, these data indicate that PRIMPOL activity is targeted to the leading-strand template immediately after polymerase stalling, which limits the size of the daughter-strand gap to generally <50 nucleotides on this template.

a, Schematic of the predicted products generated from digestion of replication products with SalI and NruI. b, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction processed as in a. c, Schematic of the DNA template in which a 162-nt sequence after the CPD was replaced with an alternative sequence. d, Urea polyacrylamide gel of a 40-min replication reaction containing PRIMPOL, processed as in a. Pol δ was omitted from the experiments in b and d. Und, undamaged.

Sources indicate that previous work established that PRIMPOL exhibits sequence preferences for the initiation of primer synthesis23,24,25. We therefore reasoned that the distinct pattern of restart products in our experiments was a consequence of the DNA sequence downstream of the CPD. To test this, we modified a 162-nt region downstream of the CPD (Fig. 2c). Replication of this modified template in the presence of PRIMPOL generated a distinct pattern of restart products to those from the original CPD template (Fig. 2d, compare lanes 3 and 4). This reveals that leading-strand repriming by PRIMPOL in the context of the human replisome is modulated by DNA sequence. Importantly, despite the altered sequence, most restart products were again initiated within <50 nucleotides of the CPD, with one prominent product initiated about 100 nt from the CPD (Fig. 2d, lane 4). This is consistent with both templates containing multiple close matches to the preferred tri-nucleotide primer initiation sequence for PRIMPOL25.

The discovery that PRIMPOL-mediated repriming occurred a short distance from the CPD on two distinct templates suggested that an efficient mechanism directs PRIMPOL to the exposed leading-strand template. We hypothesized that this was mediated by the RBMs in the PRIMPOL C terminus11, recruiting PRIMPOL to RPA bound to the leading-strand template following polymerase stalling at the CPD and continued template unwinding by CMG. To examine this, we generated two PRIMPOL mutants defective in RPA binding: one lacking both RBMs and the other carrying a mutant in RBM-A (RBM-ARA) that abolished PRIMPOL localization to chromatin in human cells11 (Fig. 3a). Figure 3b highlights that both PRIMPOL mutants promoted leading-strand restart with comparable efficiency to wild-type PRIMPOL. Moreover, analysis of restart products showed that both mutants exhibited the same repriming site pattern as wild-type PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c). We conclude that RBM-mediated interactions between PRIMPOL and RPA are non-essential for replication fork restart with reconstituted human replisomes.

Sources indicate that a, Primary structure diagrams showing full-length PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL point mutants and truncations. b, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction with the indicated PRIMPOL mutants. c, Urea polyacrylamide gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction on the CPD template performed with the indicated PRIMPOL RPA binding mutants. Products were digested post-replicatively with SalI and NruI. d, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction with dropouts of non-essential replisome components on undamaged and CPD templates in the presence of PRIMPOL. e, Silver-stained SDS–PAGE analysis of a pull-down experiment with the indicated proteins. WT, wild type.

Industry observers note that the non-essentiality of the PRIMPOL RBMs for fork restart, together with the very close proximity of repriming to the lesion, prompted us to explore the idea that PRIMPOL might be directed to stalled forks through an interaction with the core replisome. Omission of all non-essential core replisome components individually did not abolish leading-strand restart (Fig. 3d). We therefore hypothesized that PRIMPOL might be recruited directly by the CMG helicase. Consistent with this idea, the pull-down experiment in Fig. 3e shows that PRIMPOL interacts specifically with CMG.

Industry observers note that to investigate how PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG, and how this might facilitate efficient leading-strand repriming, we determined a structure of PRIMPOL bound to CMG by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Table 1). Well-resolved cryo-EM density was recovered for the PRIMPOL AEP domain alongside the ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 that form part of the C-terminal tier (C-tier) of the two-tiered hexameric MCM ring (Fig. 4a,b). This arrangement is mediated by a conserved 21-aa α-helix at the N terminus of PRIMPOL binding to MCM7 and an approximately 20-aa loop immediately downstream of the helix that is sandwiched between a shallow groove on MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). The PRIMPOL AEP domain is positioned laterally adjacent to the exit of the MCM central pore, through which the unwound leading-strand template emerges. Moreover, superimposing the crystal structure of PRIMPOL bound to primer-template DNA26 onto the AEP domain in our structure demonstrates that its catalytic core is oriented to support primer synthesis directly as template DNA is fed from CMG (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 4c).

According to recent reports, a, Cryo-EM density map of the CMG–PRIMPOL structure coloured by subunit occupancy. b, Close-up view of PRIMPOL bound to MCM4 and MCM7. The atomic model is shown in ribbon representation; the cryo-EM density is shown as a semi-transparent surface. c, Primary structure diagram of PRIMPOL with the regions visible in the cryo-EM structure shown in pink. d, Model illustrating the possible path of DNA from CMG to PRIMPOL. The protein structure shown is the CMG–PRIMPOL structure from this study. The DNA in the model was generated by superpositioning the PRIMPOL–DNA structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 5L2X) and CMG-forked DNA structure (PDB: 7PFO) onto the PRIMPOL–CMG structure in this study.

Guided by our cryo-EM structure, to evaluate the role of the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction in replication fork restart, we removed the first 39 aa of PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL∆1–39) (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). Figure 5b highlights that wild-type PRIMPOL but not PRIMPOL∆1–39 was robustly pulled down by CMG, confirming that the PRIMPOL N terminus harbours the primary CMG interaction motifs. PRIMPOL∆1–39 retained primase activity on a ssDNA template (Extended Data Fig. 5b) but was unable to promote fork restart by leading-strand repriming in the human replisome (Fig. 5c,d, lane 4). This defect was not rescued by Pol δ addition (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We conclude that the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is essential for leading-strand repriming by reconstituted human replisomes.

a, Primary structure diagrams of PRIMPOL focusing on the regions in the N terminus that bind to MCM7 and MCM4. Mutants generated within that region are shown. b, Silver-stained and western blot SDS–PAGE analysis of a pull-down experiment with the indicated proteins. c,d, Denaturing agarose (c) and urea polyacrylamide (d) gel analysis of 40-min replication reactions with PRIMPOL mutants. Samples in d were digested post-replicatively with SalI and NruI. e, Close-up view of the interaction between PRIMPOL and MCM4. The model is shown in ribbon representation in semi-transparent cryo-EM density. Amino acid residues targeted for mutagenesis are depicted (sticks). f, Denaturing agarose gel analysis of a 40-min replication reaction on the CPD template with the indicated PRIMPOL concentrations. g, Cisplatin sensitivity assay performed for the TK6 cell lines specified. The data are the average of three biological replicates, and error bars represent the standard deviation. P values are the result of statistical testing using two-way analysis of cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (see Extended Data Table 2 for all P values); pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL∆1–39 P** = 0.0064554, primpol/pcnaK164R compared with +PRIMPOL P* = 0.024598.

According to recent reports, we next investigated whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG functions exclusively in PRIMPOL recruitment or whether accurate positioning of the AEP domain is necessary for efficient replication fork restart. Abolishing PRIMPOL interaction with MCM7 by removing the α-helix at the extreme N terminus of PRIMPOL (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL∆1–21) resulted in a modest reduction in leading-strand restart (Fig. 5c, denaturing, lane 5), with a disproportionate effect on initiation events that occurred closest to the CPD (Fig. 5d, Urea PAGE, lane 5). Retaining α-helix 1–21 but substituting the ensuing loop (aa 22–39) with a glycine–serine linker (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOLGS22–39), or substituting six residues in the loop to alanine (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL6A loop), resulted in complete loss of restart products (Fig. 5c,d, lanes 6 and 7). These results highlight the importance of this loop, which sits between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain, for leading-strand restart.

Furthermore, targeting three loop residues that sit at the interface with MCM4 (Arg31, Leu32 and Ser33; Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL3A loop) resulted in a less severe defect than a mutant targeting the side chains of Tyr28 and Arg29 to disrupt the bridging interaction between MCM4 and the PRIMPOL AEP domain (Fig. 5a, PRIMPOL2A loop) (Fig. 5c–e). This observation strongly suggests that rigid PRIMPOL positioning alongside the MCM C-tier is necessary for efficient leading-strand restart in the human replisome.

According to recent reports, in our reconstituted system, the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG (Fig. 5c), but not between PRIMPOL RBMs and RPA (Fig. 3b), is essential for fork restart. Therefore, because PRIMPOL RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL activity in cells9,11,16,17, we hypothesized that the RBM-mediated interaction might serve to increase the local concentration of PRIMPOL at the replication fork. This function may not be required under our standard in vitro reaction conditions, which use a relatively high concentration (20 nM) of PRIMPOL. To test this idea, we performed a titration of wild-type PRIMPOL and PRIMPOLΔRBM. With wild-type PRIMPOL, leading-strand restart became less efficient only when the protein concentration was reduced to 0.1 nM (Fig. 5f and Extended Data Fig. 5d). By contrast, leading-strand restart was compromised at 1 nM PRIMPOLΔRBM and was barely detectable at 0.1 nM. These findings are consistent with a model in which the RBM-mediated interaction between PRIMPOL and RPA facilitates PRIMPOL localization at the replication fork.

Loss of PRIMPOL does not sensitize many human cell lines to DNA damage because of redundant DNA damage tolerance pathways27,28,29. Therefore, to evaluate whether the interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG is required for PRIMPOL function in human cells, we took advantage of our recent finding that loss of PRIMPOL sensitizes translesion synthesis (TLS)-deficient TK6 lymphoblastoid cells to cisplatin, most prominently observed in cells unable to ubiquitinate PCNA at lysine 164 (ref. 27). PRIMPOL was removed by CRISPR–Cas9 targeting in pcnaK164R cells. Figure 5g indicates that loss of PRIMPOL further sensitized pcnaK164R cells to cisplatin, consistent with our previous work27. Whereas expression of wild-type PRIMPOL fully rescued this phenotype, expression of PRIMPOL∆1–39 did not complement the additional cisplatin sensitivity of pcnaK164R cells (Fig. 5g, Extended Data Fig. 6 and Extended Data Table 2). These data indicate that the interaction between CMG and PRIMPOL, which is essential for fork restart in vitro, is important for PRIMPOL-mediated DNA damage tolerance in human cells.

In a recent development, on the basis of our results and previous work, we propose the following model for replication fork restart by PRIMPOL-dependent repriming (Fig. 6a). Our biochemical reconstitution has demonstrated that the PRIMPOL RBMs are not essential for leading-strand repriming in vitro. However, they do become important for fork restart at low PRIMPOL concentrations, and evidence from cellular studies highlights that RBM-A is required for PRIMPOL recruitment to chromatin and fork progression during replication stress9,11,16,17. To accommodate these observations, we propose that the interaction of PRIMPOL with RPA, which is low affinity11 and therefore likely to be transient, serves primarily to localize PRIMPOL to actively replicating genomic loci, which may be necessary because PRIMPOL is a relatively low abundance protein in human cells15,30 (Fig. 6a).

It has been revealed that a, Model for CMG-directed replication fork restart by PRIMPOL after the replisome encounters a leading-strand DNA lesion (red triangle). Two non-mutually exclusive mechanisms are shown. In (i), PRIMPOL is recruited to CMG only after fork stalling at the lesion. In (ii), PRIMPOL can associate with CMG and travel with the replisome before fork stalling. b, Composite model of the human replisome showing the positions of PRIMPOL, Pol ε and Pol α–primase. The model is a composite of the following PDB files: 8B9D, 7PFO and 9F6D. The position of the Pol ε catalytic domain (9F6D) is based on a yeast replisome structure42.

On encountering a DNA lesion, leading-strand synthesis by Pol ε is blocked, but CMG continues to translocate along the template at a greatly reduced rate1,2, exposing ssDNA on the leading-strand template between the helicase and polymerase (Fig. 6a). Through its interactions with MCM4 and MCM7, PRIMPOL is positioned to capture the exposed ssDNA to initiate leading-strand repriming (Fig. 6a, pathway (i)). After primer synthesis, Pol ε must reengage the leading strand for optimal fork progression to resume. The anchoring of PRIMPOL on CMG suggests a pathway in which the primer might be handed off directly to the leading-strand PCNA loader CTF18-RFC and then to Pol ε. Alternatively, Pol δ might facilitate the recoupling of leading-strand synthesis by extending the primer made by PRIMPOL until it reaches CMG, at which point the 3′ end is transferred to Pol ε. This pathway has been observed following leading-strand lesion bypass by TLS in the yeast replisome31.

Industry observers note that the direct interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG raises the possibility that PRIMPOL could travel with CMG to facilitate its immediate deployment on helicase–polymerase uncoupling (Fig. 6a, pathway (ii)). In this regard, it is noteworthy that PRIMPOL does not clash with any known core replisome protein, including Pol ε (Fig. 6b). However, because the MCM4 and MCM7 ATPase domains undergo conformational changes during CMG translocation that could affect PRIMPOL binding, single-molecule studies will be required to determine if PRIMPOL can stably associate with moving replisomes.

It has been revealed that the mechanism of PRIMPOL recruitment via MCM4 and MCM7 ensures that repriming is tightly coupled to CMG progression to limit the size of the ssDNA gap that is left for post-replicative repair pathways. Our work further establishes that PRIMPOL displays a sequence preference for primer synthesis. Based on prior studies, this sequence is short and somewhat degenerate25, which should enable efficient repriming at most genomic loci. However, regions of the genome devoid of optimal priming sites are likely to exist, for example in repetitive DNA, which could limit repriming and bias fork restart and stabilisation towards alternative pathways.

Industry observers note that the two-stage model for PRIMPOL recruitment involving both RPA and CMG interactions is analogous to a mechanism proposed for the recruitment of TLS polymerases to the replication fork32. This mechanism has been observed in the E. coli replisome for the TLS polymerase PolIV, where an interaction with the single-stranded DNA-binding protein SSB concentrates PolIV at the fork to promote its interaction with the sliding clamp β33. We also note that RPA will accumulate on the leading-strand template during prolonged uncoupling, which should enhance PRIMPOL recruitment to stressed replication forks.

Sources indicate that apart from its low abundance, PRIMPOL activity is regulated by checkpoint and cell cycle kinases6,34,35,36, suggesting that excessive repriming and daughter-strand gap formation is deleterious. Tight regulation of PRIMPOL might also indicate a capacity of the enzyme to interfere with normal replisome function. We reasoned that this could be a consequence of PRIMPOL being directed to the leading strand by CMG, causing it to interfere with Pol ε by competing for the nascent leading strand. Consistent with this idea, addition of PRIMPOL mildly slowed fork progression on an undamaged template, and this effect was exacerbated by omission of CTF18-RFC, which compromises PCNA loading on the leading strand (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Importantly, this inhibition was dependent on the interaction of PRIMPOL with CMG but not on primase activity (Extended Data Fig. 7b).

The widespread phylogenetic distribution of PRIMPOL37, and the conservation of its CMG interaction motifs, indicates an evolutionary pressure to keep replication forks moving by repriming. It also indicates that in the absence of chronic replication stress, repriming might be the default response of the replisome to impediments to leading-strand synthesis. This raises the possibility that leading-strand synthesis might be considerably more discontinuous in human cells than previously appreciated. It is also interesting to consider that PRIMPOL could access the leading strand for priming potentially in any instance where synthesis is paused, for example during PCNA loading on the leading strand by CTF18-RFC. This is possibly a frequent occurrence because PCNA abundance is reported to be similar on leading and lagging strands in yeast38.

Industry observers note that multiple pathways collaborate to protect and restart stalled replication forks during replication stress. Ablating replication fork reversal factors has been found to promote fork progression in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner6,34,39,40,41, suggesting an interplay between repriming and replication fork remodelling. The factors that dictate the balance between repriming and other fork processing pathways (for example, fork reversal), and how this is influenced by the CMG–PRIMPOL interaction, is an crucial area for future study, especially given that PRIMPOL promotes chemoresistance in BRCA1 deficient cells34.

Sources indicate that for decades, prokaryotic and eukaryotic replisomes were thought to function with a single primase to initiate DNA synthesis on both template strands. This changed with the discovery of PRIMPOL as a second primase in many eukaryotic species, including humans7,8,9. However, although it has been demonstrated that PRIMPOL facilitates replication fork progression during replication stress in a range of metazoan cell lines, evidence for PRIMPOL primase activity being directed specifically to the leading-strand template, and a plausible mechanism for this targeting, was lacking. The work presented here demonstrates that, through its interactions with CMG, PRIMPOL is a dedicated leading-strand primase, establishing a division of labour in the human replisome: Pol α–primase acts on the lagging strand14, while PRIMPOL operates on the leading strand. Our data, together with the strong conservation of CMG-binding motifs in the PRIMPOL N terminus, indicate that many eukaryotic replisomes rely on strand-specific primases to maintain efficient replisome progression, and that this specificity is governed by helicase-directed primase recruitment to the replication fork.

In a recent development, replication reactions were performed essentially as described previously, with the following modifications. Reactions were assembled stepwise: DNA (2.4 nM) was first incubated with CMG (50 nM) for 10 min in replication buffer supplemented with 0.1 mM AMP-PNP. Following this pre-incubation, the mixture was diluted two-fold with replication buffer containing 30 μM dATP and dCTP. Additional replication factors (20 nM PCNA, 20 nM RFC, 20 nM Pol ε, 10 nM Pol α, 20 nM CLASPIN, 20 nM TIM–TIPIN, 20 nM AND1 and 20 nM CTF18-RFC) were included at this stage unless stated otherwise. Replication was initiated by adding a concentrated start mix supplying 4 mM ATP; 30 µM dTTP and dGTP; 200 µM GTP, CTP and UTP; 33 nM α-[32P]-dCTP; and 100 nM RPA. When present, 20 nM PRIMPOL was added 2–3 min after replication had started. For reactions containing Pol δ, potassium glutamate was increased to 250 mM, and the polymerase was added at 2 nM immediately before the start mix. Leading-strand restart reactions were typically incubated for 20–40 min and terminated with EDTA to 50 mM. Unincorporated radiolabel was removed using Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns. Replication products were separated by alkaline agarose electrophoresis (0.7% agarose, 30 mM NaOH, 2 mM EDTA) run for 16.5 h at 24 V, fixed in cold 5% trichloroacetic acid, dried on Whatman paper, and visualized using an Amersham Typhoon phosphorimager scanner.

For analysis under native conditions, terminated reactions were supplemented with SDS (0.1%) and proteinase K (0.2 mg ml−1; New England Biolabs) and incubated for 10 min at 37 °C. DNA was purified by phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol extraction (25:24:1; TE-equilibrated) and passed through Illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns to remove unincorporated nucleotides. Samples were then digested with SapI–PciI for 30 min at 37 °C to remove the template ends and prevent end-labelled species in gels. Following digestion, reactions underwent a second SDS/proteinase K treatment and phenol:chloroform extraction to ensure complete protein removal. DNA was ethanol-precipitated, washed with 70% ethanol, resuspended in native loading dye (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM EDTA, 10% Ficoll 400, 2% N-lauroylsarcosine sodium salt solution), and resolved on 1% agarose gels run overnight at 24 V in modified 1× TAE buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.9, 40 mM sodium acetate, 1 mM EDTA pH 8.0). Gels were dried and imaged as described above.

It has been revealed that for two-dimensional (2D) gel analysis, samples were prepared as for native conditions and loaded into two lanes of a native agarose gel, with 10% of the reaction applied to one lane and the remaining 90% to the other. After electrophoresis, the lane containing the bulk of the sample was excised and placed horizontally along the top of a 0.7% denaturing agarose gel for the second dimension, which was run for 16.5 h at 27 V. Gels were then processed and imaged as described for alkaline gels.

It has been revealed that for analysis on denaturing polyacrylamide gels, samples were prepared as for native conditions, but digested with SalI–NruI instead, and resuspended in loading dye (95% formamide, 20 mM EDTA, 0.04% Bromophenol Blue and 0.04% xylene cyanol). Samples were boiled for 5 min at 75 °C and resolved on a 40 cm × 20 cm 3.5% denaturing polyacrylamide gel. Gels were run in 1× TBE for 150 min at 40 W and dried as described above.

It has been revealed that DNA substrates were prepared following previously published methods1,20. Gapped pZN3 was produced by introducing two adjacent Nt.BbvCI nicks and heating the plasmid to release the short intervening oligonucleotide, which was subsequently displaced using a sequestering oligonucleotide. The resulting gapped plasmid was purified on a Sepharose 4B (Sigma-Aldrich 4B200) gel filtration column. A 10-fold molar excess of a short oligonucleotide containing a CPD lesion, an abasic site or an undamaged control sequence (listed in Supplementary Table 1) was then annealed into the gap and ligated to generate the damaged or control templates. Finally, the DNA was digested with SapI, ligated to a pre-annealed fork structure, and purified again over a Sepharose 4B column.

Replication proteins were expressed in either E. coli or insect cells (Sf9 and Hi-5) and were purified following the methods described previously20,43. For more details about the purification steps, see Supplementary Table 2.

Relevant plasmids for protein expression were transformed into Rosetta2 cells using standard bacterial transformation protocols. A single transformant colony was selected and cultured in 1 l LB media supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and 10 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol overnight at 30 °C without agitation. The following morning, the culture temperature was increased to 37 °C and incubated with shaking at 210 rpm. On reaching an optical density (OD600) of 0.6–0.8, protein expression was induced by the addition of 1 mM IPTG for 3 h. Cells were subsequently harvested, washed with PBS and flash-frozen for storage.

Recent findings suggest that wild-type and mutant PRIMPOL proteins were purified using the following protocol. Cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM TCEP and protease inhibitors (cOmplete, EDTA-free; Roche). The cells were lysed by sonication (three cycles of 1 min each, consisting of 5 s ‘on’ and 5 s ‘off’ pulses at 40% amplitude), and insoluble material was removed by centrifugation at 235,000g for 50 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with 1 ml Strep-Tactin XT Superflow high-capacity resin for 1 h at 4 °C. The resin was then collected and washed extensively with 100 ml lysis buffer, followed by sequential washes with 25 ml lysis buffer containing 0.55 M NaCl and 35 ml lysis buffer containing 0.1 M NaCl to reduce the salt concentration. Bound protein was eluted in 1 ml fractions using eight column volumes of 0.1 M NaCl lysis buffer supplemented with 30 mM biotin. Protein-containing fractions were pooled and loaded onto a 5 ml HiTrap Heparin HP column pre-equilibrated in 0.1 M NaCl buffer. The protein was eluted with a 20 column volume linear gradient from 100 mM to 1 M NaCl. Peak fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 1 l of storage buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 0.3 M potassium acetate, 10% glycerol, 0.02% NP-40-S and 0.5 mM TCEP. Finally, the protein was concentrated using a 30 kDa molecular weight cut-off spin concentrator (Amicon Ultra-30), flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Sources indicate that reactions (20 µl) were performed in buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 150 mM potassium glutamate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 0.05% NP-40, and 1 mM DTT. CMG (5 pmol) was incubated with PRIMPOL (10 pmol; wild-type or Δ1–39) for 30 min on ice. A 2 µl aliquot was removed as input, and the remaining mixture was incubated with 5 µl α-Flag magnetic beads equilibrated in buffer for 30 min at 4 °C with shaking (1,250 rpm). Beads were washed three times with 100 µl reaction buffer, and bound proteins were eluted for 30 min at 4 °C at 1,250 rpm in 20 µl buffer containing 0.2 mg ml−1 Flag peptide. Eluates were mixed with loading buffer and analysed by 4–12% SDS–PAGE alongside input samples, followed by silver staining and western blotting.

Protein samples from pull-down assays with purified proteins were resolved on NuPAGE Novex 4–12% Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher) in MOPS buffer and transferred to PVDF membranes using the iBlot Dry Transfer System (Life Technologies). Membranes were blocked for 30 min at room temperature in 5% milk-TBST. For the detection of PRIMPOL, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with anti-PRIMPOL (Proteintech; 29824-1-AP, see Supplementary Table 3) followed by a secondary antibody incubation for another hour at room temperature (anti-rabbit-HRP, see Supplementary Table 3). For the detection of strep-SLD5, membranes were incubated for 2 h at room temperature with anti-strep-HRP antibody. Both membranes were subsequently incubated with Amersham ECL western blotting detection reagent, and the emitted chemiluminescence was detected on film and developed in an automatic film processor. The films were scanned using an Epson Scan V850 pro.

For the detection of PRIMPOL from TK6 extracts, protein was extracted from cells by lysing cells directly with RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher) supplemented with 1× protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma) for 10 min on ice. To quantify protein concentration, a BCA assay was performed using the Pierce Protein Assay Kit (Thermo) as per kit instructions. Protein lysate (20 µg) was prepared with 1× Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad), supplemented with 10% β-mercaptoethanol. Denatured protein was run using NuPAGE Novex 4–12% Bis-Tris gels (Thermo Fisher). The samples were then transferred onto a PVDF membrane. The membranes were blocked in 5% BSA in Tris-buffered saline (TBS) with 1% Tween (TBS-T) for 2 h at room temperature with rocking. The blocked membranes were incubated in blocking buffer with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 3) at 4 °C for 12–20 h. Membranes were incubated with Licor IRDye 800CW Rabbit secondary antibody at 20,000× dilution in blocking buffer for 30 min at room temperature. Membranes were washed three times with 10 ml fresh TBS-T for 5 min at room temperature with rocking. Antibody detection and image capture were carried out using the Bio-Rad ChemiDoc.

Industry observers note that reactions were adapted from a previously described study11. Human RPA (240 nM) was first incubated with 5 nM M13 single-stranded DNA (Upcoming England Biolabs) for 10 min at 37 °C in 10 µl reactions containing 25 mM HEPES-KOH (pH 7.6), 100 mM potassium acetate, 10 mM magnesium acetate, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, 0.1 mg ml−1 BSA, 400 µM rNTPs, 80 µM dNTPs, 3 mM ATP and 33 nM α-[32P]-dCTP. PRIMPOL (400 nM; wild-type or mutants) was then added, and reactions were incubated for a further 30 min at 37 °C. DNA synthesis was stopped with 50 mM EDTA, and unincorporated radiolabel was removed using illustra MicroSpin G-50 columns. The samples were mixed with loading buffer (95% formamide, 20 mM EDTA, 0.04% Bromophenol Blue and 0.04% xylene cyanol), heated at 75 °C for 5 min, and resolved on a 40 cm × 20 cm 10% denaturing polyacrylamide gel run at 40 W for 105 min. The gels were dried and imaged as described above.

PRIMPOL, purified as described above, was concentrated using an Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter with a 30 kDa MWCO and injected onto a 2.4 ml S200 increase 3.2/300 column equilibrated with 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT. The peak fractions were collected and adjusted with buffer to a concentration of 5.7 µM. CMG was dialysed overnight against 40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.6, 80 mM KOAc, 1 mM DTT, mixed with 1.3-fold molar excess of PRIMPOL, supplemented with 3.3 mM ATP and incubated on ice for at least 20 min before cryo-EM grid preparation. After incubation on ice, 2 µl of the sample was applied to freshly glow-discharged (Edwards Sputter Coater S150B, 45 s at 30 mA) UltrAuFoil R1.2/1.3, manually blotted on the top face for 2 s and immediately plunged into liquid ethane at liquid nitrogen temperature. Two datasets of 8,160 and 8,103 raw movies, respectively, were acquired using a 300 kV TFS Titan Krios microscope equipped with a Falcon 4i direct electron detector operated in electron counting mode using ThermoFisher EPU with AFIS enabled. The movies were collected over a defocus range of −1.0 µm to −2.6 µm, at an effective pixel size of 0.84 Å per pixel.

The data processing pipeline is shown as a schematic in Extended Data Fig. 4a. Raw movies were motion-corrected and dose-weighted using the implementation of a MotionCor2-like program of RELION44,45 (Extended Data Table 1) and then imported to CryoSPARC v.4.7.1 (ref. 46) for further processing. For each dataset, the particles were first ‘blob’-picked and extracted with 4-fold binning (336 Å box size). The 2D classification was run on a subset of 50,000 particles, and classes showing features for CMG in 2D-class averages were selected. Ab initio reconstruction was performed with the selected particles and, separately, with the remaining particles to generate three-dimensional (3D) volumes for either CMG or ‘noise/junk’-classes. The obtained volumes were provided as 3D references in two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement of all extracted particles, the first round of which the particles of the best class were selected for the second round. Independently, 2D class averages were used for template-based picking, and the resulting particles were also subjected to two iterative rounds of heterogeneous refinement as described above. The particles of the best 3D class from each picking strategy were combined and duplicate particles were removed. The resulting particles were used for homogeneous refinement with minimization over per-particle scale enabled, after which the particle population with poor signal (relative per-particle scale below 0.75) was removed. The remaining particles were subjected to 3D classification using a focus mask around the C-tier of the MCM ring, and particle classes with good definition for secondary structure features in the MCM C-tier were selected. At this stage, particles from datasets 1 and 2 were combined and locally refined using a focus mask around the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The resulting 3D reconstruction displayed density for the AEP domain of PRIMPOL around which a local mask was drawn for 3D classification. The largest class (135,661 particles) also exhibited the strongest signal for PRIMPOL. The particles were recentred on a mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7, re-extracted (280-pixel box, downsampled to 160 pixels, 1.47 Å per pixel) and subjected to signal subtraction with an inverted mask around PRIMPOL and ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7. The subtracted particles were used for 3D classification from which the classes with the best density for the PRIMPOL AEP domain were selected (65,500 particles). The 30,000-particle subset with the best per-particle scale was then used for 3DFlex47 to reconstruct the final map for the PRIMPOL AEP domain near the AAA+ ATPase domains of MCM4 and MCM7 (map 1, 3.5 Å resolution). The same particle subset was reverted to the original (non-subtracted) images, re-extracted from the original micrographs without binning (440-pixel box, 0.84 Å per pixel) using particle poses from global refinement on the CMG helicase. The obtained particles were subjected to homogeneous refinement to reconstruct a consensus map (map 2), or to local refinements with either a focus mask on CMG components GINS, CDC45 and the N-tier of the MCM ring (map 3, 3.1 Å resolution), or a focus mask on the C-tier of the MCM ring (map 4, 3.3 Å resolution). Maps coloured by estimated local resolution are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4c. Fourier shell correlation plots are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4d. Focus maps (maps 1, 3 and 4) were fitted into the consensus volume (map 2) using ChimeraX48. An initial atomic model was obtained by rigid-body fitting previously reported structures of CMG (6XTX, 7PFO) and PRIMPOL (5L2X) into the consensus EM volume using ChimeraX26,43,49. The fit-to-density was subsequently refined using ISOLDE50 inside ChimeraX. ATP–ADP ligands and gaps in the model were built de novo in Coot51. The molecular model was then used together with the consensus map and all focus maps to generate a composite EM map using phenix.combine_focused_maps by Thomas Terwilliger. Model geometry and atomic displacement parameters were refined against the composite map using phenix.real_space_refine52, after which model validation was carried out using MolProbity53 inside Phenix. Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. Root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between PRIMPOL–CMG (this study) and PRIMPOL–DNA (5L2X) was calculated in PyMOL (www.pymol.org) for 1,987 pairs of common atoms (RMSD = 1.723) or 253 pairs of common Cα atoms (RMSD = 1.374).

It has been revealed that viscous culture medium (5 ml) consisting of 11.9 g l−1 RPMI 1640 powder with l-glutamine supplement (Gibco), 2 g l−1 sodium hydrogen carbonate (Sigma-Aldrich), 10 g l−1 4,000 cP methylcellulose (Thermo Fisher), 100 U l−1 penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco) and 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco) was added to wells of six-well plates. The plates were equilibrated at 37 °C, 10% CO2 for a minimum of 1 h. The cells were treated with the indicated dose of cisplatin for 1 h at 37 °C and 10% CO2. The cells were then pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in fresh growth media to stop the cisplatin treatment. Then, 500,000, 50,000 or 5,000 cells were added to duplicate wells of the six-well plates for each cell line or condition. The plates were incubated at 37 °C, 5% CO2 until well-defined colonies were visible.

According to recent reports, flow cytometry was used to confirm the expression of GFP in TK6 primpol/pcnaK164R cell lines. A total of 1 × 106 cells were pelleted at 1,200 rpm for 5 min and resuspended in 1 ml PBS supplemented with 2% FBS. The cells were analysed by flow cytometry using a Becton Dickinson LSRFortessa. TK6 primpol and TK6 wild-type cells were used as negative controls for GFP expression. Cell sorting of GFP-positive cells was performed using a Becton Dickinson FACSAria Fusion, with cells sorted into single cells per well of a 96-well plate. Flow cytometry data were plotted using FlowJo.

According to recent reports, for the colony survival assay in TK6 human cells in Fig. 5g, individual colonies in each well were counted using a custom macro-script in ImageJ, and the percentage survival relative to untreated cells was calculated to assess clonogenic survival. Statistical testing was performed by the R package CFAssay using two-way analysis of the cell survival data by fitting a linear quadratic model with maximum likelihood (Extended Data Table 2).

Statistics for cryo-EM data acquisition, processing and molecular model refinement are summarized in Extended Data Table 1. RMSD between PRIMPOL–CMG (this study) and PRIMPOL–DNA (5L2X) was calculated in PyMOL (www.pymol.org) for 1,987 pairs of common atoms (RMSD = 1.723) or 253 pairs of common Cα atoms (RMSD = 1.374).

DNA replication assays were quantified using ImageJ, and data were plotted in Prism.

The experiments in Figs. 1b, 2b,d, 3b,c,e and 5c,d,f and Extended Data Figs. 1b,f, 2a, 3a, 5a,b, 6a,b were performed a minimum of three times. Experiments in Figs. 1c, 3d and 5b and Extended Data Figs. 1a,c–e, 2b, 3b, 5c and 7a,b were performed twice. Colony survival assay in TK6 human cells (Fig. 5g) was performed three times, testing two independent clones of primpol/pcnaK164R + PRIMPOLΔ1–39. Cryo-EM sample preparation was performed twice.

#1922. Latest Update: England: How many games Elliot Anderson will miss after Spain red card

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (468 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: England: How many games Elliot Anderson will miss after Spain red card

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (468 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elliot Anderson is facing a suspension after being sent-off in England’s Nations League win over Spain.
  • Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White had the Three Lions cruising to victory at 3-0 on Sunday night, before Anderson’s challenge on Lamine Yamal produced both a red card and a penalty.
  • Mikel Oyarzabal successfully converted the spot-kick before substitute Nico Williams reduced deficit with 15 minutes plus stoppage time remaining.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elliot Anderson is facing a suspension after being sent-off in England’s Nations League win over Spain.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White had the Three Lions cruising to victory at 3-0 on Sunday night, before Anderson’s challenge on Lamine Yamal produced both a red card and a penalty.

Mikel Oyarzabal successfully converted the spot-kick before substitute Nico Williams reduced deficit with 15 minutes plus stoppage time remaining.

Ultimately, England held on for a famous win and topped Group A3 as a result.

England will discover their quarter-final opponents later this week, but they will be without Anderson for the first-leg because of the red card.

UEFA rules stipulate “a player or team official sent off by the referee is automatically suspended for the next match in the competition.

“In the event of a serious offence, the UEFA disciplinary bodies are entitled to augment this punishment, including by extending it to other competitions.”.

Due to Anderson being given his marching orders in the Spanish capital for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity, rather than violent conduct, his punishment will be a one-game ban.

Therefore, the Manchester City midfielder will be available for the second leg in March 2027 - if named in the England squad by Thomas Tuchel.

Tuchel, meanwhile, slammed the decision as a ‘double punishment’ during his post-match press conference, dissecting a classic England performance after becoming the first team to beat Spain in 43 competitive matches.

Tuchel commented: “The red card and the penalty is always a big decision - and I need to understand why it's a double punishment.

In a recent development, "Then it was a long, long 30 minutes - but I don't want to focus on that. There was so, so many positive things about the result after 60 minutes. It was well deserved.”.

England made the perfect start in the Spanish capital, with Declan Rice claiming post-match that, “The first 10 minutes was the best we’ve played” as Luis de La Fuente’s side struggled to live with England’s pressing.

Recent findings suggest that england triumphed by the same scoreline and in similar fashion to their previous visit to Spain back in October 2018 - in another Nations League encounter played out in Seville, this time. Again, they achieved success by being proactive as opposed to parking the bus.

Fabulous counter-attacking strikes from Raheem Sterling (2) and Marcus Rashford put the visitors 3-0 up to silence the Spanish hordes. It was the prelude to a strong home fightback in the second half, but no victory.

According to recent reports, for too long in the past, certainly before that 2018 occasion in Seville, England had been cowed on their visits to Spain. In their previous four matches, all defeats, they failed to score. Ever since Gary Lineker, then at Barcelona, struck all four goals in a stunner at Madrid's Bernebeu Stadium in February 1987.

Spain's previous defeat was back in March 2023 against Scotland in Glasgow.

Paris Saint-Germain are reportedly prepared to compete with Barcelona for a Premier League defender the Catalan club dream of lining up in central defence alongside Pau Cubarsi. According to El Nacional, that defender is Manchester City’s Josko Gvardiol.

It is no secret that Barcelona want to use the January transfer window to sign a upcoming centre-back. Germany international Jonathan Tah, whom Bayern Munich have no intention of losing, is no longer an option, but the Catalan hierarchy have activated other profiles. Hansi Flick’s side have also positioned themselves for Gvardiol.

According to recent reports, able to play in central defence, the Croatia international is most often used as a left-back by boss Enzo Maresca. Across the Premier League and the Champions League, the 24-year-old has started nine times in that position since the beginning of 2026-27. But it is for central defence that Barcelona are thinking strongly about his arrival, with an improbable chance of success as early as January 2027.

According to recent reports, according to El Nacional, the plan is to make him a future ‘ideal partner’ for Cubarsi, in an area where Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen are options with limited time left. Barcelona will have to convince Manchester City to sell a player of this calibre, who has a contract until 2031 and a reported market value of around £64m.

Recent findings suggest that another obstacle for Barcelona is fierce competition from other European powers. According to the same source, PSG, Liverpool, Bayern Munich and Chelsea are also interested in the former Dinamo Zagreb player.

Like their illustrious rivals, the French capital club are closely monitoring possible sanctions against Manchester City, who are threatened with relegation because of their financial irregularities and who, if such a sentence is confirmed, could be forced to sell all of their leading players.

PSG’s reported interest runs into two questions, however. Until proven otherwise, the double Champions League holders are not prioritising a left-back, preferring a right-sided centre-back and a right-back to back up Achraf Hakimi.

Gvardiol may also be more tempted by a challenge at Barcelona, in a squad where competition looks less fierce than at PSG, with Willian Pacho in central defence and Nuno Mendes on the left.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

According to recent reports, emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

Ben White has scored only 12 goals in his senior career but two have been for England, including the eventual winner in a famous win in Madrid.

Has had to field booing from sections of England fans since his return to the international fold in March after he walked away from their World Cup squad in 2022, but is rebuilding his England career successfully and will be thought of by Tuchel as one of his most well-balanced right-back options now.

Hopes to climb above Reece James and become first choice.

Hall has come back stronger and this month backed up his encouraging displays from the last international break.

Solid in the 2-1 win over Croatia, he was on another level entirely in Madrid, taking care of the threat of Lamine Yamal and finding a perfect balance between defence and attack as he helped England to victory in the world champions’ own backyard.

The No3 shirt is his to lose now.

And after his heroics in Spain, even more so there is a debate to be had over whether it is time for England’s first-choice goalkeeper to be Leeds United’s Trafford rather than his Everton counterpart.

Pickford has never let England down in 94 caps, but Trafford made a string of stellar saves in Madrid and is eight years his junior.

The Bayer Leverkusen defender has become accustomed to the bulk of his England game time being at right-back during this calendar year, but a shortage of centre-back options this month saw him start in the middle in both games.

Trent Alexander-Arnold has struggled to secure regular game time at Real Madrid this season, but a return to Liverpool in January appears to be out of the question.

The 28-year-old joined Madrid from Liverpool in the summer of 2025 and has made 43 appearances for the Spanish giants across all competitions.

However, the England international has managed just four starts in La Liga this season, with a further three appearances coming off the bench.

Alexander-Arnold has lost his place to Federico Valverde, with Jose Mourinho preferring to deploy the midfielder at right-back ahead of two recognised full-backs.

This has fuelled speculation that a potential return to Liverpool could be on the cards, but Fabrizio Romano has poured cold water on those rumours.

Romano has dismissed suggestions that all three parties are involved in discussions over a potential transfer.

Alexander-Arnold rose through Liverpool's academy to establish himself as one of the best right-backs in world football, although his departure from Anfield was not universally well received.

"Let’s immediately clarify one thing, there is zero ongoing between Trent Alexander-Arnold, Real Madrid and Liverpool, zero at all," said Romano to DAZN Football, as relayed by Roundtable.

The Italian journalist further emphasised that, while Alexander-Arnold retains enormous affection for the Reds, his priorities remain firmly in the Spanish capital.

It has been revealed that "Trent obviously respects and loves the club but that’s it, it’s in the past. Trent is fully focused on Real Madrid and there is no contact or negotiation at all with Liverpool.".

The England right-back would have been a fantastic addition to Andoni Iraola's system, but it appears unlikely that the Reds have any plans to bring him back.

Jeremie Frimpong has struggled to make a significant impact, but Ronald Araujo, who joined on loan from Barcelona, has done a decent job at right-back so far.

Conor Bradley remains sidelined through injury and is unlikely to return before the end of the year, but bringing in another right-back is not currently a top priority for Liverpool.

The 2026-27 Nations League draw for the quarter-finals takes place this week, as the business end of the competition comes into focus.

England are among the five teams to have qualified for the knockout phase, as things right now stand, with Thomas Tuchel’s side enjoying a near perfect group phase.

Their only defeat came against reigning world champions Spain on matchday one in September, though the Three Lions exacted revenge on Sunday night as they held on after being reduced to 10-men to seal a famous victory.

As a result, England topped Group A3 at Spain’s expense due to a superior goal difference and that means they are likely to avoid another European heavyweight in the quarter-finals.

Elsewhere, France sealed top spot in Group A1 with a 2-1 win over Turkey, while Belgium thumped Italy 4-1 to finish as runners-up.

Portugal’s position in Group A4 is still to be confirmed after they were humbled at home by Denmark in their first game since Cristano Ronaldo unveiled his retirement from international football.

The Nations League draw for the 2026/27 quarter-finals will take place on Friday, November 20, following the conclusion of the group phase fixtures.

As well as the quarter-final draw, the promotion/relegation play-offs draw will also be conducted.

Coverage of the draw is due to start at 11am GMT, with the draw itself expected to begin shortly afterwards.

The Nations League draw will take place in Nyon, Switzerland.

TV channel: In the UK, the draw will be televised live UEFA TV.

Live stream: You can also stream the draw for free online via the UEFA YouTube page.

Live blog: You can follow the draw as it happens on the day through Standard Sport’s live blog.

The four group winners will face the four runners-up in a two-legged Nations League quarter-final.

In a recent development, the group winners will all be seeded and will have home advantage in their respective second leg ties. Teams from the same group cannot be paired together in the knockout stage, therefore England and Spain - for example - will be kept apart.

The four group winners will be seeded in Pot 1, with the four runners-up will be unseeded in Pot 2.

Pot 1: France, England, TBC, TBC.

Pot 2: Belgium, Spain, TBC, TBC.

*Portugal are guaranteed a Nations League quarter-final spot, though can still finish first or second in Group A4.

The Nations League quarter-finals, as well as the League A/B and League B/C promotion/relegation play-offs, will be played in March 2027.

The first-legs are scheduled for March 25-27, with the return legs scheduled for March 28-30.

The final tournament is scheduled for June 2027.

Aberdeen have appointed former Liechtenstein international Mario Frick as their upcoming head coach.

The 52-year-old will take charge at Pittodrie, subject to the completion of UK visa formalities, following a successful spell with Swiss side FC Luzern.

Frick arrives in the north-east after five years in charge of Luzern, where he transformed the club’s fortunes after taking over in December 2021 with the team rooted to the bottom of the Swiss Super League. He guided them away from relegation trouble before leading them to a fourth-place finish and qualification for European football.

Announcing the appointment, Aberdeen chief executive Adrian Bevington remarked the club had undertaken an extensive recruitment process before selecting Frick as the man to lead the Dons forward.

Bevington stated: 'We are delighted to welcome Mario Frick and his assistant coach Roman Matter to Aberdeen Football Club.

In a recent development, 'Mario has significant experience as a head coach and has delivered impressive results with both Vaduz and Luzern. He has a proven track record of building competitive teams and developing young players.

'Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team.'.

Sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel also welcomed the appointment and believes Frick has the qualities to make a major impact at Pittodrie.

Pfannenstiel said: 'Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play. He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment.

Aberdeen have appointed Mario Frick as their new manager.

'We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I’m convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact.'.

Recent findings suggest that before his spell with Luzern, Frick managed FC Balzers and FC Vaduz, winning promotion to the Swiss Super League with the latter. Across almost 290 senior matches as a head coach, he built a reputation for developing young talent, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players.

As a player, Frick represented clubs including FC Basel, FC Zürich, St Gallen, Grasshopper, Siena and Ternana. A striker who could also operate in defence, he won 125 caps for Liechtenstein between 1993 and 2016 and remains his country’s record goalscorer with 16 international goals.

Frick said: 'I’m excited to be joining Aberdeen FC. It’s a club with a proud history, passionate supporters and massive ambitions.

'Together with the staff, my aim is to create an environment where the players can thrive, develop and perform at their very best, while working towards our goals as a team.'.

Frick and assistant coach Matter are expected to arrive in Aberdeen at the start of the week and will begin preparations for next weekend’s Premiership clash with Kilmarnock.

💡 Key Takeaways
