  • Tunisia will be looking to repair their faltering Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign when they travel to the 11 June Stadium in Tripoli to face Libya on Tuesday.
  • The Mediterranean Knights moved onto four points from three Group H matches with Friday's victory in Sfax, while the Eagles of Carthage sit bottom of the table with two points, still waiting for their first win of the campaign.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 15 Nov 2026 21:42.

Tunisia will be looking to repair their faltering Africa Cup of Nations qualifying campaign when they travel to the 11 June Stadium in Tripoli to face Libya on Tuesday.

The Mediterranean Knights moved onto four points from three Group H matches with Friday's victory in Sfax, while the Eagles of Carthage sit bottom of the table with two points, still waiting for their first win of the campaign.

Libya opened their AFCON qualifying campaign with a 2-2 draw at home to Botswana, coming from two goals down through Marwan Al-Habashi's strike in the 87th minute and Ezoo El Mariamy's penalty deep into stoppage time.

They then suffered a 1-0 defeat away to Uganda, with Arnold Vula scoring the only goal, leaving them bottom of Group H before Friday's result moved them towards the top end of the table.

Coach Youssouph Dabo, the Senegalese who replaced Ali Cisse, had not won a competitive match in charge before Friday, making the victory all the more significant.

In Sfax, Libya took the lead after Ali Maaloul fouled Muaid Issa in the box, allowing Ali Youssef to convert from the penalty spot in the 44th minute, before Hamdou El Houni doubled their advantage on the counter-attack shortly after the hour mark.

The result marked Tunisia's heaviest home defeat in AFCON qualifying and the first time they had trailed by two goals on home soil in the competition.

It also ended more than 25 years without a two-goal home defeat in the qualifiers, prompting angry supporters to throw bottles and set off flares, while players and staff confronted referee Hamza El Fariq, who was subsequently escorted from the stadium.

Coach Mouine Chaabani has since apologised to supporters and admitted that the defeat was deserved, although Tunisia's decline stretches further back than the current qualifying campaign.

They lost all three matches at the 2026 World Cup, suffering defeats against Sweden (5-1), Japan (4-0) and the Netherlands (3-1), and have now gone nine games without a win, including September's draws against Uganda (1-1) and Botswana (2-2).

Before this campaign, Tunisia had qualified for each of the last 17 AFCON finals, the longest active streak of any nation, but with only one team besides co-hosts Uganda able to progress from Group H, they are running out of room for error.

Their record against Libya remains encouraging, however, as the visitors had won the previous six meetings before Friday's encounter, including a 5-2 away victory in 2021 and 3-0 and 1-0 wins in 2023.

Libya Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

Tunisia Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

Tunisia form (all competitions):.

Libya are expected to rely heavily on home-based players from clubs in Tripoli and Benghazi, with Youssouph Dabo naming a 27-man squad for the double-header.

Al Hilal Benghazi forward Ezoo El Mariamy is among the main attacking options, while Hamdou El Houni will be hoping to recover from the injury that forced him off during the first leg after scoring.

Tunisia have also named a 27-man squad built around experienced internationals Ferjani Sassi, Aissa Laidouni, Ali Maaloul and Montassar Talbi, while Moetez Zemzemi and Mohamed Ali Ben Hammouda are among the fresh additions.

Elias Achouri was ruled out through injury before the first leg and has not been included in the squad for the trip to Libya.

Libya possible starting lineup:.

Al-Tihar; Jaddour, Elfadli, Musrati, Salama; Al-Shuraimi, Al-Hbeishi; Eissa, Ellafi, Tajouri; El Maremi.

Tunisia possible starting lineup:.

Dahmen; Ghram, Talbi, Maaloul; Drager, Laidouni, Ben Romdhane, Gharbi; Letaief, Saad; Chaouat.

Tunisia desperately need a victory, but they have scored just three goals in three qualifiers while conceding five, and Libya showed how dangerous they can be on the counter-attack in Sfax, with another positive result likely to leave the hosts in a strong position.

The visitors should be more assertive away from the pressure of their own supporters and possess greater individual quality, but their recent struggles suggest they could again enjoy plenty of possession without creating enough clear-cut opportunities.

#1893. Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Container ships were forced to dock at ports in the United Arab Emirates and other Middle Eastern nations after the Iranian government announced that it would close the Strait of Hormuz in July.Credit: AFP via Getty Images.
  • In a recent development, protesters burnt tyres and blocked roads in Syria over fuel prices.
  • These were just some of the many knock-on effects of the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran that began in February.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Container ships were forced to dock at ports in the United Arab Emirates and other Middle Eastern nations after the Iranian government announced that it would close the Strait of Hormuz in July.Credit: AFP via Getty Images.

In a recent development, protesters burnt tyres and blocked roads in Syria over fuel prices. French fishers blockaded a fuel depot and clashed with police. Government and household budgets were squeezed around the world as interest rates rose and the sales of electric vehicles roughly doubled year-on-year in several countries, including Australia, Brazil and India.

These were just some of the many knock-on effects of the US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran that began in February. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 25% of the world’s oil trade and 20% of exported liquefied natural gas previously passed, caused what the International Energy Agency (IEA) called “the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market”, as fuel prices spiked worldwide.

Industry observers note that the resulting strain has exacerbated the economic pressures already felt from previous shocks, including the Russia–Ukraine war, the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2008 global financial crash, as well as from the continuing effects of climate change. The current global energy-security picture is “really bad on all fronts”, says Dan Marks, an energy-security researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London. “It’s something of a perfect storm.”.

It has been revealed that governments seeking to improve national energy security are taking a variety of approaches — from measures to reduce demand and increase electrification to infrastructure updates and incentive programmes to encourage renewable-energy investment. Researchers, meanwhile, are doing their bit, driving scientific and technological advances that have the potential to deliver a stable and sustainable future energy mix.

Sources indicate that human energy consumption is both growing and changing (see ‘Powering the planet’). Use of global primary energy — naturally occurring energy sources that have not undergone any processing by humans — more than doubled between 1980 and 2025. Over that period, consumption increased from around 85,000 terawatt hours (TWh) annually to 178,000 TWh. That’s approximately 71 times the yearly primary-energy consumption of France.

Sources indicate that electrification — the replacement of technologies that burn fossil fuels with alternatives powered by electricity — is advancing in many countries as various industries look into switching to renewables. Worldwide, electricity demand is predicted to increase by around 40% by 2035, compared with current levels (see ‘The road ahead’). Despite this, many industries are still reliant on fossil fuels. Close to 99% of aviation and more than 90% of shipping relies on fossil fuels, for example. One-quarter of extracted natural gas is used to heat industrial buildings, and around 21% is used for heating and cooking in homes worldwide. Most of the rest (40%) is used to generate electricity. Although the share of primary energy generated by renewables is growing, oil, coal and gas still account for about 80% of energy production.

Industry observers note that the IEA defines energy security as reliable, affordable access to all fuels and energy sources. Marks and others highlight that priorities vary internationally, with reliability often seen as of primary importance in high-income countries and affordability taking precedence in low-income nations. The impacts of global shocks to fuel supplies and prices also vary according to how reliant countries are on imported fossil fuels. “There isn’t one global energy-security picture, but many different context-dependent pictures,” says Severin Borenstein, an energy economist at the University of California, Berkeley.

In a recent development, economies that rely on imported oil products are particularly vulnerable to the current shocks. The World Food Programme, part of the United Nations, estimated in March that the US–Iran war could push an extra 45 million people into acute hunger, taking this year’s total to 363 million, as increasing oil and gas costs push up the prices of fuel, food and other crucial products such as fertilizer. “If, like in a lot of African countries, people are dependent on travelling long distances in vehicles and on other imported oil products, large oil-price increases can be existentially problematic,” indicates Marks. Some high-income nations have also been hit hard. In Japan — which was importing more than 90% of its crude oil from the Middle East before the conflict — household electricity bills have risen to their highest levels in three years, and government borrowing costs have risen to a 30-year high.

According to recent reports, by contrast, nations with domestic fuel supplies have been partially insulated. Although car consumers in the United States have seen big fuel-price increases, the country’s ample supplies of natural gas have shielded the nation from severe economic hardships. “In most developed free-market economies, there isn’t an energy-security concern in the sense of availability,” claims Borenstein. “There are price and macro-economic problems. Some countries, like the United States, are better protected than others.”.

It has been revealed that global oil prices have jumped since the US–Iran war broke out. Brent Crude futures contracts, a global oil-price benchmark, hit US$126 a barrel in April — up from around $70 before the conflict. This has affected consumers and businesses, but not as much as some previous energy crises. During the Yom Kippur War, coordinated action by oil-producing countries caused prices to more than triple between October 1973 and January 1974. And oil prices more than doubled after the 1978–79 Iranian revolution.

Many economists think that the global economy is better placed to avoid the soaring inflation, unemployment and recessions seen in many industrialized nations after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks. The ‘oil intensity’ of the global economy, that is, how much oil is needed to generate a unit of gross domestic product (GDP) in the form of goods and services, has fallen by more than 50% since the 1970s. And the IEA, established after the 1973 oil crisis, also requires its 32 member countries to keep reserves of at least 90 days’ worth of crude oil to guard against supply shocks. “For most of the developed world, it’s a big inconvenience, and, for some, a substantial budget squeeze, but it’s not the complete disruption of the economy seen in the 1970s,” says Borenstein.

According to recent reports, but economic and energy-security challenges are also expected to grow owing to climate change. Droughts are becoming more frequent and severe, resulting in major reductions in hydropower generation in nations such as China, Brazil, the United States, Spain and Zambia. Low water levels in rivers, including the Rhine and Danube in Europe, the Amazon in South America and the Yangtze in China, have caused freight delivery problems. The other effects of climate change include reduced wind-energy generation and increased demand for power to run air-conditioning units.

Industry observers note that governments, policymakers and others who are working to tackle energy-security challenges have various options. Reducing energy demand, especially for oil and gas, by electrifying industrial processes and home heating, for example, helps with these issues, especially in nations that are heavily reliant on imported fossil fuels. Managing demand volatility through improved energy storage and ensuring that power grids can transition towards greater energy generation from renewables are also part of the picture, Marks notes.

Sources indicate that although governments and business leaders have parts to play in energy-demand management, electrification and infrastructure investments, researchers are driving scientific and technical innovations that support energy security. Tapping underground heat to produce geothermal energy, for example, emits only small amounts of greenhouse gases and can be used to generate electricity or to heat buildings. However, at present, geothermal energy produces less than 1% of electricity globally because few locations have the right combination of accessible underground heat, water and permeable rock.

That could change thanks to advances in enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), in which underground fractures are expanded or created in hot areas, and then fluids are pumped down, heated up and transferred back to the surface, usually to drive turbines and generate electricity.

Sources indicate that russia has been experiencing a fuel crisis since mid-June caused by increased Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries. Credit: Contributor/Getty Images News.

There have been small-scale EGS research operations since the 1970s, but drilling times and costs have fallen substantially in the decades since thanks to techniques adapted from the oil and gas industries. These include the fracturing of rock with pressurized fluids, known as fracking, horizontal drilling to increase the exposure of fluid to heat reservoirs and the use of tougher, faster polycrystalline diamond compact drill bits. “It’s hard to overestimate how much of a game changer the upcoming techniques have been,” states Roland Horne, a geothermal-energy engineer at Stanford University in California.

Sources indicate that these innovations are driving investments in large commercial plants. One of the biggest of these is the Cape Station project operated by Fervo Energy near Milford in Utah, which began delivering power in September and plans to build the capacity to generate 500 megawatts (MW) by 2028 — enough electricity to power around 500,000 US homes.

It has been revealed that however, there are obstacles to overcome. A number of EGS projects have been halted owing to earthquakes that geologists linked to increased underground forces generated by the EGS process. A magnitude-5.5 earthquake that injured 90 people was probably triggered by hydraulic fracturing at an EGS plant in Pohang, South Korea, in 2017. Lessons have been learnt from this and other incidents. For example, EGS developers are deploying networks of sensors to better predict seismic risks and using multistage stimulation. This involves the use of pressurised fluids or chemical agents to fracture rock sequentially and more gently at several points rather than at fewer locations.

Horne says that he expects the levelized cost of electricity — the average cost of generating a unit of electricity across a power plant’s lifetime — for EGS to drop to a commercially competitive $80 per megawatt hour (MWh) by 2027. The IEA says that this could drop to $50 by 2035 and that geothermal energy could generate 8% of global electricity supplies by 2050.

Sources indicate that efforts to develop more efficient solar cells could also help countries to improve their energy security by increasing sustainable domestic electricity supplies. In 2025, 9% of the world’s electricity came from solar, up from 3% in 2020. Today’s solar cells are mostly silicon-based and can typically convert light into electricity with efficiencies of around 20–24%.

A worker inspects newly installed solar panels at the Fuendetodos II solar park near Zaragoza, Spain.Credit: Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images.

In a recent development, when sunlight hits a solar, or photovoltaic, cell, electrons inside the semiconductor material that it is made from are knocked loose, creating an electrical imbalance that produces a voltage and generates electricity. Researchers are now developing next-generation solar cells that use metal halide perovskites, a family of crystalline compounds with high light absorption and charge-transport capabilities.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Luis de la Fuente has stated the “best is yet to come” from Spain following their loss to England.
  • England’s 3-2 victory away in Madrid on Sunday evening ended Spain’s run of 43 straight games without defeat, handing the World Cup winners their first loss since March 2024.
  • Under De La Fuente, Spain have won a European Championship, a World Cup and a Nations League title in 2023 - as well as reaching the final of the latter in 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Luis de la Fuente has stated the “best is yet to come” from Spain following their loss to England.

England’s 3-2 victory away in Madrid on Sunday evening ended Spain’s run of 43 straight games without defeat, handing the World Cup winners their first loss since March 2024.

Under De La Fuente, Spain have won a European Championship, a World Cup and a Nations League title in 2023 - as well as reaching the final of the latter in 2025.

However, defeat to England means that Spain will enter the quarter-finals stage of the 2026-27 Nations League as an unseeded runner-up, potentially setting up a showdown with France in March next year.

Reflecting on the game, De La Fuente mentioned: “In the first 30 minutes, they knocked us out of our rhythm and were better than us. After that, we fought back, and I thought we were going to get the draw.

“But I’ll use a phrase that I’ve used before when we were unbeaten: ‘The best is yet to come’.”.

De La Fuente also shared his belief that England approached the game in Madrid as a ‘final’, with Spain not as motivated for the game - which allowed the Three Lions to ‘trample’ over La Roja.

It has been revealed that "The fact that the whole world wants to beat Spain is a great feeling,” he added. “This was a 'final', and in this type of game, you have to be spot on, in great shape, and if not, then an opponent like England, France, Portugal or Italy can trample all over you.”.

The Spanish head coach went on to state that his side’s ambitions of winning the Nations League remained in place, with his side ‘determined’ to make amends.

According to recent reports, he continued: "We'll try to be exactly the same in defeat as we were in victory. Okay, we haven't often tasted defeat, but we stay proud; we stay determined - in March, we're in the quarter-finals, and we'll go to those knockouts with the intention of winning, and winning the tournament.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Joshua Cole | 15 Nov 2026 21:42.
  • Niger will be looking to respond to their heavy defeat in the first meeting when they face Morocco again in Tuesday's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying fixture at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat.
  • The Mena suffered a 5-1 defeat in Casablanca on Friday, leaving them with three points from three Group A matches, while the Atlas Lions maintained their perfect start to the campaign and moved onto nine points after winning all three of their qualifiers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joshua Cole | 15 Nov 2026 21:42.

Niger will be looking to respond to their heavy defeat in the first meeting when they face Morocco again in Tuesday's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying fixture at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat.

The Mena suffered a 5-1 defeat in Casablanca on Friday, leaving them with three points from three Group A matches, while the Atlas Lions maintained their perfect start to the campaign and moved onto nine points after winning all three of their qualifiers.

Niger began their qualifying campaign with a 2-1 victory over Lesotho, but they were unable to build on that result when they travelled to face Gabon, suffering a 2-0 defeat in their second Group A fixture.

They then lost by the same scoreline to Algeria in an international friendly in October, before Friday's 5-1 defeat against Morocco extended their losing run to three matches across all competitions.

Their latest defeat was particularly frustrating because they managed to reduce the deficit to 2-1 before half-time through Mohamed Abdouramane's header, and were handed an opportunity to equalise shortly afterwards when a penalty was awarded for a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.

However, Yassine Bounou saved Ousseini Badamassi's spot kick, and Achraf Hakimi restored Morocco's two-goal advantage with a free kick in first-half stoppage time before the Atlas Lions added two more goals after the break.

The Mena have now conceded nine goals in their last three outings, including a 2-1 friendly defeat to Algeria, while scoring just twice during that period, leaving coach Nabil Neghiz with plenty to address after a difficult start to his tenure.

Morocco have now scored nine goals and conceded just once in their opening three qualifiers, having started the campaign with consecutive 2-0 victories over Gabon and Lesotho before Friday's emphatic win.

The Atlas Lions also drew 1-1 with Mali in a friendly in October, but their competitive form has been considerably more impressive, with the latest result extending their winning run in AFCON qualifying to nine matches.

Morocco have also won their last 16 home matches in major tournament qualifiers, covering both the Africa Cup of Nations and World Cup, marking their longest-ever winning streak on home soil in such fixtures.

With Tuesday's match also taking place in Morocco, with Rabat serving as Niger's adopted home for this fixture, Mohamed Ouahbi's side will remain on familiar territory and look to make further use of that advantage.

Morocco have consequently won the last three encounters between the sides by an aggregate score of 12-2 and boast a perfect record in this fixture, having won all seven meetings across all competitions.

Niger Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

Morocco Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

Morocco form (all competitions):.

Niger named a 25-man squad for the November double-header, with nine players based in the domestic league and the rest drawn from clubs in Europe, Asia and other African countries.

Rahim Alhassane, who plays for Bologna, is expected to remain an important figure in defence, while Oumar Sako, Ali Mohamed, Daniel Sosah and experienced winger Tidjani Amadou Moutari are among the other notable selections.

Morocco are also working with the 26-man squad named by Ouahbi for the two matches, although several established internationals are missing, including Ismael Saibari, Azzedine Ounahi, Ayoub El Kaabi, Soufiane Rahimi, Chadi Riad and Hamza Igamane.

Youssef En-Nesyri returned to the squad and scored after coming off the bench in the first meeting, while Ayoub Oufkir marked his first senior call-up with a late goal, with both forwards now hoping to earn starting places after their contributions in Casablanca.

Niger possible starting lineup:.

Tanja; Camara, Sako, Abdouramane, Alhassane; Oumarou; Moutari, Ali Mohamed, Badamassi, Amoustapha; Sosah.

Morocco possible starting lineup:.

Bounou; Hakimi, Diop, Aguerd, Mazraoui; Bouaddi, Targhalline; Diaz, El Khannouss, Ezzalzouli; Zabiri.

Morocco have already demonstrated the gulf in quality between the sides, scoring five goals in Friday's meeting and extending their winning run in this fixture.

Niger have conceded nine goals in their last three games, and their inability to defend consistently makes it difficult to see them preventing another defeat against the Group A leaders.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have been hit with a fresh injury concern as Patrick Dorgu has withdrawn from international duty with Denmark.

The 22-year-old suffered a hamstring injury during Denmark’s 2-0 win over Wales in September and was out until he made his return in United’s 4-4 draw with Aston Villa last Sunday.

Dorgu had been called up to Denmark’s squad for their Nations League fixtures against Portugal and Norway.

But the versatile left-sider will not feature in either game for Denmark and has returned to United due to his injury.

Speaking on Friday, Denmark’s team doctor, Morten Boesen, said: ‘We have carried out a series of tests on Dorgu, and he has not performed well enough to be ready to play in the two matches.

‘He needs further recovery time after his injury, so we are sending him home for additional rehabilitation.’.

Meanwhile, Mauricio Pochettino was officially confirmed as United’s fresh head coach on Friday following the club’s decision to sack Michael Carrick.

Pochettino will take charge of the United States’ games against Haiti on November 14 and 17 before travelling to Manchester ahead of United’s next Premier League game away to Liverpool on November 22.

During a press conference on Friday, Pochettino was in tears as he was asked why he took the United job having signed a new four-year contract with the United States Soccer Federation in August.

‘I never said I wanted to go back [to the Premier League] but they know there aren’t too many opportunities that happen in your career like Manchester United. When it arrives, it’s difficult to turn down.’.

By Ben Knapton | 15 Nov 2026 21:48, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 22:02.

England inflicted Spain's first defeat in 43 games on the World Cup winners with a sensational 3-2 victory in the Nations League, thus progressing to the quarter-finals as group winners.

Evidently learning their lessons from their gut-wrenching World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, the Three Lions exploded out of the blocks in the Spanish capital, but Luis de la Fuente's backline weathered the early storm.

The world champions soon began to threaten James Trafford's goal too, but England got the reward their endeavours warranted on the stroke of the break, as Harry Kane dispatched a controversial penalty.

Neither the home nor away fans could then comprehend what they witnessed inside the opening 15 minutes of the second half, as Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White incredibly extended England's lead, but the visitors were then forced to strap in for a nail-biting ending.

Barely moments after England's third went in, Elliot Anderson was sent off for a last-man foul and Mikel Oyarzabal dispatched the resulting penalty, before an Anthony Gordon error ended with Nico Williams cutting the arrears further.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England goalkeeper James Trafford has been singled out for praise from both managers after the heroic 3-2 win over Spain.

Thomas Tuchel’s side finished top of their Nations League group above the world champions on goal difference after they avenged September’s 3-2 defeat at Wembley with victory by the same scoreline in Madrid.

England played the last half an hour with 10 men following Elliot Anderson’s red card.

Tuchel handed Jordan Pickford and Trafford two matches each during the last international break and again split their game time, with the Everton stopper playing in Thursday’s 2-1 win over Croatia and Trafford coming into the team against Spain.

The Leeds shot-stopper made a string of crucial saves late in the game as 10-man England held on for a famous win that brought an end to Spain’s 43-match unbeaten run.

Trafford’s double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Aymeric Laporte was particularly eye-catching, and his team-mates immediately mobbed him to praise him for those smart stops in added time.

The performance of the 24-year-old - vying with Pickford for the No1 shirt ahead of Euro 2028 - drew praise not only from Tuchel but also from his opposite number, the Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente.

“We did generate some chances, but England’s goalkeeper produced a fantastic performance and stopped two or three potential goals in the last 10 or 15 minutes,” De la Fuente remarked afterwards.

“I want to say how fantastic England were on the night,” he added.

Trafford’s own head coach was similarly impressed by the Leeds man’s influence on a high-stakes clash at the Metropolitano Stadium.

“The obvious save, where he deserves full credit, is the double save at the very end,” Tuchel said.

“Absolutely brilliant. There was a lot to do in the deep build-up as well, which he did very, very well, with everyone around him.

“Never lose the concentration, never lose the focus, never lose the vision where to find the free men to overcome the press and put the game to the opponent’s half. [Along] with everyone else, he was part of a fantastic team performance.”.

In a recent development, asked whether Trafford had closed the gap to long-time No1 Pickford, Tuchel said: “[He was] very good. That is his job: to close the gap. We want competition in all positions. We need to see Trafford in high-pressure moments.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mauricio Pochettino has been urged to wield the axe and ‘move on’ club captain Bruno Fernandes in one of his first acts as the new Manchester United manager.

Pochettino will take charge of the United States’ two games against Haiti before beginning life as United boss after signing a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick.

And the Argentine will not have much time to work with the squad before his first Premier League match in charge of the Red Devils away to Liverpool on November 22.

Pochettino might be hopeful that the January transfer window might offer him the chance to reshape his squad after a disappointing summer transfer window left several holes in United’s squad.

And former Red Devils assistant manager Rene Meulensteen has suggested that Pochettino consider cashing in on Fernandes after his sluggish start to the season.

‘In terms of Bruno, Bruno has been a fantastic servant for Manchester United over many, many years,’ Meulensteen told talkSPORT.

‘He’s not hit the same levels this year round. I think he’s also been, to some extent, maybe even mentally damaged by all the negativity that has surrounded the club and himself.

‘To be fairly honest, I think he’s been a great servant, but I would not be too sad if he decided to leave the club.

‘I think there’s many more people, more players that I think need to move on, and we need to create a different kind of dynamism in the team.’.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

Fernandes won the PFA Players’ Player of the Year last year after a superb second half of the season under Carrick, but has not hit those same heights so far this campaign.

The 32-year-old is out of contract at the end of the season, with The Athletic reporting that the midfielder recently turned down a second contract offer from the club.

Fernandes can talk to foreign clubs about a potential free transfer from January, but United do have the option to trigger a 12-month extension until the summer of 2028.

The Red Devils are also said to be considering a move for talented Como midfielder Nico Paz if they do decide to part ways with Fernandes in the coming months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 15 Nov 2026 21:57, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 22:05.

Africa Cup of Nations co-hosts Tanzania will be seeking their first win of the qualifiers when they welcome Nigeria to the Amaan Stadium on Tuesday.

While the match carries little significance for the hosts - already assured of a place at next year’s finals - the visitors remain fully focused, as a win would all but secure their own qualification.

Recent findings suggest that no team in AFCON history has recorded more podium finishes (17) than Nigeria, who are regulars at the competition. After wins over Madagascar and Tanzania, either side of a 3-0 defeat to Guinea Bissau, the West Africans are on course to reach the tournament finals once again.

Despite missing several key attacking players, Eric Chelle’s men scored three goals in a competitive match for the first time since January, hinting at attacking depth across the squad, which is crucial given their overreliance on Victor Osimhen at times.

The Super Eagles have topped their AFCON qualifying group in each of the last four campaigns but at the moment trail Guinea Bissau by three points, so they cannot afford further slip-ups if they hope to finish as group winners.

Winless in their last four outings (D2, L2), Tuesday's visitors have been underwhelming away from home lately, so supporters travelling to Zanzibar City will be wary of further disappointment, with September’s heavy defeat in Bissau still fresh in the memory.

Converting just 10% of their chances so far, Nigeria need a much sharper edge in front of goal, especially given their ongoing defensive woes, having now gone six matches without a clean sheet since a 3-0 win over Jamaica in May.

While the result was inconsequential in the grand scheme, Tanzania were largely competitive in the first half of their 3-1 defeat to Nigeria, but a lacklustre second-half display set the stage for a second defeat in three outings.

In a recent development, miguel Angel Gamondi’s men would have hoped the AFCON qualifiers might provide a preview of what to expect on their fifth appearance at the competition next year. However, based on recent results, hopes of a fairytale showing on home soil are rapidly diminishing.

The Taifa Stars have now won just one of their last 16 matches across all competitions - a run that includes two meetings with Nigeria, who are unbeaten in seven previous encounters, winning five.

Tanzania are still awaiting their first competitive home victory since being awarded a 3-0 win over Congo in March 2025. As a result, some sections of the nation's faithful will approach this clash hoping for the best but expecting the worst.

A good start would help settle any nerves, but Tuesday’s hosts have conceded first in five of their last seven outings, and a repeat of that would be catastrophic, to say the least, given their current dry patch.

Ademola Lookman and Victor Osimhen are both ruled out with knee injuries, after Lookman was forced off just before half-time on Friday.

Igoh Ogbu (Achilles) and Samuel Chukwueze (thigh) are also unavailable for the visitors, who continue to monitor the fitness of Frank Onyeka.

Tolu Arokodare came off the bench to score twice last time out and could be rewarded with a start here as he looks to continue his impressive run of form.

Ibrahim Hamad is Tanzania’s most notable absentee due to a knock, following an impressive display at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium.

This should open the door for Charles M’Mombwa to come into the hosts’ starting XI, although Evastus Lukanima could also be considered.

Manula; Mligo, M’Mombwa, Mwamnyeto, Mnoga; Miroshi, Mkami, Msanga, Chilambo; Kachwele, Kibu.

Nigeria possible starting lineup:.

Nwabali; Aina, Bassey, Fredrick, Bewene; Yusuf, Iwobi, Ndidi, Nnadi; Arokodare, Adams.

Despite the Super Eagles being far from full strength, anything less than a win here would be considered an underperformance.

With two leaky defences on display, goals are likely at both ends, but we expect the away side to come out on top when all is said and done.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Premier League referee Graham Scott has named Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta as the toughest person to deal with on the touchline.

Last month, Arteta received his second yellow card of the season during Arsenal’s 2-0 win over Everton but said after the game that he had a dossier of other managers committing similar offences which have gone unpunished.

The Arsenal manager now faces a one-match touchline ban if he receives a third yellow card.

Scott, who refereed in the Premier League for a decade before retiring in 2025, claims Arteta ‘does push all the limits all of the time’ and described the Spaniard as ‘hard work’.

When asked who was the worst manager to deal with on the touchline, Scott told The Athletic: ‘Well, the trite answer is all of them when they’re losing.

‘The honest answer, I’m afraid, I know whatever I say at this point just gets me pelters but it is Arteta. He is the hardest work.

Industry observers note that ‘He really does push all the limits all of the time. I don’t mind that in many ways, he’s trying to get a competitive advantage for his team. That’s fine. That’s part of his job. And of course, he’s entitled to do it, and it’s for us to place them, but he does make your life extremely difficult.

‘He’s out of his box [technical area] all the time. I watched him recently in the game against Everton and every time Everton had the ball anywhere near the touchline on his side, he was like joining in the press, his toes are on the touchline.

Industry observers note that ‘As fourth official, it’s a nightmare, because if you step forward and do anything about it, you’re being pedantic, being petty. He does get away with rather too much. The officials do need to be a bit tighter. And I was one of them who let him do that. I’m not going to deny that. But he was just hard work. Really, really hard work all the time in a way that others tended to be hard work some of the time.

In a recent development, ‘And let’s not pretend the others are all, by comparison, angelic. Some were very controlled. Graham Potter would be an example. Didn’t have anything to do with you, just very, very calm, quiet. But then, of course, he got some stick at times for not showing that he cared enough. So I guess managers can’t win either way.’.

By Lewis Nolan | 15 Nov 2026 23:18.

AC Milan owner Gerry Cardinale is obsessed with the idea of signing Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk, the latest report has revealed.

The Reds' centre-back has so far enjoyed a strong season in England, helping the Merseysiders keep four clean sheets in their first 10 Premier League games.

However, fans are worried about the Dutchman's future given his contract is set to expire at the end of the campaign.

The 35-year-old has hinted that he would like to stay at Anfield, but there has seemingly been little movement regarding an extension.

Italian outlet Gazzetta dello Sport now claim that AC Milan's majority shareholder Cardinale is obsessed with the idea of signing Van Dijk.

Liverpool owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG) have implemented a policy focused on rewarding younger stars at the club, while also moving on experienced players before they decline beyond the point of use.

There have been exceptions to those rules, with Van Dijk and Mohamed Salah both signing deals in 2025 following impressive seasons.

However, Salah struggled considerably in 2025-26 before leaving for free in the summer transfer window, and it would be understandable if the club were reluctant about handing another deal to a player in the twilight of their career.

Van Dijk's performances may be deserving of a contract offer, but FSG are unlikely to be swayed by any sentiment shared by fans, and they will instead make an emotionless judgement call in 2027.

Van Dijk is still one of the most physically imposing defenders in Europe, with the centre-back having won 75% of his duels in the Premier League this season.

Losing his experience would place significant pressure on Jeremy Jacquet next term, and the 21-year-old would benefit from spending more time without being the main man at the back for Andoni Iraola.

Liverpool are also likely to lose Alisson Becker and Joe Gomez for free in the summer, so ensuring there is someone at the club that has been through the peaks and troughs of life at Anfield would be sensible.

This is according to the Telegraph, who claim the Nigeria international will feature prominently on a list of potential left-footed central defensive targets for the new Man United head coach.

Capable of playing at left-back but at the moment deployed by Fulham boss Alvaro Arbeloa at centre-half, Bassey has played every single minute of the Cottagers’ Premier League campaign so far - including the 1-1 draw with Manchester United back in September.

Valued at £23.3million on transfermarkt, Bassey is approaching the final six months of his contract at Craven Cottage,.

However, Fulham do hold an option to extend his stay by another year and Arbeloa revealed that the club are keen on agreeing a upcoming deal.

Everton’s Jarrad Branthwaite, meanwhile, is another left-footed defender in the Premier League that Man United are reportedly tracking, although the Toffees would likely demand a far more expensive transfer fee for the 24-year-old England international.

Man Utd’s defence has come in for heavy criticism in recent weeks, with club legend Gary Neville sharing his belief that the current backline will lead to relegation for the Red Devils.

No senior defender has been signed by Man United since wing-back Patrick Dorgu arrived at Old Trafford from Lecce in January 2025.

The signing of another left-footed defender would raise questions over Lisandro Martinez’s future at Old Trafford.

A World Cup winner with Argentina, Martinez has struggled on the pitch in recent seasons - while creating controversy off the field by calling out the club’s hierarchy over a perceived lack of investment in the transfer market.

Former Southampton, Manchester United and Everton midfielder Schneiderlin played alongside the France international for one season at Nice back in 2021, convinced then of his world class ability.
